title: 3D watermelon fur render comparison
text:
prompt

Build a single self-contained HTML page (no build step) showing an interactive 3D "Fluffy Watermelon" covered in long fur, rendered with WebGL using three.js r147 (UMD build: https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three@0.147.0/build/three.min.js). All UI text in English.

SCENE & LOOK
- Full-screen canvas on a soft watermelon-flesh pink studio background: vertical gradient #ECB3AB → #F7CFC7 (lighter band in the middle) → #E8A9A0, used as the scene background.
- A big oblong watermelon lying on its side along the X axis: half-length 1.38, radius 0.98, blunt barrel-like ends, small dimples at both ends, slightly flattened belly, subtle surface unevenness. Start in a 3/4 view (about -0.32 rad around Y, 0.1 rad tilt), camera FOV 30°, framed to fill ~80% of the height.
- Rind pattern under the fur: light green (#A8D66B) with 16 dark green (#1C4D1C) stripes running stem to blossom, with ragged finger-like edges (sine meander + value noise), plus a pale cream "field spot" on the underside. Each hair takes the colour of its own root, so the stripes stay crisp through the fur.
- A short, dried, ribbed stem stub at one end with a slightly domed pale cut cap, and a thin curly helical tendril springing from beside it.
- One directional light from upper-left-front, wrap diffuse, Kajiya-Kay anisotropic highlight along the hair tangent, darker roots (occlusion by hair height), slight per-hair brightness variation.

FUR (most important: it must look crisp, never blurry)
- Fur length 0.2 units. Hairs grow out along the normal, then bend: combed from the stem end toward the blossom end and draped down the flanks (no whorls at the ends), plus slight gravity.
- Undercoat: shell texturing with ~64 instanced shells of the body mesh that reach only 50% of the fur length. Procedural hair cells in UV space (density scaled so one cell is ~3.4 device pixels at the default view), two hair populations (long + fine underfur), hairs gathering into locks toward their tips, analytic anti-aliased coverage, alpha blending, shells write depth. Fade shells out where the surface is seen edge-on and discard faint fragments, so no dotted rim appears at the outline.
- Guard hairs: ~90,000 individual tapered, camera-facing ribbon strands (instanced, 7 segments each) that follow exactly the same bend function, with a minimum width of ~0.75 px so they stay sharp. Draw them twice: once before the shells and once after (depth-tested), so faint edge fur never hides them and they always lie crisply on top.
- Always render at the device's full pixel ratio (capped at 2) and NEVER lower it for performance. If frames are slow, reduce the shell count first (down to 32), then the guard-hair count.

INTERACTION
- Drag to rotate freely (trackball style) with inertia after a flick. The fur lags behind the rotation through a damped spring and flops back. Gentle idle breeze in the fur; after 3 s without input, a slow auto-turn.
- Mouse wheel / pinch to zoom (smooth dolly). Double-click or "0" resets with an eased animation. Arrow keys rotate.
- Custom cursor: the native grab hand plus a thin dark 46 px ring that follows the pointer and shrinks while dragging. Hovering gently parts the fur under the cursor, as if stroking it.
- Respect prefers-reduced-motion (no idle spin, no breeze).

UI & ROBUSTNESS
- Bottom-left caption: "Fluffy Watermelon" and a hint "Drag to rotate · Scroll to zoom · Double-click to reset" (on touch devices: "Drag to rotate · Pinch to zoom") that fades after the first interaction. Font: Onest from Google Fonts with system fallbacks.
- Guard against a zero-sized container at load: clamp width/height to at least 1 and, every frame, recover from any non-finite camera distance or rotation state.
- Show a small on-page note if the WebGL context is lost or a shader fails to compile, and a fallback message if WebGL is unavailable.

title: Electric motor 3D animation comparison
text:
For sure my friend:

Create a high-end cinematic and educational 3D animation in Three.js explaining how a Tesla-style electric motor works.

The animation must have an EXACT FIXED DURATION OF 40 SECONDS.

Do not make the animation shorter or longer than 40 seconds.

Final output:
Exact duration: 40.0 seconds
Resolution: 1920x1080
Aspect ratio: 16:9
Frame rate: 30 FPS
Total frames: 1200
High-quality anti-aliasing
High-resolution textures
Smooth deterministic animation
Extremely realistic visual quality

The overall visual quality should resemble a premium automotive engineering visualization or a high-end technical product commercial.

Build a detailed electric motor assembly inspired by the permanent-magnet AC motors used in modern Tesla vehicles. Do not use Tesla logos or branding.

FIXED TIMELINE

0–5 seconds — Hero introduction
Show the fully assembled electric motor suspended in a dark premium studio environment.

Use:
cinematic lighting
realistic brushed aluminum
copper
steel
magnets
insulation
bearings
realistic reflections
ambient occlusion
realistic shadows
subtle depth of field

Use a slow cinematic orbit around the motor.

During the final part of this section, make the outer housing partially transparent to reveal the internal structure.

5–11 seconds — Internal components
Move the camera closer and reveal the internal motor components.

Clearly show:
stator
copper windings
rotor
permanent magnets
motor shaft
bearings
housing
cooling channels
electrical connections

Highlight the important components one at a time.

Use floating labels with short technical names.

Keep non-highlighted components slightly darker or semi-transparent.

11–19 seconds — Exploded view
Create a dramatic and highly detailed exploded-view animation.

Separate the motor into many individual mechanical components along the motor axis.

Include:
outer housing
front cover
rear cover
bearings
shaft
rotor core
rotor magnets
stator core
copper windings
cooling components
seals
electrical connectors
fasteners

Keep every component perfectly aligned.

The viewer must clearly understand where every piece belongs.

Move the camera slightly through the exploded assembly while highlighting the major components.

Near the end of this section, smoothly begin reassembling the motor.

19–28 seconds — Electromagnetic operation
Finish reassembling the motor.

Explain how electricity creates rotation.

Visualize three-phase AC current flowing through the stator windings.

Use animated electrical pulses inside the copper coils.

Visualize the rotating magnetic field around the stator using elegant semi-transparent magnetic field lines, arrows, or vector effects.

Show how the rotating magnetic field interacts with the permanent magnets inside the rotor.

Clearly visualize magnetic attraction and repulsion.

The rotor should begin rotating slowly and gradually accelerate.

Display these short explanations:

"Three-phase current creates a rotating magnetic field."

"The magnetic field interacts with the rotor."

"This interaction generates torque."

28–34 seconds — Technical close-up and power flow
Show a close-up cross-section of the stator and rotor.

Visualize:
magnetic north and south poles
rotating stator magnetic field
rotor magnetic field
electric current direction
torque direction
rotor rotation direction

Optionally show three small animated sine waves representing phases A, B, and C, separated by 120 degrees.

Then visualize the complete energy conversion process:

Electrical energy
→ stator current
→ rotating magnetic field
→ electromagnetic torque
→ rotor rotation
→ mechanical output through the shaft.
Use clean animated arrows to show the energy flow.
34–38 seconds — High-speed operation
Show the motor operating at high RPM.
The rotor should spin smoothly while the stator remains stationary.
Add subtle motion blur.

Show cooling flow through the housing using translucent fluid paths.

Visualize heat being removed from the stator and copper windings.
38–40 seconds — Final hero shot

Transition back to the fully assembled motor.

Show a slow cinematic rotation.

Briefly use a transparent cutaway so the spinning rotor can still be seen inside.

Finish with the text:

"Electrical energy → Electromagnetic torque → Mechanical rotation"
The animation must end exactly at 40.0 seconds.

VISUAL QUALITY

The animation should be:

photorealistic

cinematic

technically believable

futuristic

premium
educational
clean and uncluttered
Avoid cartoon styling.
Use realistic:
machining details
bolts
screws

copper winding geometry

segmented magnets
bearing geometry
cooling channels
metallic surfaces
manufacturing details
Use physically based materials with:
metallic properties
roughness variation
normal maps
realistic reflections

subtle surface imperfections
CAMERA
Use only smooth cinematic camera movement:
slow orbit shots
macro close-ups
controlled dolly-ins

exploded-view fly-throughs

cross-section shots

internal motor views
Avoid:
shaky camera movement
sudden cuts
excessive zooming
unrealistic camera acceleration

ANIMATION REQUIREMENTS
All transitions must be smooth and deliberate.
The exploded-view sequence should be one of the main visual highlights.
All mechanical components must separate and reassemble with precise motion.
Electrical currents, magnetic fields, torque indicators, and rotor rotation must remain synchronized.

The entire animation must use the same fixed 40-second timeline on every execution so the prompt can be used as a repeatable benchmark between different AI coding and 3D generation systems.

title: Orbit landing page with and without TasteSkill
text:
THE PROMPT: (With image attached!)

Build a complete, production-quality landing page for Orbit, a project management platform for small product teams.
Orbit combines projects, tasks, discussions, documents, and weekly progress updates in one workspace. Its core purpose is to let teams understand what is happening without constantly asking for updates or scheduling status meetings.
Technical requirements
Build the website using Next.js, React, and TypeScript.
Use TSX components and a proper Next.js project structure. Do not create a plain HTML/CSS website.
The implementation should be clean, componentized, responsive, and production-quality. Use modern CSS or Tailwind CSS for styling where appropriate.
Do not merely describe the implementation. Build the complete working page.
Visual reference
Use the provided reference image as the primary art-direction reference.
Match its overall visual character very closely: typography treatment, density, spacing philosophy, texture, contrast, borders, surface treatment, visual weight, image treatment, and general design atmosphere.
However, do not copy the reference website or recreate its content.
Do not copy its:
branding
text or copy
logos
illustrations
exact layout
individual components
imagery
proprietary visual assets
Instead, understand the design language behind the reference and reinterpret it for Orbit.
For example, if the reference uses grain, paper texture, sharp borders, muted surfaces, unusual typography, dense layouts, editorial spacing, or a particular treatment of imagery, use those qualities as inspiration while creating an original design.
The finished page should clearly belong to the same visual world as the reference while still being an original website.
Page
The hero should immediately explain Orbit and show a convincing view of the actual product.
Throughout the page, create realistic Orbit UI showing projects, tasks, assignees, discussions, documents, statuses, deadlines, and weekly updates.
Include the sections that genuinely help sell the product, such as:
Hero
Product demonstration

Core workflow
Features
Team use cases
Integrations
Customer proof
Pricing
FAQ
Final CTA
You may change, combine, reorder, or remove sections when doing so produces a stronger page.
Design quality
Avoid the stereotypical AI-generated SaaS aesthetic.
No purple gradient hero.
No glowing blobs.
No glassmorphism.
No giant collection of rounded cards.
No endless 3-column feature grids.
No random floating icons.
No meaningless charts.
No fake AI functionality.
No excessive pills.
No generic startup illustrations.
No repetitive centered sections.
Do not make every element a card or container.
Use typography, composition, whitespace, texture, product UI, imagery, and hierarchy to create visual interest.
The product UI itself should be detailed and believable. Keep names, projects, dates, statuses, and other information consistent across different product previews.
Copy should be concise and specific. Avoid phrases such as “supercharge your workflow,” “unlock your potential,” and other generic SaaS language.
Add subtle, intentional interactions and motion where they improve the experience. Avoid animation for animation's sake.
Make the page excellent on desktop and mobile.
The final result should feel designed, not generated.
Take the reference image seriously. Analyze its design system first, then translate that design language into an original Orbit website.
Do not ask me to choose colors, fonts, layouts, libraries, or design direction. Make those decisions yourself and implement the complete site.

title: Interactive 3D jelly orange in browser
text:
PROMPT

Build "Whole Orange Jelly" — a single self-contained HTML file (inline JS/CSS, no libraries): a real-time WebGPU soft-body whole orange made of jelly. The user can grab and stretch it, and cut it with a knife into wheels, wedges and small pieces. Every piece is its own wobbling body.

Shape and pieces
- The orange is a signed distance field: a gently oblate ellipsoid (polar half-length 1.27 along x, equatorial radius 1.36) lying on its side, with a softly flattened seat on the floor.
- Every piece is that field clipped by the half-spaces n·X ≤ c of the cuts that made it, with the fresh edges rounded (smooth max, k ≈ 0.085). All pieces share the orange's original rest frame, so the anatomy stays where it grew.
- Per piece:
  - a surface-nets render skin (0.042 grid) projected onto the field;
  - a hex lattice for the simulation in the piece's own principal frame, with boundary nodes snapped to the surface;
  - barycentric embedding of render vertices into the lattice tets.
- Up to 30 pieces; slivers are rejected.

Anatomy (all in rest space, so every cut shows it where it really is)
- Zest (0.07 deep) with oil-gland pores, a mottled tone, a green stem button at one end and a small navel at the other.
- White pith (to 0.19 deep).
- 11 segments around the stem axis, with thin milky membrane walls (slightly jittered, bowed and wandering along the axis) and a pithy core along the axis.
- Juice vesicles: teardrop sacs fanning out from the core within each segment.
- 16 pale citrus pips near the core, pointed end inward; a few small bubbles in the flesh.
- A pip that a cut goes through is kept by the side holding its centre and eased just under the new face.

Physics (XPBD)
- Per piece: hex cells with co-rotational shape matching plus volume constraints on their five tets.
- Zest and pith firmer than the flesh.
- Edge and deformation damping; floor contact with Coulomb friction and a little rolling resistance.
- Piece–piece contact against each other's exact rest shape in a best-fit frame.
- Sleeping pieces that wake on touch; fixed 60 Hz step with small substeps.

Knife
- A nakiri-style knife: draw a stroke across the orange.
- The stroke, read on the top of what it crosses, fixes a vertical blade plane, carried into each crossed piece's rest frame by its best-fit rotation and added as a half-space.
- The new pieces are built incrementally while the knife lines up, presses a groove and cuts straight down. They take over the position and speed of the jelly they came from, and the blade wedges the faces apart.

Rendering (WebGPU / WGSL)
- Procedural photo studio. Soft PCSS key shadow tinted by the jelly, plus contact AO from a height map.
- Back-face thickness; refraction of the scene, with each tap dimmed by its own path length.
- A volumetric march through the jelly in rest space, using a per-vertex inverse deformation gradient:
  - zest, pith, membranes/core and flesh each absorb with their own colour (Beer–Lambert);
  - scattering is grey (only absorption is coloured), so light scattered out of orange flesh stays orange.
- The white pith, the membrane star and the core read crisply on cut faces.
- Back-lit glow at thin edges, Fresnel studio reflections, GGX highlights, sugar-crystal glints.
- Post: Khronos PBR Neutral tone mapping, sRGB, dither.

UI (editorial "Material Studies / No. 032", English)
- Italic serif title "Whole / Orange." with the caption "Eleven segments, set in jelly. Zest, pith and juice. Cut it as small as you like."
- Status pill "WEBGPU · LIVE".
- Tools: Hand / Knife. Varieties: Navel, Blood, Cara Cara.
- Firmness and Internal damping sliders; Give it a nudge, Reset, Pause; ¼ speed and Show mesh.
- Readouts: Mass (g, 1 unit ≈ 3 cm at 1.3 g/cm³), Volume (% of rest), Kinetic (mJ), Pieces.
- A collapsible "Inside the experiment" with notes on the method.
- Fallback without WebGPU. Stacked mobile layout with no horizontal scroll.

title: Jelly pumpkin render comparison
text:
If you don't believe me, try this prompt

Build a single self-contained HTML file: a simple 3D "Jelly Pumpkin" demo using three.js from a CDN. Keep the code short and basic.

SCENE
- One orange pumpkin in the centre made from a low-poly sphere (about 24x16 segments) with 8 shallow ribs, flat shading.

- Jack-o'-lantern face made of flat black 2D shapes (two triangle eyes, triangle nose, zigzag mouth) placed just in front of the pumpkin surface. No glow from inside.
- Simple green cylinder stem on top.
- Three small low-poly pumpkins (purple, green, orange) and four small flattened spheres as candy around it.
- White background, ambient light plus one directional light, basic hard shadows on the floor.

INTERACTION
- Click the pumpkin: it squashes slightly (scale Y down, X/Z up) and springs back quickly with no extra wobble.
- Drag the stem: draw a straight thin green cylinder from the stem to the cursor. Dragging upward lifts the whole pumpkin rigidly; release and it falls, with one small bounce.
- "Carve Face" button: instantly swap to a second face (two black circle eyes, round mouth).
- "Glow" slider: changes the emissive intensity of the pumpkin a little.
- "Add Candy" button: drops 16 small spheres from above; they fall, bounce once on the floor and stop. No collision with the pumpkin.

UI

- Top right white box with border: colour buttons (Orange, Purple, Green), Glow range input, "Carve Face" and "Add Candy" buttons with default browser styling.

title: Landing page 3D scroll
text:
<inputs>
Ask me for: my landing page link, my brand name and logo mark, a two-part closing line (a statement, then a short italic tail), and a 15 second track (optional).
</inputs>

<direction>
A 14.5 second 3D fly-over of my landing page, 1440x1152 at 60fps. The page lies flat on a bright studio floor (#f9fbfb in the middle, #f2f3f6 in the corners) with a soft wide shadow around it and 24px rounded corners. One continuous camera, never a cut: it starts low over the hero and glides backwards down the page at one steady speed while looking up it, rises straight overhead to show the whole page as one strip, dives into the hero and lands it as a card under a two-line title. Focus is razor thin in front of the subject and almost none behind it, so everything near the lens melts. Cards float a little above the page with soft shadows; photos, chips and the testimonial lift off and stand up toward the lens as the camera passes them. Four small tiles of my logo lift off beside the hero button and stay with the film until the end card. The title is Geist 500, the italic tail Instrument Serif.
Banned: cuts, crossfades, stops or surges in the glide, the camera turning or swinging sideways, zooming in and back out, glows, any text laid over the page before the end card.
</direction>

<structure>
14.5 seconds: flight 0-8.2s, rise 7.75-9.25s, overhead 9.25-9.47s, dive 9.47-9.97s, title card 9.97-14.5s.
The camera 56° off straight-down and 1360px from the point it looks at, centred on the top half of the hero, the phone or product mockup sharp, four 32px logo tiles beside the button → 0-0.6: the glide eases in from rest → 0.1-1.35: the tiles lift, grow to 140-200px and hang just outside the page's top corners while the hero's chips rise to 60-80px and stand up 30° → 1.25-1.6: the glide doubles to cruising speed as the hero falls behind → 1.6: the second section's title passes the centre of the frame, its photos blurred near the lens → 1.35-2.7: that section's main photos lift to 100-130px and stand up 46°, two of its chips fly up to about 200px, stand up 54° and pass the left and right edges at 2.5 → 1.2-2.4: the tiles trail the camera 300px down the page, then drift out of the top → 3.0-7.3: every following section passes through at the same steady speed, each one sharp as it crosses the middle of the frame and soft below it; a logo tile drifts past the left edge close and blurred at 5.4 → 5.45-6.3: the testimonial card rises from 22 to 112px, stands up 30° and shows a 34px white edge → 7.3-8.2: the glide eases off as the footer arrives, the footer title sharp at 8.0 → 7.75-9.25: the rise, zooming out at an even rate while the tilt flattens (8.15-8.95) and the page's bottom edge settles 42px above the frame bottom → 9.25-9.47: the whole page as one centred strip, creeping 3.5% closer → 9.47-9.97: the dive, the page's top edge pinned to the frame top while it grows, everything below the hero fading out, then the top drops to y 283 so the hero lands as a 1018px wide card with 38px corners and a soft shadow; two logo tiles sit on its top corners, one crisp at the right edge, two huge soft blurs drift in at the bottom corners → 10.02: a white badge pill (logo + brand, 21px) fades in at y 44 → 10.12: line 1 at 74px, one word every 0.06s → 10.36: the italic tail at 82px in grey #8b8b92, one word every 0.05s, each word rising 16px out of a 12px blur in 0.34s → 10.6-14.5: hold, the card creeping 2% closer, the tiles drifting a few px.
</structure>

<build>
1. Open my link in headless Chromium (Playwright) at 1440px wide, device scale 2, and scroll to the bottom once so lazy images and scroll animations finish. Mark the pieces that lift (cards, phone or product mockups, chips, feature photos, the testimonial, the hero button) with data-layer. Screenshot the full page with them hidden, then each piece alone on a transparent background with 28px padding, and save every piece's page position to a JSON.
2. One WebGL2 film page, 1440x1152, every frame computed from time inside seek(t): no timers, no CSS transitions. The page is a textured quad on the floor and each piece its own quad at its height, drawn lowest first with no depth buffer. Use mipmaps and 16x anisotropic filtering or the far text shimmers.
3. Drive the camera from one speed curve, never from a position key every half second. Focal length 1880px, 56° tilt, distance easing out from 1360 to 1700px and never back in, no turning. Speed down the page as a share of cruise (cruise is about 770 page px/s): 0 at 0s, 0.5 by 0.6s, held at 0.5 to 1.25s, 1.0 by 1.6s, held between 0.94 and 1.1 to 7.3s, then easing to 0.12 by 8.3s. Integrate it into the page position.
4. Depth of field per pixel: blur radius = 75 x (focus - depth) / depth in front of the focus and 6 x (depth - focus) / depth behind it, capped at 120px, 40 taps on a golden-angle disc, each tap read from a mip level matched to the blur. Keep the focus on whatever crosses the middle of the frame.
5. A lifted piece stands up by turning about its own middle, top edge rising toward the lens. Each casts a shadow on whatever is under it: the same picture in flat #1a2133, offset (0.10z, 4 + 0.36z), blurred 7 + 0.5z, 26% opacity.
6. Rise: zoom out in log scale with a smooth trapezoid speed (speeding up 7.75-8.35s, even 8.35-8.95s, slowing to a stop at 9.25s) and hand the glide over to a camera that holds the page's bottom edge at that 42px line from 8.3 to 8.65s. Dive: log scale on a quadratic ease in-out, then solve the look-at point from the pinned edge. A rounded-rect mask morphs from the full page to the hero, 24px to 38px corners.
7. Render with Playwright on the real GPU (--use-angle=d3d11 --enable-gpu --ignore-gpu-blocklist): 60fps, 16 subframes across 0.7 of a frame for motion blur, H.264 MP4. The track's hit goes on 9.97s, whooshes on 8.66 and 9.80.
</build>

<gotchas>
If you can't run code on my computer, tell me straight away that you can only make a live preview here and that the MP4 needs Claude Code. Phones or cards that fade out with transparency show whatever is behind them, so fade them into the haze colour first and only cut to transparent at the very end. Keep most lifts tiny (20-40px) and lock the page before timing anything, because any change in a section's height shifts everything after it. Before the final render, measure a quick 30fps preview with optical flow: the speed down the page must never dip and the zoom must never turn into a zoom-in during the flight.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for the inputs, capture my page, then show me stills at 0, 1.6, 2.5, 5, 6.5, 9.3 and 11 seconds before you render.
</start>

title: 3D canal and windmill scene model comparison
text:
PROMPT

Build "Lock Jelly." — a single self-contained HTML file (WebGPU + WGSL, no libraries, no network, works from file://), part of a "Material Studies" series of jelly dioramas. If WebGPU is missing or the adapter fails, show a clean fallback card instead of the scene.

CONCEPT
A square block of clear coloured jelly (about 5.2 × 5.2 units, ~2 units high) holding a little English canal scene. The canal runs along the FRONT edge of the block, so the block's front face cuts the water lengthways: you see the lock chamber in cross-section, the water inside it rising and falling between the gates, fish swimming, the boat's hull below the waterline. All cut faces show candy-coloured soil strata; under the pounds a blue-grey puddle-clay lining, under the chamber a brick invert on a concrete bed, under the fields brown earth and turf.

LAYOUT (left to right along the front)
- Upper pound on the left at the higher level, opening into a round winding hole (a bay for turning boats); near the lock it narrows between brick wing walls.
- The lock chamber in the middle: brick walls with dressed-stone quoins and coping, a slimy band between the two water levels and weed below, an iron ladder, a gauge board, a stone cill under the top gate, recesses that the open gates fold into.
- Below the bottom gate a short walled tail, then the lower pound bends away from the front face, runs under a humpback brick bridge into a basin with a willow-covered island, lily pads in its corners and a sunken bicycle on the bed.
- The ground steps down from an upper terrace to a lower one along a grassy bank.
- Behind the lock: stone setts around the chamber, bollards, a gravel towpath, a lane, the keeper's whitewashed cottage with a slate roof, green door, picket-fence garden full of flowers and washing flapping on a line, a gas lamp, a bench, a white windmill with turning lattice sails, oaks, willows, poplars, a hedge, sheep, reeds on the soft banks.

WATER
- Linear shallow-water waves on a staggered grid (~168²) with a little surface tension, so short ripples are springy like jelly; damping and firmness are adjustable.
- Three separate bodies of water — upper pound, chamber, lower pound — each with its own rest level. Faces between bodies stay shut unless the gate between them is open and the levels are equal. The chamber's level is moved bodily when paddles are drawn (Torricelli-style flow), with boils, white water and a dimple at the intake.
- Rendering: refraction of the scene behind, flavour-coloured absorption, sun caustics on the bed, soft light shafts, foam (wakes, paddle churn), a meniscus line on the cut faces. Split the surface mesh along the gate lines so the step in level at a shut gate is a clean wall hidden by the gate leaf, not a ramp.
- The block itself can be tipped by dragging its side; the jelly shears and wobbles, the water sloshes, and it settles back.

THE LOCK AND THE KEEPER
- Two single-leaf timber gates (planks, rails, diagonal brace, iron straps, a walkway with a handrail), each with a white balance beam with black bands. Ground-paddle pedestals with toothed racks that rise when wound.
- An articulated lock keeper (flat cap, navy jumper, cords, windlass in hand; torso, arms, thighs and shins as separate parts). He walks with a proper gait, plans his route around the bench, pedestals, bollards and any beam lying across his way (going round the beam's end), leans his back on a beam and walks it round backwards to swing a gate, winds the windlass with his arm circling the spindle, and sits on his bench between jobs. He sets off for the gate as the boat comes in.
- The cycle: the boat lies in the full chamber → keeper shuts the top gate → winds up the bottom paddles → the chamber empties into the tail with white water → winds them down → opens the bottom gate → the boat leaves, runs the tail, swings round the bend, ducks under the bridge, goes round the island and comes back into the chamber bow first → shut bottom gate → round to the top paddles → chamber fills with boils → open the top gate → the boat goes up the pound, turns in the winding hole and comes back. Repeat forever. A gate may only open when the levels match.

BOATS
- A traditional narrowboat "Wobble": black lofted hull, a green cabin with red lining-out, brass portholes, a cratch board and cover at the bow, a chimney with brass bands (puffing smoke), a painted Buckby can, plank and pole on the roof, rope fenders, a headlamp, a brass swan-neck tiller and a steerer in a red jumper. It follows smooth filleted routes (check the stern never swings out through the block's face), slows near the gates, heaves, pitches and rolls on the local surface, and hands its displaced volume back to the water so it makes bow waves and wakes.
- Three moored narrowboats in the basin in different liveries with flowerpots on the roofs and one ginger cat, tied to bank pins with stretchy mooring lines.

LIFE
- Roach, perch and bream as boids that stay in their own body of water (they can only move between pound and chamber while a gate is open), under the surface and hulls, off the bed, scattering from the boat and splashes.
- Mallards (drakes, ducks) and a duck with four ducklings that follow exactly along her trail; a pair of mute swans in the basin. They paddle the surface, ride the chamber down and up, upend now and then, get out of the boat's way and come for bread.
- A grey heron that wades in the shallows or stands on a moored boat's roof, stabs at fish (sometimes catching one), and flaps off somewhere quieter when the boat passes or someone toots.
- Chimney smoke from the boat and the cottage.

UI (editorial, like a print magazine)
- Top-left: small caps eyebrow "MATERIAL STUDIES", a huge italic serif title "Lock / Jelly.", a short subtitle. Top-right: a status pill "WebGPU · Live / Paused / Unavailable".
- Right: a frosted-glass control panel (a bottom sheet on mobile) with: buttons Hurry (speeds the keeper, paddles and boat), Toot (horn; also Space), Throw bread, Rubber duck (drops a yellow rubber duck that floats upright, can be picked up and thrown, rides the lock, is stopped by gates and shoved by boats); a liveliness meter; tallies Trips · Lockfuls · Fed; a status line "Wobble — Emptying the lock 62%" telling the story step by step; three flavours Greengage, Elderflower, Blackcurrant (change the water colour/absorption and strata); sliders Firmness, Wave damping, Paddle speed; Reset, Pause, Sound on/off, View.
- Bottom-left: "How to play — Throw bread. Toot the horn. Hurry the keeper." with a small line of instructions.
- Interaction: drag across the water to make waves, drag the block's side to tip it, pick up and throw rubber ducks, drag empty space to orbit, scroll/pinch to zoom; touch works.
- Soft studio lighting on a warm paper backdrop with the block's tinted, caustic-flecked shadow; WebAudio sounds: the boat's horn, the gate thudding shut, a creak, the windlass ratchet, and the rush of water that swells with the flow.

QUALITY
Keep it smooth (fixed-step physics, cheap per frame), no console errors, no page scroll, works at phone width. Test it headlessly: a full round trip happens, levels go exactly from upper to lower and back, no gate opens across a step, the keeper never walks into the water or through obstacles, the boat never touches a gate leaf, and every button works.

title: Jelly lego bricks model comparison
text:
PROMPT

Build a single self-contained HTML file: an interactive 3D toy called "Jelly Bricks" - translucent gummy candy bricks you can grab, stretch, stack into a tower and knock over. Use three.js (import from a CDN) and any lightweight physics library you like. Everything must run by opening the file in a browser.

LOOK
- Bricks are classic stud-on-top building bricks (2x1, 2x2, 3x2, 4x2) in red, orange, yellow, green and blue. No brand names or logos anywhere.
- Material must read as real gummy candy: glossy, translucent, light passing through, deeper colour where the brick is thicker, soft rounded edges and rounded studs. Use MeshPhysicalMaterial with transmission, thickness, attenuation colour, clearcoat, and an environment map for reflections.
- Soft shadows plus a faint coloured glow on the floor under each brick, tinted by its colour.
- Clean white background, slight slow camera drift so the scene feels alive.

JELLY BEHAVIOUR (most important)
- Grab a brick and it stretches toward the cursor before it lifts off, like pulling taffy. Release it and the stretch snaps back with a decaying wobble.
- A brick lagging behind the cursor tilts slightly in the direction it's moving.
- Every landing squashes the brick flat, then it springs back up with a few wobbles (spring-damper squash and shear, done in the vertex shader).
- Dropping a brick on the stack snaps it in place, and the whole tower sways like pudding: each brick's wobble shifts the bricks above it, so the top moves the most.
- Pulling a brick out of the middle of the tower collapses it: the bricks above tumble, bounce off the floor and each other, and scatter a little - lively, not explosive.

UI (minimal editorial style)
- Top left: small caps label "Nº 09 / SOFT GOODS", big serif italic title "Jelly / Bricks." with "Bricks." in red, and a one-line subtitle.
- Floating panel on the right: flavor colour swatches, a "Wobble" slider that controls jelly softness, live "Stack height" and "Bricks" counters, and a black "Pour more bricks" button that drops a handful of new bricks from above with random spin.
- Bottom left hint: "Grab to lift · Drop to snap · Space to wobble". Space shakes the tower.
- Custom round cursor that shrinks while holding a brick.

Start with one 4x2 brick in the centre as the tower base and about 9 bricks scattered around it. Keep it at 60fps on a laptop.

title: Arctic jelly iceberg diorama comparison
text:
PROMPT 

Build "Iceberg Jelly" — the next piece in my "Material Studies" series of jelly dioramas: a single self-contained HTML file using WebGPU (WGSL), no external libraries, English UI.

THE SCENE
A square block of jelly (5.2 × 5.2 units) standing on a pale, cool-grey paper studio backdrop with a soft floor shadow. Inside it, a polar bay:
- At the back left, a glacier flows down a valley between jagged mountains and ends in an ice cliff standing in deep water. The cliff has vertical runnels and blue bands. The glacier surface has chevron crevasses along its margins, transverse crevasses and seracs near the front, and grey lateral moraines. Its tongue is flanked by moraine banks, so only its front stands in the water.
- Mountains: a peaky left range and a spur on the right of the glacier, with a snowy ridge along the back. Dark volcanic rock with orange lichen, and snow in ragged patches on flatter and higher ground (not everywhere).
- At the back right, a low peninsula with an Adélie penguin rookery: an organic, irregular patch of round pebbles stained pink with krill, with pebble-ring nests. Behind it, a small research station (red and yellow huts on stilts, fuel drums, a radio mast with guy wires, a flag, a turning anemometer, a snowmobile) and a timber quay.
- A ragged skerry of two low rocks off to the front right, where Weddell seals haul out.
- The sea floor is grey gravel with shells, sponges, sea stars and swaying anemones, visible through the clear jelly front face.
- The cut faces of the block show candy-coloured strata, dark basalt columns under the land, and layered blue glacier ice with a dirty basal layer under the glacier.

PHYSICS
- Shallow-water simulation on a ~168² grid for the bay: waves, wakes, foam, refraction, caustics on the floor, light shafts, and absorption that depends on the flavour.
- Every piece of ice is a rigid body: tabular, dome, pinnacle and wedge bergs, growlers, pancake floes, and glacier slabs. Each is a star-shaped faceted mesh (superellipsoid plus lobes plus two octaves of noise), a lattice of mass points for buoyancy and drag, and contact spheres for ground, walls, each other and the ship. Settle stable poses at load so nothing capsizes at the start.
- Calving: three slabs stand along the cliff. About once a minute (or on demand) one breaks off with a crack, a puff of ice dust, a splash, spray and a wave, then capsizes until it finds a stable way up. The glacier slowly pushes a new slab out. Old slabs melt away.
- The displaced water is handed back to the waves without feedback: wakes only when a piece moves fast, splashes when it plunges in. Slow drift makes no waves.
- The jelly block itself wobbles, shears and squashes, and can be tipped by dragging its side.

LIFE
- An icebreaker, "Polaris" (red hull with a spoon bow, white superstructure, yellow funnel with smoke, a turning radar, a helideck), lies at the quay. Now and then (or on demand) she casts off, shoulders round the bay through the pack, pushing floes and bergs aside, and comes back alongside. A status line shows Alongside / Casting off / Under way / Breaking ice / Coming alongside, with a countdown or progress.
- 22 Adélie penguins: blue-black backs, white shirt fronts, white eye rings, pink feet. They stand on nests and look about, have the odd ecstatic display, waddle or toboggan to the beach, dive in, "fly" underwater with beating flippers, porpoise, leap out onto floes and bergs, and slide off when a floe tips. They chase silverfish and thrown fish.
- 3 Weddell seals (spotted grey) haul out on the skerry and floes, lift their heads, and go for swims.
- An orca (proper eye patch and grey saddle) patrols deep water, surfaces to blow and dives. Penguins keep clear of it.
- Schools of silverfish; gentle snowfall.

UI (same layout as the rest of the series)
Masthead "Material Studies / Iceberg Jelly." with a one-line description. A "WebGPU · Live" status pill. A glass control panel on the right that turns into a bottom sheet on mobile:
- Buttons: Calve (shows "Wait…" while no slab is ready), Cast off / Full ahead, Throw fish, Horn (Space).
- A water-energy meter; tallies for Calved, Capsized, Fed; the ship status line.
- Flavours: Glacier mint, Blue raspberry, Blackberry. Each changes the water's absorption, its tint and the strata.
- Sliders: Firmness, Wave damping, Snowfall.
- Reset, Pause, Sound on/off, View.
- A "How to play" footer.
Interaction: pick up and throw floes and bergs; drag across the water to make waves; drag the ground or the side of the block to tip it; drag empty space or right-drag to orbit; scroll or pinch to zoom.

Web Audio sounds: calving crack and rumble, splashes, a capsizing groan, ice knocking on the hull, a deep two-reed ship's horn, penguin plops, and wind that rises with the snowfall.

Show a fallback screen when WebGPU is unavailable. Respect prefers-reduced-motion. No network requests.

QUALITY BAR
Low-poly faceted ice with chalky snowy tops, glassy blue underwater parts, blue bands, sparkles and translucency. Soft shadows. Cool polar light. Performance around 60 fps on a laptop. Test headlessly: no NaNs over long soaks, a calm start, calving plus capsize, a full ship round trip, feeding, picking up ice, the mobile sheet, and no console errors.
Deliver the HTML file and publish it as an artifact.

title: Soft-body jelly kiwi wedge simulation
text:
PROMPT
Build "Kiwi Jelly Wedge" — a single self-contained HTML file (inline JS/CSS, no libraries): a real-time WebGPU soft-body gummy kiwi wedge you can grab, stretch, lift and twist.
Object
One sixth of a thick kiwi slice: a pie-shaped wedge with 30° half-angle, radius ≈ 1.8 and thickness 0.56. Rounded corners (iq's exact pie SDF minus a rounding radius) and bevelled top/bottom edges.
Regions, measured from the tip in rest space:a cream core at the tip with a slightly lobed edge;
thin pale rays fanning out of the core every 2π/56, each with its own random brightness and length;
a darker, glassier ring around the seeds (blushes red in the Ruby variety);
bright juicy outer flesh with radial cell grain and a lighter band just under the skin;
a thin brown fuzzy skin on the arc wall.

Seeds:small flattened black teardrops, pointed end toward the core, in radial rows between the rays, at four depths;
the face layers break the cut surfaces like real seeds; the others float inside and show through the jelly;
wet glossy shading.

A few small air bubbles in the outer flesh.
Varieties: Green, Gold, Ruby.
Physics (XPBD tetrahedral soft body)
Mesh: 2D Delaunay of the rounded outline plus a hex lattice, extruded into prisms → tets.
Co-rotational per-tet shape matching (warm-started quaternion) plus volume constraints.
Stiffer skin and core tets; edge-velocity damping; floor contact with Coulomb friction.
Soft patch grab with bounded reach; scroll or a second finger twists the held patch.
Fixed 60 Hz step with 10 substeps; gentle settling.
Seeds and bubbles are separate meshes embedded in the tets by barycentric weights, so they ride with the flesh.
Rendering (WebGPU / WGSL)
Procedural photo-studio cyclorama with softboxes. Soft PCSS key shadow tinted green, plus contact AO from a top-down height map.
Seeds and bubbles are drawn in the scene pass. A back-face pass gives the view-ray thickness.
Jelly:refraction of the scene, with per-tap Beer–Lambert absorption by material (flesh, glassy seed ring, milky core and rays, opaque skin);
scattering, back-lit glow at thin edges, Fresnel studio reflections and GGX highlights;
a velvet sheen on the fuzzy skin;
sparse sugar glints in the flesh.

Post: exposure, Khronos PBR Neutral tone mapping, sRGB, dither.
UI (editorial "Material Studies / No. 028", English)
Italic serif title "Kiwi / Jelly." with the caption "An emerald wedge. A halo of seeds. A gentle wobble."
Status pill "WEBGPU · LIVE".
Panel "The Specimen": variety chips (skin / core / flesh bands); Firmness ("trembling → set") and Internal damping ("lively → syrupy") sliders; Give it a nudge, Reset, Pause; ¼ speed and Show mesh.
Readouts: Mass (g, 1 unit ≈ 1.6 cm at 1.3 g/cm³), Volume (% of rest), Kinetic (µJ).
A collapsible "Inside the experiment" with notes on the method.
Fallback "This kiwi needs WebGPU." Stacked mobile layout with no horizontal scroll.

title: Red panda Koda and the giant peach
text:
Seedance 2.5 prompt:

Create an exactly 30-second vertical 9:16 premium 3D animated adventure-comedy short. Use the attached @ Koda character sheet as the exact visual reference for Koda. Maintain his identical face, amber-brown eyes, cream facial markings, rust-red fur, dark legs, rounded ears, compact proportions and enormous ringed fluffy tail throughout every frame. The reference defines Koda's appearance only.
The entire story takes place on one continuous sunny green mountain hillside surrounded by distant forested mountains. One old peach tree grows from the slope. It has a thick stable trunk, several strong main branches and one thinner flexible outer branch. One enormous ripe golden-orange peach hangs near the end of that thinner branch. A large dense leafy bush grows directly below that side of the tree. A long fallen bamboo pole lies several meters away on the same hillside. Farther downhill, a narrow wooden footbridge crosses a shallow mountain stream. Keep this geography fixed throughout the entire video.
Koda desperately wants the enormous peach. His first idea is simply to climb the tree. He reaches the fruit but moves too far onto the thin outer branch, causing the branch to bend gradually under his weight. He almost touches the peach, loses traction and slides off into the huge soft bush below. Koda refuses to give up. He returns with the long fallen bamboo pole, places it diagonally against a strong fork in the tree and climbs it like a simple ladder. This time he reaches the peach and pulls it free. The peach is far heavier than expected, drops onto the clearly sloping hillside and begins rolling downhill because of gravity. Koda chases it, jumps onto the rolling fruit and accidentally begins riding it. He becomes thrilled and celebrates until he notices a narrow wooden footbridge directly ahead. The peach is much wider than the bridge entrance. It wedges between the entrance posts, stops instantly and Koda's forward momentum sends him harmlessly into a giant pile of dry leaves beside the bridge.
Open at 0:00 with a low wide tracking shot of Koda already sprinting uphill through tall green grass toward the peach tree. His short legs move rapidly and his huge fluffy tail streams naturally behind him. As he reaches the tree, he suddenly looks upward and sees the enormous peach glowing among the leaves. He skids to a stop, stares at it, looks at the trunk and immediately becomes determined.
From 0:02 to 0:05, follow Koda as he rapidly climbs the thick trunk using all four paws. His claws visibly grip the bark while his hind feet push upward. His tail stays naturally attached behind him and reacts only to his body movement. He pulls himself onto a strong main branch and begins moving toward the peach.
From 0:05 to 0:08, show a clear wide side view of Koda carefully stepping from the thick branch onto the thinner outer branch. The peach is just beyond his reach. As Koda moves farther away from the trunk, his weight causes the thin branch to bend downward gradually. The branch does not bend before Koda steps onto it and does not move for any unexplained reason.
From 0:08 to 0:11, Koda slowly stretches one front paw toward the peach. His paw almost reaches it. He leans slightly farther forward and briefly touches the peach's fuzzy surface. He smiles. His rear paws then lose traction on the increasingly sloped branch. Koda freezes, his eyes widen and he begins sliding backward along the branch.
From 0:11 to 0:13, Koda slides completely off the branch and falls directly downward into the large dense bush below. He disappears into the foliage with a huge soft leafy FWUMP. The bush shakes. After a short comedic pause, Koda's head slowly rises from between the leaves. Small leaves cling to his fur. He looks upward toward the peach again and his dazed expression changes into stubborn determination.
From 0:13 to 0:16, Koda jumps from the bush, runs several meters across the same hillside and grabs the end of the long fallen bamboo pole using both front paws. He drags it across the grass toward the peach tree. The bamboo scrapes naturally over the ground. Koda struggles because the pole is much longer than his body, but he never uses or removes his tail as a tool.
From 0:16 to 0:18.5, show the complete setup clearly in one wide shot. Koda positions one end of the bamboo on the grassy ground near the tree. He lifts the other end with both front paws while the grounded end remains in contact with the earth. As Koda walks forward underneath the rising pole, the bamboo rotates upward around its grounded end until the raised end settles securely against a strong fork in the thick tree. The bamboo now forms a stable diagonal climbing pole. Koda steps back, studies it and smiles proudly.
From 0:18.5 to 0:21, Koda climbs the angled bamboo with all four paws. His front paws pull while his hind feet push against the bamboo surface. The bamboo remains stable against the tree. His fluffy tail remains physically connected to his body and trails naturally behind him. He reaches the upper end beside the enormous peach.
From 0:21 to 0:23.5, Koda braces his hind feet against the bamboo and grabs the peach with both front paws. He pulls once and nothing happens. He adjusts his grip and pulls much harder. The short fruit stem stretches under the force. With one final effort the stem breaks with a clear POP. Koda is suddenly holding the enormous peach and gives a huge triumphant smile.
From 0:23.5 to 0:25.5, the peach's weight immediately pulls downward. Koda cannot support it. The peach slips from his paws and drops onto the steep grassy slope below with a heavy THUMP. Because the ground visibly slopes downhill, the peach naturally begins rolling. It starts slowly and then accelerates. Koda quickly descends from the bamboo and runs after it.
From 0:25.5 to 0:27.5, use a dynamic downhill tracking shot. The enormous peach rolls rapidly through the grass. Koda catches up and jumps onto its upper surface. At first he lies belly-first and panics, but after a moment he gets his paws underneath himself and manages to balance on top. His expression changes from fear to pure excitement. He stretches his front paws outward while his huge attached tail streams behind him. Koda begins enjoying the ridiculous ride.
From 0:27.5 to 0:29, track backward in front of the rolling peach. Koda rides proudly with a huge smile while his fur moves in the rushing air. He suddenly looks ahead. His smile disappears. Pull the camera backward enough to reveal the narrow wooden footbridge directly downhill. The entrance is obviously narrower than the giant peach. Koda's eyes widen. He has no time to stop.
From 0:29 to 0:30, show the bridge entrance in a clear wide side view. The rolling peach reaches the two wooden entrance posts and wedges firmly between them with one heavy THUD. The peach stops instantly. Koda's momentum carries him forward off the fruit and into a large soft pile of dry leaves beside the bridge. Leaves burst upward around him. His head immediately rises from the pile, completely unharmed and dazed. One small green peach leaf drifts down and lands gently on top of his head. Koda slowly looks upward with only his eyes. Cut to black.
Use a premium photorealistic 3D CGI animated-feature aesthetic with detailed soft fur, realistic bark, leaves, grass and peach fuzz, cinematic daylight, rich natural colors and expressive physical comedy. Keep the daylight warm and consistent. Use believable gravity, momentum, friction, collisions and character weight beneath the exaggerated comedy.
Koda has exactly one fluffy tail, permanently attached to the base of his spine throughout all 30 seconds. Never detach it, duplicate it, turn it into a prop or place it in Koda's paws. Koda manipulates objects only with his paws and body weight.
The peach remains attached to the same branch until Koda physically pulls it free. The thin branch bends only because Koda moves his weight farther outward. The bamboo moves only because Koda physically drags and raises it. The peach rolls only after falling onto the visibly downhill slope. The peach continuously travels downhill toward the existing bridge. Do not teleport objects, change geography, create duplicate props or introduce unexplained movement.
No humans, no additional animals, no dialogue, no text, no subtitles, no logos and no HUD.
Use playful adventurous orchestral music throughout. Include rapid soft paw footsteps, mountain wind, grass and leaf movement, claw-on-bark sounds, subtle branch creaking, the soft leafy FWUMP of Koda landing in the bush, bamboo scraping over grass, bamboo contact sounds, the fruit-stem POP, heavy peach THUMP, increasing rolling rumble, stronger wind during the downhill ride, an abrupt musical stop when Koda sees the bridge, a heavy THUD when the peach wedges between the posts, a soft POOF when Koda lands in the leaves, brief silence, gentle leaf flutter and one tiny comedic orchestral note when the peach leaf lands on Koda's head.

title: Japanese shrine scene comparison
text:
PROMPT

Build a single-file interactive WebGL diorama (one index.html, no build step) with Three.js r160 loaded via an import map from http://cdn.jsdelivr.net, plus OrbitControls and BufferGeometryUtils (mergeVertices, mergeGeometries) from three/examples/jsm. Everything is procedural — no external models or textures.

CONCEPT
"Torii at High Tide": a miniature Japanese shrine island inspired by Itsukushima, inside a 10×10 block of clear water with rounded edges (vertical corner radius ~0.6, top edge radius ~0.26), on a thin sand-colored base slab, on a warm washi-paper background with a soft floor shadow that fades out with distance (so long dusk shadows never streak across the page).

TERRAIN (heightfield ~400×400, clipped to the rounded block, with a boundary "skirt" so the cross-section shows through the water)
- Work in a local frame facing the camera (u = across, v = toward the viewer).
- A forested dome-shaped hill at the back (~2.4 high), a low sandy shrine terrace at its foot, then a wide, gently sloping tidal flat in front (from ~-0.06 down to ~-0.46), dropping to ~-1.0 at the front and sides.
- Two rocky granite headlands framing the bay, each with 1–2 leaning bonsai-style pines (segmented trunks + flattened canopy pads).
- A flattened clearing on the hill flank for the pagoda.
- Terrain shader: granite rock on steep slopes (speckled, darker wet band just above the waterline, algae-dark below it), sand with a wet line, darker wet intertidal sand below the high-tide mark, moss/grass on the hill and in patches on the terrace, snow on upward-facing surfaces in winter, procedural animated caustics under water. CPU-baked horizon AO per vertex plus canopy-cover darkening.

ARCHITECTURE (merge everything into one vertex-colored mesh + one emissive "glow" mesh; write a small Builder that adds boxes/cylinders/spheres/custom geometry with a color and a transform, then mergeGeometries)
- Ryōbu-style torii standing in the bay on the axis of the shrine (~1.9 tall): vermilion tapered main pillars with black base sheaths, four supporting sode-bashira legs with black caps and two connecting beams each, nuki tie beam, central strut with a dark plaque, shimaki, and a curved kasagi (extruded shape with upturned ends) with a black top layer. Pillars must end inside the shimaki, not poke through the kasagi.
- Shrine on stilts over the tidal flat: plank deck (with plank-gap strips and dark edge beams) on a grid of wooden stilts reaching the seabed; a main hall and a smaller front hall (white walls, vermilion posts and tie beams, shoji-style front panels = glow panels behind a thin dark lattice), a lower front stage with vermilion railings, and two roofed vermilion corridors on stilts running sideways then back to the shore.
- Roofs: a hip-roof generator with a concave profile and lifted eave corners (top surface dark cypress-bark brown, warm wood underside, pale fascia trim, black ridge cap).
- A five-storey pagoda on the hill clearing: stone plinth, white walls with vermilion posts, bracket layer, flared roofs decreasing in size, bronze finial with rings.
- Stone tōrō lanterns on the terrace and on the stage (hexagonal base, post, firebox with emissive windows, small roof, jewel).

VEGETATION
- ~4–5k canopy blobs (InstancedMesh of icospheres with vertex-noise displacement + fragment bump), clustered 2–4 per tree, per-instance AO from neighbour occlusion, brighter tops.
- Four kinds via an instance attribute: broadleaf, cherry, maple, pine (flattened pads). Cherries cluster lower on the hill and as 5 feature trees with visible trunks on the terrace; pines dominate the summit and the headlands.
- Colors come from per-kind dark/light palette uniforms that the JS blends across seasons.

SEASONS (cyclic 0..4 = spring, summer, autumn, winter; animated transition from a dock button)
- Spring: pink sakura, falling petals. Summer: lush green, no particles. Autumn: red maples, orange/yellow broadleaf, falling maple leaves. Winter: bare-ish brown deciduous blobs shrunk ~38%, snow on canopy tops, roofs, decks, rocks and ground; snowfall that melts instantly on the water.

WATER (realistic, not jelly)
- Pipeline: opaque scene → MSAA HalfFloat target with DepthTexture; copy to a second target, then draw the water with a custom ShaderMaterial doing a manual depth test; then floating particles; final fullscreen pass with ACES tone mapping, sRGB, subtle tilt-shift. Transparent canvas over the CSS background.
- Color from real thickness: reconstruct the depth behind each water pixel, Beer–Lambert absorption toward a deep scatter color derived from the user's water color (pale over the flats, blue in the deep; side walls get extra path length so they read as a water volume).
- Screen-space refraction, Fresnel sky reflection, sun glints from fine animated detail normals.
- Screen-space reflections (~26 ray-march steps against the depth buffer, fewer on mobile) so the torii, shrine and lit lanterns reflect in the water.
- Ripples: GPU wave equation on a 256×256 HalfFloat ping-pong target, fixed 60 Hz steps, land-mask texture so waves reflect off the shore. Cursor movement injects capsule drops along its path; a click makes a splash.
- Shore foam only where the terrain is near the water level AND gently sloped (no white outlines around cliffs, stilts or the torii pillars); foam band width scaled by slope; broken by noise.
- Tide: a dock toggle animates between high tide (0) and low tide (-0.55): the water block's rim moves and its sides stretch; at low tide the whole flat is exposed and the torii stands on wet sand.

PARTICLES (petals / leaves / snow, ~700 instanced quads, CPU-simulated)
- Spawn from cherry blobs (spring), deciduous blobs (autumn) or the sky (winter); flutter while falling; a gusting wind blows from the island toward the bay so they reach the water.
- Landing: on water they become floating (vertex shader lifts them by the same ripple + wave height as the water), drift slowly, get pushed by the cursor's movement and blown away by click splashes, strand when the tide drops, re-float when it rises; on land they rest and fade.
- Shapes drawn in the fragment shader: notched petal, five-lobed maple leaf, soft snow disc. Manual depth test against the scene depth.

KOI
- 7 koi (lathe body + forked fan tail + pectoral fins, merged), InstancedMesh with a swimming sway in the vertex shader and procedural patterns per type (kohaku, sanke, showa, ogon, plain orange). They wander, steer away from shallow water and the block walls, and flee the cursor and splashes. Rendered under the water so they are refracted and tinted.

TIME OF DAY (slider, shown as a clock from 11:00 to ~19:10)
- Sun elevation, color and intensity, hemisphere colors, and the water's sky reflection shift from noon to golden hour; towards dusk the shoji panels and lanterns glow (emissive) and three warm point lights light the shrine, the stage and the torii.

UI (editorial, minimal, English)
Brand "shiosai°" with a small torii mark, headline "A gate that / stands in the sea.", eyebrow "Shrine and tide, in miniature", a vertical caption "A study of tide and seasons", a location label "Shrine Cove · 34°16′ N · 132°19′ E", a floating pill dock (reset, season cycle with the current season name, High tide / Low tide toggle, Tune, fullscreen), hints and an adaptive FPS + "Season · time" readout in the footer, a glassy settings panel (season, time of day, falling petals; water color, tide level, wave height, ripple strength, clarity, caustics; sun azimuth, tilt-shift), and a "How it's made" card. Vermilion accent, light and dark themes via CSS tokens, responsive to 390 px (panel becomes a bottom sheet), prefers-reduced-motion respected, adaptive pixel ratio and a lighter mode for touch devices. Intro: the water fills the block while the camera eases in.

title: Three.js Tesla-Style Electric Motor 40-Second Educational 3D Animation
text:
Create a high-end cinematic and educational 3D animation in Three.js explaining how a Tesla-style electric motor works.

The animation must have an EXACT FIXED DURATION OF 40 SECONDS.

Do not make the animation shorter or longer than 40 seconds.

Final output:
Exact duration: 40.0 seconds
Resolution: 1920x1080
Aspect ratio: 16:9
Frame rate: 30 FPS
Total frames: 1200
High-quality anti-aliasing
High-resolution textures
Smooth deterministic animation
Extremely realistic visual quality

The overall visual quality should resemble a premium automotive engineering visualization or a high-end technical product commercial.

Build a detailed electric motor assembly inspired by the permanent-magnet AC motors used in modern Tesla vehicles. Do not use Tesla logos or branding.

FIXED TIMELINE

0–5 seconds — Hero introduction
Show the fully assembled electric motor suspended in a dark premium studio environment.

Use:
cinematic lighting
realistic brushed aluminum
copper
steel
magnets
insulation
bearings
realistic reflections
ambient occlusion
realistic shadows
subtle depth of field

Use a slow cinematic orbit around the motor.

During the final part of this section, make the outer housing partially transparent to reveal the internal structure.

5–11 seconds — Internal components
Move the camera closer and reveal the internal motor components.

Clearly show:
stator
copper windings
rotor
permanent magnets
motor shaft
bearings
housing
cooling channels
electrical connections

Highlight the important components one at a time.

Use floating labels with short technical names.

Keep non-highlighted components slightly darker or semi-transparent.

11–19 seconds — Exploded view
Create a dramatic and highly detailed exploded-view animation.

Separate the motor into many individual mechanical components along the motor axis.

Include:
outer housing
front cover
rear cover
bearings
shaft
rotor core
rotor magnets
stator core
copper windings
cooling components
seals
electrical connectors
fasteners

Keep every component perfectly aligned.

The viewer must clearly understand where every piece belongs.

Move the camera slightly through the exploded assembly while highlighting the major components.

Near the end of this section, smoothly begin reassembling the motor.

19–28 seconds — Electromagnetic operation
Finish reassembling the motor.

Explain how electricity creates rotation.

Visualize three-phase AC current flowing through the stator windings.

Use animated electrical pulses inside the copper coils.

Visualize the rotating magnetic field around the stator using elegant semi-transparent magnetic field lines, arrows, or vector effects.

Show how the rotating magnetic field interacts with the permanent magnets inside the rotor.

Clearly visualize magnetic attraction and repulsion.

The rotor should begin rotating slowly and gradually accelerate.

Display these short explanations:

"Three-phase current creates a rotating magnetic field."

"The magnetic field interacts with the rotor."

"This interaction generates torque."

28–34 seconds — Technical close-up and power flow
Show a close-up cross-section of the stator and rotor.

Visualize:
magnetic north and south poles
rotating stator magnetic field
rotor magnetic field
electric current direction
torque direction
rotor rotation direction

Optionally show three small animated sine waves representing phases A, B, and C, separated by 120 degrees.

Then visualize the complete energy conversion process:

Electrical energy
→ stator current
→ rotating magnetic field
→ electromagnetic torque
→ rotor rotation
→ mechanical output through the shaft.
Use clean animated arrows to show the energy flow.
34–38 seconds — High-speed operation
Show the motor operating at high RPM.
The rotor should spin smoothly while the stator remains stationary.
Add subtle motion blur.

Show cooling flow through the housing using translucent fluid paths.

Visualize heat being removed from the stator and copper windings.
38–40 seconds — Final hero shot

Transition back to the fully assembled motor.

Show a slow cinematic rotation.

Briefly use a transparent cutaway so the spinning rotor can still be seen inside.

Finish with the text:

"Electrical energy → Electromagnetic torque → Mechanical rotation"
The animation must end exactly at 40.0 seconds.

VISUAL QUALITY

The animation should be:

photorealistic

cinematic

technically believable

futuristic

premium
educational
clean and uncluttered
Avoid cartoon styling.
Use realistic:
machining details
bolts
screws

copper winding geometry

segmented magnets
bearing geometry
cooling channels
metallic surfaces
manufacturing details
Use physically based materials with:
metallic properties
roughness variation
normal maps
realistic reflections

subtle surface imperfections
CAMERA
Use only smooth cinematic camera movement:
slow orbit shots
macro close-ups
controlled dolly-ins

exploded-view fly-throughs

cross-section shots

internal motor views
Avoid:
shaky camera movement
sudden cuts
excessive zooming
unrealistic camera acceleration

ANIMATION REQUIREMENTS
All transitions must be smooth and deliberate.
The exploded-view sequence should be one of the main visual highlights.
All mechanical components must separate and reassemble with precise motion.
Electrical currents, magnetic fields, torque indicators, and rotor rotation must remain synchronized.

The entire animation must use the same fixed 40-second timeline on every execution so the prompt can be used as a repeatable benchmark between different AI coding and 3D generation systems.

title: Anime opening edit of a martial arts clip
text:
Opus Prompt: Edit this video in the style of an anime opening. Add color grading,  also dynamic cuts, transitions, visual effects, motion graphics and impactful editing to give it that authentic anime opening feel.

Seedance 2.5 Prompt:
References:
@[ref1]: The martial artist's face. Identity, dark tousled hair, eyes, and the look of the painted flame around her open hand.
@[ref2]: Her body, costume, setting, and effects. Pale pink short-sleeve top, red wrist wraps and red sash, dark loose trousers, her low kneeling stance, the misty blue void with its dark floor, the looping pink ribbon arcs, and the spark burst.

Visual style: Painterly digital illustration in motion: thick, loose brushstrokes and palette-knife texture, deep blue-teal shadows and haze, figures built from broad painted planes. Every effect is painted, not rendered: flame-like ribbons of orange, hot pink, and violet with white-hot cores, exactly as in @[ref1] and @[ref2].

Avoid: No subtitles. No background music. No clean 3D particle fire, glossy CG effects, or lens-flare glare. No weapons or opponents.

A solo karate kata in a misty blue void, where painted flame grows with every strike and ends in an explosive palm strike into the floor. Vertical 9:16 frame, real-time speed except one brief speed ramp at the final impact. She performs toward screen right, faces screen left after her turn, and faces the lens for the finale; the camera stays on the same side of her line. The flame starts in her right hand; after the first punch it ignites on whichever limb strikes, and each technique leaves its own shape. Warm colors stay on the effects; the setting stays blue-teal. Crackling flame, sharp whooshes, foot stamps, cloth snaps, breath, one kiai, and heavy impact thuds land on the cuts.

Scene 1: Continuous, the misty blue void, its dark floor dusted pale blue.
Shot 1 (0-2s): [Extreme close-up on her eyes, slow push in] Stillness. A single ember drifts across her face as she breathes in. Cut on a sharp inhale.
Shot 2 (2-4s): [Close-up on her right hand, low angle, quick push toward the lens] Her open right hand thrusts at the lens in teisho-uchi, fingers spread as in @[ref1]. Painted flame ignites in the palm and curls up her forearm. Cut as the flame flares.

Scene 2: Continuous, the first form.
Shot 3 (4-6s): [Low wide, fast lateral track] She steps into zenkutsu-dachi and drives a right oi-zuki toward screen right; the flame stretches behind her fist in one long straight ribbon. Cut as the punch locks out.
Shot 4 (6-7s): [Tight side view at waist height] A left gyaku-zuki snaps out past the retracting right fist, and the flame catches on her left fist too. Cut as it locks out.
Shot 5 (7-9s): [Medium, camera whipping around to face her] Her right mae-geri kicks straight at the lens, flame fanning off the foot in a short burst. Cut as the kick retracts.
Shot 6 (9-10s): [Ground level, close on her feet] The kicking foot stamps down, throwing a ring of pale blue dust and orange sparks. Cut as she pivots.
Shot 7 (10-13s): [Orbiting camera with a whip pan] She turns 180 degrees through a right, then left shuto-uke, and her burning hands wrap her in looping pink ribbon arcs as in @[ref2]. She now faces screen left. Cut as the arcs close.

Scene 3: Continuous, the pause and the escalation.
Shot 8 (13-15s): [Low frontal medium, locked] She sinks into kiba-dachi, both fists drawn to her hips. The flames shrink into tight glowing cores in her fists and the dust settles; only her breath is heard. Cut on a sharp exhale.
Shot 9 (15-16s): [Snap zoom into her face] Her kiai rings out, flame reflected in her eyes, hair whipping. Cut at the peak of the shout.
Shot 10 (16-18s): [Low wide] She explodes into ushiro-mawashi-geri, the burning heel drawing one full ring of fire around her. Cut as the ring closes.
Shot 11 (18-19s): [Close tracking on her right fist] An uraken-uchi snaps through the frame toward screen left, its trail cracking like a whip. Cut on the snap.
Shot 12 (19-20s): [Medium from behind her shoulder] Her right empi-uchi drives toward screen left, a short burst flaring off the elbow. Cut as the elbow locks.
Shot 13 (20-22s): [Low angle, camera rising] She crouches and launches into nidan-geri, a spiral of flame climbing around her through both kicks. Cut at the apex.

Scene 4: Continuous, the finale.
Shot 14 (22-24s): [High angle, camera diving down with her] She descends from the apex, turning to face the lens, and drops onto one knee, right palm driving toward the floor. Cut just before contact.
Shot 15 (24-25s): [Ground-level close-up] Her right teisho-uchi hits the floor: a white-hot core flashes and erupts into orange sparks, pink paint flecks, and lifted blue dust, as in @[ref2], with a brief speed ramp at contact. Cut at the peak of the burst.
Shot 16 (25-30s): [Low frontal wide, slow push in to medium] She holds the low kneeling stance from @[ref2] as the burst's ribbons settle into drifting embers and fade. She raises her eyes to the lens and holds.

title: Gummy bear soft-body physics scene
text:
PROMPT

Build "Gummy Bears" - a single self-contained HTML file (three.js from a CDN is the only dependency): a handful of translucent gummy bears on a white table that you can grab, stretch, squash, throw and pour.

The bears
- Classic gummy bear silhouette: round head with two ears, short snout, plump body, stubby arms and legs, tiny molded eyes and nose
- Every part melts smoothly into the next - build the body as an implicit surface (metaballs / marching cubes), not separate spheres
- Material: real gummy candy. Translucent with transmission and refraction, colored light absorption that gets deeper in thick parts, glossy clearcoat with sharp highlights
- Colors: cherry red, orange, lemon yellow, apple green, clear pineapple
- Soft colored shadow under each bear, tinted by the bear's own color

Physics (this is the whole point - it must feel like jelly, not plastic)
- Each bear is a soft body: mass points for head, ears, snout, body, belly, hands and feet, held together by volume-preserving shape matching
- Limbs and neck are rendered as stretchy strands between points, getting thinner as they stretch
- Grab any part and pull: it stretches like rubber, the rest of the bear leans after it, on release it snaps back with a damped wobble
- Pull the head up: the neck stretches, the body follows, on release the bear squashes and hops
- Press down on the head: the bear pancakes, bulges sideways, then launches itself back up
- Throw a bear: it flies, squashes on landing, bounces and pushes other bears out of the way
- Bears collide with each other and never pass through one another
- Idle bears do small random hops with squash and stretch
- "Pour more bears" drops a handful from above into a wobbling, jiggling pile

UI
- Editorial product-page style on a white background. Large italic serif title "Gummy / Bears.", a short subtitle, a minimal card on the right with flavor swatches, a wobble slider, live "Stretch" and "Bounces" readouts and a "Pour more bears" button
- A subtle circular cursor that grows while grabbing
- ACES tone mapping, environment reflections, soft key and back light. Smooth 60fps

title: make an animated short that felt like Hedgehog in the Fog.
text:
make an animated short that felt like Hedgehog in the Fog. I didn’t want to copy Yuri Norstein’s film, so we went with a new story.

It runs for 6.5 minutes. All 9363 frames are drawn by JavaScript code written by Opus. No video or image generation models, just canvas.

It follows a little mouse in a red scarf. Her grandfather, an old mole, is out fishing when fog rolls over the lake. She goes looking for him with a walnut-shell lantern and a sleeping firefly inside. They have a secret knock to help them find each other: short, short, long. It means "I’m here".

Norstein used paper cutouts on layers of glass, filmed frame by frame. I wanted some of that paper texture to come through in code. So the scenes use different styles: torn-paper collage, chalk on black paper, tissue paper underwater. There’s even sand on a light table and a pop-up book.

Opus wrote the music too. It found Steinway piano samples in my Logic library and used Python to compose the score around the rhythm of that knock.

title: Build a single self-contained HTML file: a 3D marble computer, in…
text:
Build a single self-contained HTML file: a 3D marble computer, in the spirit of Wintergatan's marble machine and the Digi-Comp II, that adds two 4-bit numbers using nothing but marbles falling through mechanical toggles.

Hard rules:

1. One HTML file. Three.js from https://t.co/KCQbEZLusb via an import map, plus its OrbitControls addon. No other libraries, no physics engine, no external assets.

2. The mechanism is the computer. Each bit of the result is stored in a two-state toggle (flip-flop) that a marble physically flips as it passes. Carries happen because a marble leaving one toggle rolls on to the next. Do not compute the answer in JavaScript arithmetic anywhere. The displayed result must be read from the toggle states after the last marble stops.

3. Marbles move along tracks with believable gravity and timing. Nothing teleports. You may script motion along paths, but every toggle flip must be caused by a marble arriving at it.

4. Input: two rows of four switches (A and B, 0 to 15), set by clicking. A lever labelled RUN releases the marbles. A counter shows how many marbles have fallen.

5. Output: a row of five result toggles, most significant bit on the left, and a readout that shows the binary and decimal value read from those toggles.

6. A DEMO button runs 5+6, then 9+7, then 15+15, resetting between runs, so it can be screen-recorded without touching anything.

7. Looks: a wooden board, brass toggles, glass marbles, warm studio lighting, soft shadows, a slow camera that follows the busiest part of the machine. It should look good in a square 1080x1080 recording.

8. Short click sounds via the Web Audio API when a toggle flips, started only after the first user click.

9. It must run at 60 fps on a normal laptop and have no console errors.

Output only the complete HTML file.

title: Yohaku: 36s vertical three.js stained-glass cathedral film
text:
Please make a short vertical film in three.js: 1080×1920, 30 frames per second, about 36 seconds.

[Title]
Yohaku (Space to Breathe)

[The experience to convey]
A film that makes the viewer feel the sense of losing time while chasing efficiency, and the sense of life being filled with rich light the moment you gain some breathing room, without showing any person at all. The aim is for the viewer to catch their breath at the stained-glass light that finally spreads across the whole floor.

[Setting]
- The interior of a dim stone cathedral. On the front wall there is a single pointed-arch window, 15 m high and 10 m wide
- Strong light comes in from outside the window at a 45-degree angle, casting the shape of the window onto the stone floor
- The window holds stained glass with the Virgin Mary in the centre, two winged angels on either side, and a rose window at the top. The design is original, not imitating any existing work, and has a left-right symmetrical composition

[Timeline]
0–3s: The light coming through the window is still white, without colour. A soft white shape of light on the floor
3–11s: Grey cubes engraved with words such as "Busy", "Efficiency", "Urgent" and "Deadline" fly in one after another from the front of the room and fill the window. The pace of arrival keeps accelerating, and the more the window is filled, the darker the room becomes
11–14s: The window is completely blocked; darkness and silence

title: Rebuild Type 1 diabetes in one HTML file, from the whole body down…
text:
Rebuild Type 1 diabetes in one HTML file, from the whole body down to a single molecule.

THE BROKEN MESSAGE

Type 1 diabetes isn't caused by sugar, weight or lifestyle. It's autoimmune: the immune system destroys the beta cells in the pancreas that make insulin.

Those cells live in tiny clusters called islets, about 1–2% of the pancreas. After a meal, they sense rising glucose and release insulin. Insulin signals muscle and fat to take glucose in, and tells the liver to release less.

In Type 1, that signal disappears.
The fuel is still there. The message is missing.
So glucose builds up in the blood.

With almost no insulin, the body breaks down fat fast and the liver makes ketones. They can build up into diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), a medical emergency.

Insulin therapy doesn't cure Type 1. It replaces a signal the body can no longer provide adequately, through injections or a pump. The daily challenge is balance: too little and glucose rises, too much and it can fall dangerously low. Food, exercise, stress and timing all change the picture.

Technology helps. A CGM tracks glucose every few minutes, and automated insulin delivery (AID) adjusts insulin based on those readings.

In the build, you can compare Healthy vs Type 1 vs Type 1 + insulin on the same meal, drag one slider from INTACT to BROKEN to watch the signal fade, follow a glucose molecule through the body, and explore CGM, pumps and AID.

Type 1 diabetes changes the system.
It doesn't define the person.

Built in Three.js. Educational visualization, not medical advice.
