title: Explainer video of 9 football rules
text:
Postav mi video, které vysvětluje pravidla sportu stylem televizní analýzy s AR grafikou. Bez AI video modelů a bez stahování assetů: 3D scénu, postavy, textury, grafiku i zvuk vytvoř kódem. Pracuj samostatně a průběžně mi ukazuj kontrolní snímky.

## Parametry (pro jiný sport změň tuhle sekci a sekci Scénář)
- Sport: fotbal
- Pravidla (9): ofsajd, faul, pokutový kop, vhazování, rohový kop + kop od branky, hra rukou, přímý volný kop, žlutá a červená karta, gól (celý míč za čarou)
- Jazyk všech textů: čeština (plná diakritika, desetinná čárka)
- Délka: cca 68 s (úvod ~4,5 s, každé pravidlo 6 až 8 s, závěr ~4 s)
- Formát: 1920×1080, 30 fps, MP4 (H.264 + AAC)
- Styl postav: PS2 éra ve stylu GTA San Andreas (low-poly tvarované tělo, ručně malované textury)
- Týmy: Červení (červený dres s bílými lemy, bílé trenky), Modří (královsky modrý dres, tmavě modré trenky), rozhodčí černý s limetkovými lemy, brankáři zelený a fialový

## Technologie a pipeline
- Three.js (npm). index.html obsahuje WebGL canvas 1920×1080 a nad ním DOM vrstvu pro HUD.
- Deterministická funkce `window.renderFrame(t)`: stav scény i HUD je čistá funkce času, žádný stav mezi snímky.
- `render.mjs`: lokální statický HTTP server + puppeteer-core se systémovým Chrome (headless, na Macu `--use-angle=metal`). Pro každý snímek zavolej renderFrame(t), počkej 2× requestAnimationFrame, udělej JPEG screenshot a pošli ho rourou do ffmpeg (libx264, CRF 18, yuv420p). Režimy: `stills t1 t2 …` (PNG na kontrolu), `video`, `info` (zapíše časovou osu do out/timeline.json).
- Cesty řeš přes fileURLToPath (složky s mezerami v názvu).
- WebGLRenderer s `preserveDrawingBuffer: true`, ACES tone mapping, PCF soft shadows. EffectComposer s MSAA (samples 4, HalfFloat): RenderPass, UnrealBloomPass, vlastní grade pass (vinětace, jemné zrno, chromatická aberace, záblesk, whip blur, VHS efekt), OutputPass.
- Zvuk: Python (numpy + scipy) syntetizuje celý soundtrack do WAV, ffmpeg ho přimíchá (AAC 192k).
- Výstupy: plná kvalita + webová verze (CRF 23 až 24, maxrate 10M).

## Struktura projektu
src/util.js (easing, tmap pro freeze a zpomalení, track() pro pohyb hráčů po časovaných waypointech s fází běhu podle uražené vzdálenosti, seeded rng), src/world.js, src/player.js, src/ar.js, src/hud.js, src/grade.js, src/segments.js, src/main.js, render.mjs, http://audio.py, PROGRESS.md (průběžně zapisuj, co je hotové a jak se to pouští, ať se dá navázat po přerušení).

## Svět
- Hřiště 105×68 m. Tráva jako canvas textura (pruhy po 5,25 m, šum, skvrny) + dlaždicová detail textura přes onBeforeCompile. Čáry jako ostrá geometrie, ne textura. Vnější hrana čar = hranice hřiště.
- Branky se sítí (LineSegments), rohové praporky.
- Stadion: dvoupatrová mísa podle superelipsy, dav jako canvas textura lidí v řadách, LED pás mezi patry, střecha s žebry, řady reflektorů na hraně střechy (emisivní, bloom), vnější fasáda s osvětlenými okny, noční obloha, světla města kolem, tmavá zem.
- LED mantinely kolem hřiště s českými nápisy (PRAVIDLA FOTBALU, RESPEKT, FAIR PLAY, ZNEJ PRAVIDLA, #PRAVIDLAFOTBALU), pomalu se posouvají.
- Světla: 4 směrová světla z rohů střechy se stíny (shadow kamera zaostřená na akci daného segmentu), hemisférické světlo, jemná mlha.
- Analytický grade: do všech materiálů světa vlož přes onBeforeCompile sdílený uniform uFreeze (odbarvení do chladné šedozelené + ztmavení). AR materiály ho nemají, takže při zastaveném obrazu zůstanou syté.

## Postavy (styl GTA San Andreas)
- Hierarchický rig: root → body (pánev) → trup → hlava a ramena → lokty, kyčle → kolena → kotníky. Póza = sada úhlů (náklon a rotace trupu, flexe a abdukce ramen, lokty, kyčle, kolena, kotníky, náklon těla, výskok).
- Geometrie: trup jako LatheGeometry (široká ramena, užší pas), zúžené končetiny, klouby jako koule, dlaň s palcem, kopačka s podrážkou a zúženou špičkou, tvarovaná hlava (užší brada), nos, uši, vlasy jako slupka (krátké, objemné, ježek, holá hlava).
- Ručně malované canvas textury: obličej (oči s duhovkou a odleskem, obočí, stín nosu, rty, tváře, strniště nebo vousy, vlasová linie), dres (V-výstřih, boční pruhy, znak, sponzor, jméno a velké číslo na zádech, vrásky látky), rukávy, trenky s číslem, štulpny s pruhy.
- Každý hráč jiný: pleť, vlasy, účes, oči, vousy, barva kopaček, postava. Česká jména na zádech (NOVÁK, DVOŘÁK, RŮŽIČKA…).
- Procedurální běh (fáze z uražené vzdálenosti, ať nohy nekloužou) + knihovna póz: kop (nápřah, úder, dokopnutí), skluz, zakopnutí a pád, vhazování, výskok s paží nad hlavou, zvednutá karta, postoj ve zdi, výskok zdi, robinzonáda brankáře, hlava dolů.
- Zvýraznění: obrysová slupka (inverted hull, tloušťka podle vzdálenosti od kamery), průsvitný hologram „ducha“ pro naznačení restartu, rozsvícení paže.

## AR grafika (additive blending, depthWrite false, kreslí se postupně přes progress)
GroundLine (zářící čára na zemi), Curtain (svislá rovina: ofsajd, branková a postranní čára), GroundRing (prstenec nebo disk s pulzem, čárkováním a výsečí, třeba kruh 9,15 m), Area (vyplněné území s okrajem a skenem), Trail (trubice trajektorie míče), GroundArrow (šipka s běžícími chevrony), Marker (zaměřovač kontaktu), Beam (světelný sloup), ScanGrid (skenovací mřížka), Segment3D (měřicí úsečky), Silhouette (válec obrysu těla).
Barvy: tyrkysová = měření, červená = přestupek, jantarová = míč a území, zelená = platné rozhodnutí.
DŮLEŽITÉ: shadery musí být NaN-safe (clamp UV, žádné pow ze záporného čísla). MSAA na hranách extrapoluje UV a NaN se v bloomu rozleje do černých bloků přes půl obrazu.

## HUD (DOM, styl sportovního přenosu)
- Logo vlevo nahoře „PRAVIDLA FOTBALU / AR ANALÝZA ZÁPASU“ + počítadlo „01 / 09“.
- Vpravo nahoře stav (ŽIVĚ, ZÁZNAM, ZPOMALENĚ ×0,6, STOP · AR, PŘETÁČENÍ ◀◀, KONEC ZÁPASU) a herní čas.
- Lower third vlevo dole: číslo pravidla, název, jednověté vysvětlení, ukazatel postupu z 9 dílků.
- Panel rozhodnutí vpravo dole v barvě rozhodnutí (OFSAJD, PENALTA, GÓL…) s podtitulkem.
- Při zastavení obrazu: záblesk, rohové závorky, štítek „ZASTAVENÝ OBRAZ · AR ANALÝZA“, krátký technický řádek dole.
- AR štítky ukotvené na 3D bod (projekce kamerou) s odkazovou čarou. Drž je v bezpečné zóně (ne pod spodní grafikou, ne pod logem) a nesmí se překrývat.
- Velká grafika karty (žlutá a červená) s důvody, úvodní titulek, závěr „TEĎ ZNÁŠ PRAVIDLA.“ s mřížkou 9 pravidel, stinger přechod (šikmé pruhy navy, tyrkysová, bílá + logo) na každém střihu.
- Čitelnost: minimální velikosti (název pravidla 66 px, popis 29 px, štítek 33 px + podtitulek 21 px, technický řádek 22 px). Text vždy na tmavém podkladu, krátké texty. Line-height aspoň 1,05, aby diakritika (Ž, Č, Ř) nebyla oříznutá. Titulky neodhaluj maskou, vypadá to jako ořez: použij fade + rozostření + lehký zoom.
- Fonty: systémové s českou diakritikou (na macOS DIN Condensed + Avenir Next Condensed). Pokrytí znaků ověř předem přes fc-query.

## Scénář (vnitřní časy segmentů, natažení na čtení viz další sekce)
Úvod (3,5 s): dron sjíždí z noční oblohy přes střechu do stadionu na široký záběr středu hřiště. Skenovací mřížka přejede hřiště, pod hráči naskočí kroužky, štítek „MÍČ SLEDOVÁN“. Titulek „PRAVIDLA FOTBALU“, nad ním „TV ANALÝZA PRAVIDEL“, pod ním „9 KLÍČOVÝCH PRAVIDEL · AR ANALÝZA“.
1. Ofsajd: televizní kamera, Červený #8 přihrává, zastavení v okamžiku přihrávky. Kamera se přesune do osy ofsajdové linie. Tyrkysová rovina u nejzazší části těla předposledního obránce (Modrý #4), červená u předsunutého kolena útočníka (Červený #9), měření „+1,59 m“ (spočítej z kloubů, paže se nepočítají). Rozhodnutí OFSAJD: nepřímý volný kop, Modří.
2. Faul: záznam ×0,6 nízko u trávníku. Modrý #10 vede míč, Červený #6 jde skluzem zezadu do kotníku. Zastavení v okamžiku kontaktu: zaměřovač „KONTAKT“, „MÍSTO FAULU“ (kruh + sloup), šipka dráhy skluzu, červený obrys. Kamera obkrouží, pak pád. FAUL: přímý volný kop.
3. Penalta: Červený #9 ve vápně, Modrý #3 ho podrazí. Zastavení, jeřáb nahoru. Zvýraznění pokutového území, oblouk z místa faulu na pokutovou značku s drátěným míčem, „11 m“. PENALTA.
4. Vhazování: přihrávka Červeného #2 přejede postranní čáru (trajektorie se kreslí živě). Zastavení až ve chvíli, kdy je celý míč venku, střih na kameru za čarou. Červená rovina, „+15 cm“, „CELÝ MÍČ VENKU“, „POSLEDNÍ DOTEK · ČERVENÝ #2“, modrá šipka do hřiště a hologram modrého hráče s míčem nad hlavou. VHAZOVÁNÍ (Modří).
5. Roh + kop od branky: střela Červeného #10 tečovaná Modrým #4 za brankovou čáru → ROHOVÝ KOP. Pak efekt přetáčení (VHS) a stejná střela bez teče → KOP OD BRANKY (zvýrazněné brankové území).
6. Hra rukou: střela, Modrý #5 ve výskoku s paží nad ramenem, míč do předloktí. Paže zčervená, ramenní linie, čára paže „ÚHEL PAŽE 135°“, průsvitný válec „OBRYS TĚLA“. RUKA: přímý volný kop.
7. Volný kop: zeď na 8,00 m „ZEĎ MOC BLÍZKO“, nakreslí se kruh 9,15 m, zeď ustoupí, číslo naběhne na 9,15 m a zezelená. Kamera za exekutora, zahraný oblouk přes zeď zpomaleně, zastavení „PŘES ZEĎ“. PŘÍMÝ VOLNÝ KOP.
8. Karty: detail rozhodčího se žlutou kartou proti hráči se svěšenou hlavou + velká grafika ŽLUTÁ KARTA / NAPOMENUTÍ se 3 důvody. Střih, červená karta, vyloučený odchází + ČERVENÁ KARTA / VYLOUČENÍ.
9. Gól: střela, brankář vyrazí, míč padá na čáru. Kamera u brankové čáry. První zastavení: polovina míče na čáře, červená rovina, „−11 cm“, „ZATÍM NENÍ GÓL“. Míč se dokutálí. Druhé zastavení: celý míč za čarou, rovina zezelená, „+3 cm“, blesky foťáků v hledišti. GÓL.
Závěr (2,5 s): kamera stoupá nad hřiště (návrat k úvodnímu záběru), mřížka, „TEĎ ZNÁŠ PRAVIDLA.“ + mřížka 9 pravidel, stmívačka.

Každé zastavení obrazu: krátký záblesk, odbarvení scény, kamera se dál pomalu hýbe kolem zmrazených hráčů, AR prvky naskakují postupně. Mezi segmenty vždy stinger.

## Čas na čtení
Akce (běh, kopy, skluzy) běží ve skutečné rychlosti. Analytické části každého segmentu natáhni 1,5× až 2,1× přes warp funkci (výstupní čas → vnitřní čas segmentu), aby každé pravidlo bylo na obrazovce 6 až 8 s a všechny texty se daly v klidu přečíst. `node render.mjs info` exportuje výslednou časovou osu do out/timeline.json.

## Zvuk (procedurální, http://audio.py)
120 BPM broadcast groove (kopák, virbl, hi-haty, basa se sidechainem, arpeggio, pad), riser v úvodu, závěrečný akord. Při zastaveném obrazu hudba ztlumená low-passem. Dav (filtrovaný šum s vlněním, řev při gólu), whoosh + boom na každém střihu, kovový úder na každém zastavení, krátké „razítko“ při rozhodnutí, píšťalka, kopy do míče, zvuk přetáčení. Časy všech zvuků načti z out/timeline.json, ať sedí na obraz i po změně délky. Cílová hlasitost kolem −14 LUFS.

## Postup práce a kontrola
1. Nejdřív rozjeď pipeline (server, render, ffmpeg) s jednou scénou a ověř, že WebGL v headless Chrome běží.
2. Po každé změně vyrenderuj kontrolní snímky v klíčových časech a prohlédni je, včetně výřezů na 100 % kvůli textu a diakritice.
3. Celé video kontroluj přes kontaktní listy (ffmpeg filtr tile) a snímky kolem přechodů.
4. Hotové video ověř dekódováním (`ffmpeg -v error -i video.mp4 -f null -`) a délku a stopy přes ffprobe.
5. Do PROGRESS.md průběžně zapisuj, co je hotové a jakými příkazy se to pouští.

title: Looping product launch motion template
text:
opus 5.5 is f*cking insane at motion design

every frame is code with 0 external tools

im open sourcing the template for all these morph transitions

steal it ↓

<inputs>
Ask me for: my product's name (one lowercase word, it becomes a black wordmark with a period), the one job a user hands it before bed, the three results it reports by morning, two photos of the same place at night and by day (aligned, so a crossfade reads as a real sunrise), one sunny daytime photo for outside the logo, and a song with a big hit near its start. If I skip any, use the defaults: "nightshift", "book 10 sales calls this week", 200 leads found / 200 emails sent / 10 calls booked.
</inputs>

<direction>
A 24 second square product launch video, 1440x1440 at 60fps, 2D only, one continuous take that loops. The whole video happens inside the period of the wordmark. Outside it's daytime (the sunny photo behind a black wordmark). Inside it's the night photo under iOS-style glass panels (the blurred photo behind each panel, a tint, a rim light). Nothing cuts: every scene grows out of the last, shapes morph, dots fly, colours change under floods. Every morph glides 0.8s on cubic-bezier(.45,0,.15,1) and the camera zoom rides the same curve. Geist, the real macOS pointer, soft shadows that grow with each shape's height.
Banned: flat or gradient backgrounds made in code, camera zooms into tiny points, hard cuts, crossfades between scenes, bouncy springs, particles, glows, holds longer than 1s, cropped type.
</direction>

<structure>
Beats are the song's. The song enters on its big hit as the first pill appears.
Open: the letters slide into the period and vanish into it while it glides to the middle. The period opens like an iris onto the night inside it, and "you log off at 6", then "[product] doesn't", roll through one mask line over the night photo.
Ask: a glass "Ask [product]" pill springs in. The cursor clicks it, it glides into an input and the job types out.
Find: send shrinks the input to a dot that ripples into a 23x15 grid. A scan line sweeps it, 200 dots light up and a counter counts them.
Write: the lit dots pour into a glass email composer. A second, purple cursor labelled "[product]" types a personal opener and presses Send, and the counter runs to 200/200.
Night: the composer becomes a glass orb with a progress ring. A clock chip swaps 11:42 PM, 3:17 AM, 5:02 AM, 6:59 AM while the sky relights from night to dawn and "while you sleep" rolls in.
Results (beat 20): the orb turns black and goo-splits into the three result pills. The checks pop green.
Morning: the pills merge into a Dynamic Island that grows into a phone lock screen: the day photo, the date, a big 7:00, the bezel growing out of the screen edge. Three glass notifications stack in, and the cursor taps the first, which opens like iOS.
Proof: a week calendar (10 meetings pop in, a hover shows one's time), then a pipeline chart ($48,200 counts up, the line draws, a hover follows it). A black flood from the line's end becomes "Start your night shift →" and the cursor clicks it.
Out: the button shrinks into a dot, the whole scene closes down into it like an iris, and the letters slide back out of the period. The tagline rises. Last frame = first frame.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML canvas. Everything is a pure function of time inside seek(t): no timers, no state between frames.
2. One element morphs through every state (size, radius, colour, material) from a table of beat times, so retiming is one edit.
3. Render the inside world into an offscreen canvas and reveal it through the period with a circular mask. Never zoom the camera into the dot.
4. Glass: a pre-blurred copy of the photo clipped to the shape, then a tint and a gradient rim.
5. Goo: blur + alpha threshold on an offscreen layer for the split and the merge.
6. Sound: a downloaded SFX for every event, each placed by its measured peak. The song enters on its hit. Loudnorm to -14 LUFS.
7. Render with Playwright at 60fps with 4 motion-blur subframes. Scan every frame for single-frame jumps and fix each one.
</build>

<gotchas>
A camera zoom into an off-centre dot swings sideways and spikes, so open the dot instead. Ease a closing iris by area, not radius, or its first frames jump. A helper that sets globalAlpha must restore the caller's, or fading cards pop. Counters read the frame's time, not the subframe's, or the digits smear.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for the inputs, then show me the beat map and 6 stills (open, find, write, results, phone, out) before you render.
</start>

title: Jelly pufferfish browser comparison
text:
PROMPT:
Build an interactive 3D jelly pufferfish (fugu) as a single self-contained HTML page using three.js from a CDN.

The fish is a soft-body gummy sitting on a table. Model the body as one closed icosphere-topology skin with two rest shapes per vertex: a calm fish (blunt round head, body tapering to a short tail stalk, slightly flattened belly) and a fully inflated ball (sphere with the same tail stalk sticking out). Blend between them with an "inflation" value. Simulate with XPBD at a fixed 1/600 s substep (frame-rate independent): edge-length constraints, a global volume constraint, a soft global shape-matching pull toward the blended rest shape (rotation via polar decomposition, gently leaning upright), ground collision with friction, and damping applied to the wobble (velocity relative to the body's mean) so it jiggles but settles in about a second. Render with one Loop-subdivision pass for a smooth surface.

Behaviour: tapping the fish startles it. It gulps air three times (mouth opens on each gulp, small overshoot) until it is a round ball, stays puffed about 4 seconds, then slowly deflates while blowing iridescent bubbles from its mouth. Dragging grabs and stretches the jelly locally; dragging empty space orbits the camera; wheel or pinch zooms.

Details: ~260 soft spines that lie flat and hidden when calm, pop up one by one (staggered) as it inflates, wobble on their own springs, bend against the table, and lift the ball so it stands on its spines. Big glossy eyes (gold-green iris, large pupil, white catchlight) that follow the cursor. Puckered lips with a tiny white beak. Translucent ray-striped fins: fluttering pectorals, swaying tail fan, rippling dorsal and anal fins, all faster when alarmed. Dark freckles on the back, pale belly, a few air bubbles trapped inside the jelly.

Look: MeshPhysicalMaterial with transmission, clearcoat and sheen for a candy-gummy look; a soft environment map; a soft colored shadow with a faint caustic on a floor that matches the page background. Flavour presets Yuzu, Ramune, Momo, Matcha. Editorial "Material Studies" layout: big italic serif title "Fugu Jelly.", a side panel with flavour swatches, Firmness and Wobble sliders, Startle / Calm / Reset buttons, ¼ speed and Sound toggles, and live readouts for volume, spine angle and mood. Synthesized WebAudio sounds for gulps, a boing on tap, a hiss while deflating and tiny bubble pops. Responsive down to phone width.

title: Interactive jelly watermelon toy
text:
PROMPT:
Build "Whole Melon": a single self-contained HTML file (all JS/CSS inline, no build step, no libraries) with a big whole watermelon made of glossy jelly that you can grab, wobble and cut into pieces with a knife. Render with raw WebGPU (WGSL); if WebGPU is missing, show a clean fallback card.

SHAPE AND MATERIAL
- The melon is a signed distance field: an ellipsoid (~32 cm long) lying on its side with a softly flattened belly.
- Layers by depth under the skin: dark-green skin with irregular darker stripes running pole to pole (seamless all the way around), a pale pith band, then translucent red flesh that brightens toward the rind. Add a pale yellow field spot on the belly, a stem scar at one end and a blossom end at the other.
- About 700 seeds in a three-lobed ring at roughly two thirds of the radius (teardrops, wide end pointing outward), plus tiny air bubbles. Mesh seeds only near cut faces; a seed the knife goes through is kept by one side and eased just under the new face, so it shows through a thin film of jelly.
- Three varieties: Crimson, Golden, Rosé.

PIECES AND CUTTING
- Every piece is the melon SDF clipped by the half-spaces of the cuts that made it, with the fresh edges rounded (smooth max). All pieces share the melon's original rest frame, so rind, pith, stripes and seeds stay exactly where they grew.
- Knife tool: the user draws a line across the melon. Read the stroke on top of what it crosses to get a vertical blade plane. For each piece the plane passes through, fit the piece's best rotation, carry the plane into rest space, and split the piece in two.
- Build the new pieces cooperatively (generators with a per-frame time budget) while a steel knife (brushed blade, wooden handle with rivets) lines up over the stroke and presses a groove into the jelly. Swap the new pieces in the moment the edge breaks through, carrying over the position and velocity of the flesh they came from, and let the blade wedge them apart as it sinks. Allow up to about 24 pieces and reject slivers.
- For each piece: a surface-nets render skin (evaluate only the blocks near the surface, one Newton step onto it), a hex lattice in the piece's principal frame with boundary nodes snapped onto the surface, and a fast barycentric embedding.

PHYSICS (XPBD on the CPU, fixed 60 Hz, 6 substeps)
- Cell-wise co-rotational shape matching (8-node cells, warm-started rotation, strain stiffening), tet volume constraints for near-incompressibility, rind firmer than flesh.
- Edge damping, plus damping of each piece's deformation relative to its rigid motion (never its fall or tumble), rolling resistance on the table, and sleep when calm.
- Piece-to-piece contact against each other's exact SDF in a best-fit frame; sleeping pieces act as walls. Floor contact with Coulomb friction.
- Hand tool: grab any piece and pull (soft patch attachment, with enough reach to drag pieces across a wide table). Scroll or a second finger twists while holding. Pinch or scroll zooms; dragging the empty table orbits the camera.

RENDERING (a photographic product shot)
- Procedural studio: pale paper sweep, overhead softbox, back-left strip light, cool fill card.
- Jelly: front faces refract the scene behind by the view-ray thickness (nearest-back-face pass), with Beer–Lambert absorption per material, milky scattering in the pith, a back-lit glow at thin edges, sugar glints, Fresnel studio reflections and GGX highlights.
- Seeds, bubbles and the knife are drawn before the jelly, so they are seen refracted through it.
- Normals follow the jelly's local deformation (cofactor of the node-averaged deformation gradient).
- A soft key shadow coloured by what the light crossed first (rosy through flesh, dark through rind), plus contact occlusion from a top-down height map. MSAA, Khronos PBR Neutral tone mapping.

UI (editorial, like a material study)
- Kicker "Material Studies / No. 010" and a big italic serif title "Whole / Melon."
- A panel with Tool (Hand / Knife), Variety, Firmness and Internal damping sliders, Nudge, Reset, ¼ speed, Show mesh and Pause.
- Live readouts: mass, volume %, kinetic energy, piece count. A collapsible "Inside the experiment" note.
- Responsive down to phones.

Quality bar: it should look and move like a real glossy jelly watermelon, and every cut face should look like a sliced jelly melon with seeds just under the surface. Test headlessly with screenshots: the whole melon, mid-cut, many pieces, a close-up of a cut face, and mobile.

title: Liquid glass web hero section
text: Access this, plus 500+ website prompts. 100+ 3D scenes, 100+ interactive gradients, 300+ backgrounds, motion sections. This prompt: https://motionsites.ai/?prompt=design-world Build a single standalone index.html file (inline CSS + inline JS, no local assets, no build step) containing ONE full-screen hero section: a black "Design World" landing hero with a rotatable 3D glass cuboid in the centre that refracts a huge background headline with chromatic dispersion. Recreate it exactly to the spec below. ================================================== 1. EXTERNAL RESOURCES (use these exact URLs) ================================================== - Font: Google Fonts Poppins, weights 300/400/500/600/700/800          - Three.js r169 via importmap:   "three": "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three@0.169.0/build/three.module.js"   "three/addons/": "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three@0.169.0/examples/jsm/"   Imports: GLTFLoader (loaders/GLTFLoader.js), mergeVertices + mergeGeometries (utils/BufferGeometryUtils.js), RoundedBoxGeometry (geometries/RoundedBoxGeometry.js). - 3D model (rounded cube GLB, CORS-enabled, load directly, do NOT download or replace):   const MODEL_URL = 'https://d8j0ntlcm91z4.cloudfront.net/user_38xzZboKViGWJOttwIXH07lWA1P/hf_20260929_212926_92423081-b0e4-4f5a-b650-14af6c05c058.glb';   If it fails to load, fall back to new RoundedBoxGeometry(1, 1, 1, 8, 0.12). Page : "Design World — Explore New Ideas". ================================================== 2. PAGE STRUCTURE (HTML) ================================================== <section class="hero" id="hero">   <canvas id="scene" aria-label="Rotatable glass cube. Drag to rotate."></canvas>   <div class="ui">     <h1 class="sr-only">Explore New Ideas</h1>     <header class="nav">       <a href="#" class="logo"><i class="logo-mark"></i><b>Design</b><span>World</span></a>       <ul class="nav-links"><li><a>Home</a></li><li><a>Portfolio</a></li><li><a>Contact Us</a></li></ul>     </header>     <div class="arrows">       <button class="arrow" id="prev">[left-arrow SVG]</button>       <button class="arrow" id="next">[right-arrow SVG]</button>     </div>     <nav class="dots"><button class="dot"></button><button class="dot active"></button><button class="dot"></button></nav>     <p class="tagline">Let's Build the<br>Future of <strong>Design.</strong></p>     <div class="cta-row">       <a href="#" class="cta">Explore Now</a>       <span class="cta-line"></span>       <span class="count" aria-hidden="true">07</span>     </div>     <div class="loader" id="loader">Loading model</div>   </div> </section> Arrow SVGs: viewBox 0 0 24 24, fill none, stroke currentColor, stroke-width 2.6, round caps/joins.   prev path: "M19 12H5M11 6l-6 6 6 6"    next path: "M5 12h14M13 6l6 6-6 6" IMPORTANT: The big "Explore / New / Ideas" headline is NOT HTML text. It is drawn onto a 2D canvas inside WebGL so the glass cube can refract it (see section 4). The HTML only has a visually hidden <h1> for accessibility. ================================================== 3. CSS (exact values) ================================================== :root { --bg:#000; --fg:#fff; --pad-x: clamp(20px, 6.95vw, 120px) } html, body { height:100%; background:#000; color:#fff; font-family:'Poppins',sans-serif; -webkit-font-smoothing:antialiased } .hero { position:relative; width:100%; height:100vh; height:100svh; min-height:520px; overflow:hidden; background:#000 } #scene { position:absolute; inset:0; width:100%; height:100%; display:block; cursor:grab; touch-action:none } #scene.dragging { cursor:grabbing } .ui { position:absolute; inset:0; pointer-events:none; z-index:2 }   /* drags pass through to the canvas */ .ui a, .ui button { pointer-events:auto } .sr-only { position:absolute; width:1px; height:1px; overflow:hidden; clip:rect(0 0 0 0); white-space:nowrap } NAV .nav { position:absolute; top:clamp(24px,4.7vh,40px); left:var(--pad-x); right:var(--pad-x); display:flex; align-items:center; justify-content:space-between } .logo { display:flex; align-items:center; gap:8px; color:#fff; text-decoration:none; font-size:15px; letter-spacing:-0.01em } .logo-mark { width:20px; height:40px; background:#fff; border-radius:0 20px 20px 0 }   /* white "D" half-circle */ .logo b { font-weight:700 }   .logo span { font-weight:400 } .nav-links { display:flex; gap:clamp(20px,4.1vw,60px); list-style:none } .nav-links a { color:#fff; text-decoration:none; font-size:15px; font-weight:500; position:relative } .nav-links a::after { content:''; position:absolute; left:0; right:0; bottom:-4px; height:1px; background:currentColor; transform:scaleX(0); transform-origin:right; transition:transform .35s ease } .nav-links a:hover::after { transform:scaleX(1); transform-origin:left } ARROWS (top-right, left of the dots column) .arrows { position:absolute; top:18.9%; left:76.7%; display:flex; gap:32px; transform:translate(-19px,-50%) } .arrow { width:38px; height:38px; border-radius:50%; border:2.5px solid #fff; background:transparent; color:#fff; display:grid; place-items:center; cursor:pointer; transition:background .25s, color .25s } .arrow svg { width:18px; height:18px } .arrow:hover { background:#fff; color:#000 } PAGINATION DOTS (vertical, right edge) .dots { position:absolute; right:calc(var(--pad-x) - 7px); top:49.4%; transform:translateY(-50%); display:flex; flex-direction:column; gap:33px } .dot { width:14px; height:14px; border-radius:50%; border:2px solid #fff; background:#fff; cursor:pointer; transition:background .25s } .dot.active { background:transparent }   /* active = hollow ring, middle one active by default */ TAGLINE (bottom-left) .tagline { position:absolute; left:var(--pad-x); bottom:clamp(40px,7.5vh,70px); font-size:clamp(24px,2.65vw,44px); line-height:1.2; font-weight:300; letter-spacing:-0.01em } .tagline strong { font-weight:700; display:block } CTA ROW (button → horizontal line → giant outlined "07" bleeding off the right edge) .cta-row { position:absolute; left:45.6%; right:-1vw; top:88.7%; transform:translateY(-50%); display:flex; align-items:center } .cta { flex:none; padding:0 15px; height:48px; display:inline-flex; align-items:center; border:1.5px solid rgba(255,255,255,.85); border-radius:6px; background:rgba(0,0,0,.15); color:#fff; font-size:14px; font-weight:400; text-decoration:none; cursor:pointer; transition:background .25s, color .25s } .cta:hover { background:#fff; color:#000 } .cta-line { flex:1; height:1.5px; background:rgba(255,255,255,.8); min-width:40px } .count { flex:none; font-size:clamp(140px,19.8vw,360px); font-weight:400; line-height:1; letter-spacing:-0.02em; color:transparent; -webkit-text-stroke:1.5px rgba(255,255,255,.9); transform:translateY(6%); user-select:none } LOADER .loader { position:absolute; left:50%; top:50%; transform:translate(-50%,-50%); font-size:12px; letter-spacing:.2em; text-transform:uppercase; opacity:.6; transition:opacity .6s } .loader.done { opacity:0 } RESPONSIVE @media (max-width:900px), (max-aspect-ratio:1/1) {   .arrows { left:auto; right:var(--pad-x); top:15%; transform:translateY(-50%); gap:14px }   .tagline { bottom:clamp(150px,20vh,220px) }   .cta-row { left:var(--pad-x); right:-3vw; top:auto; bottom:24px; transform:none }   .count { font-size:clamp(120px,22vw,200px) } } @media (max-width:640px) {   .nav-links { gap:16px }   .nav-links a, .logo { font-size:13px }   .dots { gap:20px; right:16px }   .dot { width:10px; height:10px }   .cta-row { right:-8vw }   .count { font-size:120px } } @media (max-width:420px) { .nav-links li:nth-child(2) { display:none } }   /* hide "Portfolio" */ No horizontal page scroll at any width. ================================================== 4. WEBGL SCENE (Three.js) ================================================== Renderer: WebGLRenderer({ canvas:#scene, antialias:true, alpha:false }), clearColor #000, outputColorSpace SRGBColorSpace, pixelRatio = min(devicePixelRatio, 2). Camera: PerspectiveCamera(fov 30, aspect W/H, 0.1, 100) at (0,0,10) looking at origin. 4a. Background headline (drawn into an offscreen 2D canvas → CanvasTexture) - Canvas size = viewport × DPR, filled #000. - mobile = (W < 768) || (W/H < 1). - fontSize fs = min(H*0.21, W*(mobile ? 0.21 : 0.118)); font = `800 ${fs}px Poppins`.   If the widest line is wider than W*(mobile ? 0.9 : 0.5), scale fs down to fit. - Lines: "Explore", "New", "Ideas". Fill #e9e9e9, textAlign center, baseline alphabetic. - Centre x = W*(mobile ? 0.5 : 0.505); centre y = H*(mobile ? 0.45 : 0.468).   Line gap = fs*1.07; cap height ≈ fs*0.7. Line i (0..2) baseline y = cy + cap/2 + (i-1)*gap. - Texture: colorSpace SRGB, LinearFilter, no mipmaps. Redraw on resize and on document.fonts 'loadingdone'. - Show it with a fullscreen quad (PlaneGeometry(2,2), ShaderMaterial, vertex outputs position.xy directly, fragment = texture2D(uTex, vUv) followed by #include <colorspace_fragment> ON ITS OWN LINE; depthTest/depthWrite false; frustumCulled false) in its own bgScene. - Wait for fonts before first draw: Promise.race([Promise.all([document.fonts.load('800 100px Poppins'), document.fonts.ready]), 2500ms timeout]) then layout() + start loop. 4b. Model loading - GLTFLoader.load(MODEL_URL). Traverse gltf.scene; for each mesh: clone geometry, delete 'uv','color','tangent' attributes, mergeVertices(g, 1e-4), computeVertexNormals(), applyMatrix4(mesh.matrixWorld). Merge all parts with mergeGeometries. - Centre the geometry on its bounding box and scale uniformly so its largest dimension = 1. - Scene graph: scene → pivot (screen position + scale) → spinner (rotation) → cube mesh. On load add class "done" to #loader. 4c. Cube placement (in layout(), on load and on resize) - visH = 2*tan(fov/2)*10; visW = visH*aspect. - Screen-fraction centre: sx = mobile ? 0.5 : 0.517, sy = mobile ? 0.45 : 0.488.   pivot.position = ((sx-0.5)*visW, (0.5-sy)*visH, 0). - On-screen edge length px = min(H*0.44, W*(mobile ? 0.45 : 0.29)); pivot.scale = (px/H)*visH. - Initial spinner rotation: Euler(-0.42, 0.62, 0.18). 4d. Glass material — custom ShaderMaterial, screen-space refraction with 6-band chromatic dispersion, rendered in two passes (back faces, then front faces). Vertex shader:   varying vec3 vNormal; varying vec3 vEye;   worldPos = modelMatrix*position; mvPos = viewMatrix*worldPos; gl_Position = projectionMatrix*mvPos;   vNormal = normalize(normalMatrix*normal); vEye = normalize(http://mvPos.xyz); Fragment shader:   uv = gl_FragCoord.xy / uResolution (drawing-buffer size).   n = normalize(vNormal); if (uBackside > 0.5) n = -n;   // do NOT use gl_FrontFacing, three.js flips winding for BackSide   eye = normalize(vEye).   LOOP = 16 iterations; slide = i/LOOP * 0.045.   For each band compute refract(eye, n, 1.0/ior) with iorR/Y/G/C/B/P and sample uTexture at     uv + refr.xy * (uRefractPower + slide*k) * uChromatic, with k = 1 (R), 1 (Y), 2 (G), 2.5 (C), 3 (B), 1 (P):     r = tex(R).x*0.5     y = (tex(Y).x*2 + tex(Y).y*2 - tex(Y).z)/6     g = tex(G).y*0.5     c = (tex(C).y*2 + tex(C).z*2 - tex(C).x)/6     b = tex(B).z*0.5     p = (tex(P).z*2 + tex(P).x*2 - tex(P).y)/6     R = r + (2p + 2y - c)/3;  G = g + (2y + 2c - p)/3;  B = b + (2c + 2p - y)/3     color += vec3(R,G,B)   color /= LOOP; saturation adjust: mix(luma(color), color, uSaturation) with luma weights (0.2125, 0.7154, 0.0721).   Specular (Blinn-Phong, light vector = normalize(-light), view = -eye):     spec = specular(uLight, uShininess, uDiffuseness) + 0.6 * specular(vec3(1,1,-1), uShininess*0.6, uDiffuseness*0.5)     spec(x) = pow(max(dot(n,halfVec),0), shininess) + max(0,dot(n,lightVec))*diffuseness     color += spec * (backside ? 0.35 : 1.0)   Fresnel: f = pow(1.0 + dot(eye, n), uFresnelPower); color = mix(color, vec3(1), f * (backside ? 0.25 : 0.55)).   color += vec3(0.004, 0.005, 0.007). gl_FragColor = vec4(color,1); then #include <colorspace_fragment> on its own line. Uniform values:   uIorR 1.15, uIorY 1.16, uIorG 1.18, uIorC 1.22, uIorB 1.22, uIorP 1.22,   uRefractPower 0.30 (front) / 0.22 (back), uChromatic 0.5, uSaturation 1.08,   uShininess 90, uDiffuseness 0.02, uFresnelPower 5.0, uLight (-1, 1, 1),   uBackside 0 (frontMat, side FrontSide) / 1 (backMat, side BackSide). 4e. Render pipeline (every frame) - Two WebGLRenderTargets sized to drawing buffer (W*DPR × H*DPR), type HalfFloatType, default (linear) colour space: rtBack, rtFront. - backMat.uTexture = rtBack.texture; frontMat.uTexture = rtFront.texture.   1) render bgScene → rtBack   2) render bgScene → rtFront, then (autoClear=false) cube with backMat → rtFront   3) render bgScene → screen, then (autoClear=false, clearDepth) cube with frontMat → screen - This gives the look: text seen through the cube is magnified, mirrored and split into blue/yellow fringes, inner rounded edges of the cube are faintly visible, and the bevelled edges glow white. ================================================== 5. INTERACTION & ANIMATION ================================================== - Drag to rotate (pointer events on the canvas, setPointerCapture):   dx = Δx*0.008, dy = Δy*0.008; apply as world-space rotation: premultiply spinner.quaternion by axisAngle(Y, dx) then axisAngle(X, dy).   Track velocity per 16.67ms frame; add class "dragging" to the canvas while dragging. - Inertia after release: keep applying velocity, damped by 0.94^(dt*60) per frame. - Idle drift: 0.6s after release, blend in a constant slow rotation of 0.0035 rad/frame around Y and 0.0012 rad/frame around X (blend ramps 0→1 over 1s). It also runs from page load. - Prev/Next arrow buttons: smoothly rotate the cube -90°/+90° around Y (ease: each frame apply remaining*min(1, 0.09*dt*60) until remaining < 0.0005). Cancels inertia; dragging cancels the spin. - Dots: clicking a dot makes it the only .active one (hollow ring). - Hover transitions: nav link underline wipe (.35s), arrow and CTA buttons invert to white bg / black content (.25s). - Clamp frame dt to 0.05s. Recompute layout (renderer size, camera aspect, render-target sizes, uResolution, headline canvas, cube position/scale) on window resize. ================================================== 6. LAYOUT REFERENCE (desktop 1440×806) ================================================== - Logo at (100, 38), 40px tall. Nav links right-aligned, right edge ≈ 1340, vertical centre ≈ 58. - Arrow circles centred at ≈ (1105, 152) and (1175, 152). - Dots at x ≈ 1340, y ≈ 351 / 398 / 445 (middle one hollow). - Headline "Explore / New / Ideas" centred at x ≈ 727, ~170px ExtraBold, baselines ≈ 272 / 445 / 637. - Glass cube occupies ≈ x 510–1000, y 145–600, slightly right of centre, overlapping the headline. - Tagline "Let's Build the / Future of / Design." at left 100, bottom ≈ 60px, ~38px, Light with Bold "Design.". - "Explore Now" button at (657, 691), 48px tall; a 1.5px line runs right to a huge outlined "07" whose "0" starts at x ≈ 1140 and whose "7" is clipped by the right and bottom edges. - Pure black background, all UI white. Mobile (≤767px or portrait): headline and cube centred at 50% x / 45% y, headline up to 90% width, arrows move under the nav on the right, tagline sits above the CTA row, and the CTA row is pinned 24px from the bottom with "07" partly off-screen on the right. Output: one complete index.html, nothing else.

title: AI video editing workflow comparison
text:
I gave Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra and Fable 5.1 the same raw video, the same brief and my real YouTube editing process (the one I use for my own videos):

1. Give each model the same footage and reference.
2. Ask to cut the pauses and turn your words into visuals.
3. Review the first 10 seconds, then fix it round by round.

title: Gummy squid render: Opus 5.5 vs GPT-6.1 Sol
text:
PROMPT:
PROMPT:
Create “Squid Jelly” — a beautiful, interactive 3D gummy squid that users can grab, stretch, and squish directly in their browser. Deliver a complete standalone HTML file using genuine WebGPU.

ART DIRECTION

Make the squid look like a premium translucent gummy candy:
- An elongated, tapered mantle with a rounded tip.
- Two broad, thin, diamond-shaped side fins.
- Eight shorter curled arms and two longer feeding tentacles with rounded club-shaped tips.
- Small suction cups and a cute, understated face.

Use a warm off-white background, soft studio lighting, and a subtle ground shadow. Keep the squid large and centered, with an elegant, uncluttered composition.

GEOMETRY

Generate all geometry procedurally. No external models or image files.

Connect the arms, tentacles, and fins smoothly to the body. Their roots must remain embedded and attached during strong pulls, with no visible gaps or floating parts.

Suction cups and eyes must follow the deforming surface. Give the fins a thin, flexible profile and the longer tentacles slender shafts with thicker tips.

JELLY MATERIAL

Create convincing glossy, translucent jelly:
- Thickness-dependent color absorption.
- Refraction and soft internal light scattering.
- Smooth studio reflections and delicate rim highlights.
- A few tiny bubbles embedded inside the material.
- Richer color in thick areas and greater translucency along thin fins and tentacle tips.

Avoid opaque plastic, washed-out colors, blown-out highlights, visible mesh seams, and flickering transparency.

SOFT-BODY PHYSICS

Use a stable mass-spring or position-based dynamics simulation with approximate volume preservation.

The mantle should feel soft but substantial. Arms should bend independently, while long tentacles and fins should be more flexible.

Let users grab the body, fins, or tentacles at the clicked location. Pulling must deform the nearby geometry first, with the rest following elastically. Do not fake softness by scaling or rotating the entire model.

On release, the squid should wobble, recover its shape, and gradually settle. Include gravity, floor collisions, friction, and damping. Prevent appendages from passing through the floor.

Use fixed simulation steps, bounded stretching, and robust attachment constraints so repeated strong pulls cannot tear the model apart or destabilize the simulation.

INTERACTION

- Left-click or touch the squid to grab and stretch it.
- Right-drag or drag empty space to gently orbit the camera.
- Support limited zoom and mobile touch controls.
- Keep camera gestures separate from object dragging.

Add:
- Give it a nudge
- Reset
- Reset view
- Pause
- Firmness slider
- Internal damping slider
- ¼ speed toggle
- Show mesh toggle

Provide three material palettes: Coral, Lagoon, and Grape. Switching colors must not reset the simulation.

INTERFACE

Use a minimal editorial layout:
- Top left: small “MATERIAL STUDIES” label.
- Large italic serif heading: “Squid Jelly.”
- Caption: “A little ink. A little wiggle. A very sweet sea creature.”
- Top right: WebGPU status indicator.
- Right side: compact “THE SPECIMEN” control panel.
- Bottom left: a short interaction hint.

Use clean sans-serif controls, thin borders, and generous whitespace. Adapt the layout for mobile without covering the squid.

QUALITY AND PERFORMANCE

Use real 3D geometry and native WebGPU rendering with WGSL shaders, not a 2D imitation or prerecorded animation.

Reuse meshes and buffers. Do not reconstruct geometry during dragging. Prioritize stable interactions and smooth performance.

Test strong pulls, repeated releases, appendage attachments, floor collisions, palette changes, pause, reset, and camera controls.

Provide a clear fallback message if WebGPU is unavailable.

Deliver the full working HTML, not a mockup or code fragment. The result should feel like a little living gummy toy: glossy, weighty, flexible, and irresistibly satisfying to stretch.

title: Interactive jelly press toy
text:
PROMPT:
Create "Jelly Press": a single-file interactive 3D toy in HTML (all JS, CSS and WGSL shaders inline, no external assets except Google Fonts). Render with WebGPU; if WebGPU or an adapter is missing, show a clean fallback message instead of a blank page.

CONCEPT
Four translucent gummy jellies shaped like fruit slices sit one at a time on the steel bed of a hydraulic press. The player holds a big red button to lower the press. The jelly squashes and spreads, the pressure gauge climbs, and somewhere past half its height it bursts into pieces. After the burst the game does NOT end: the player can grab the pieces, drag them, throw them around, and squash them again.

THE JELLIES (chips at the bottom, keys 1–4)
1. Watermelon wedge (half-disc slab): red flesh with dark teardrop seeds, a pale rind band, a green striped skin.
2. Orange slice (half-disc): orange pulp segments separated by thin white membranes, pale pith, orange peel.
3. Fig half: pink flesh full of small golden seeds, a cream layer, a dark purple skin.
4. Pineapple ring: golden fibrous flesh with radial streaks and a hole in the middle.
Each jelly should look like real gummy candy: subsurface scattering, soft translucency, glossy specular highlights, soft shadows on a warm studio floor (cream/beige, tone-mapped).

PHYSICS (CPU, fixed 60 Hz step)
- XPBD tetrahedral soft body with 8 substeps: co-rotational per-tet shape matching, per-tet volume constraints, hard edge strain limits (0.35×–1.8×), edge velocity damping, floor contact with Coulomb friction, rolling resistance, and gentle settling when nearly still.
- Render mesh skinned on the CPU through barycentric embedding in the tets; normals recomputed from triangles every frame.
- The press die is a kinematic round platen (radius ~1.05, rounded edge, a thickness, a ram above it). It acts as a ceiling with friction below, a shelf on top, and a side wall at its rim. The two press posts are solid.
- Pressure readout in bar comes from the platen's contact load, scaled per fruit.

THE BURST
- Break at a random squash between 52% and 66% of the jelly's height.
- Plan the fracture in the background shortly after each round starts, so the burst itself is instant.
- 5–7 big pieces from 3D Voronoi cells with slightly tilted walls. On 3–4 of them, a far corner is chipped off by two cutting planes and split further into 2–4 small chips, which leaves jagged, notched edges.
- Assign tets to cells by centroid. Duplicate particles per chunk. Merge tiny islands into their neighbours.
- The new body adopts the old positions and velocities.
- Clip the skin triangles against each cell's half-spaces, and fill every cut face with a clean flat cap showing the fruit's interior (flesh, seeds, membranes). No stretched triangles, no holes.
- Kick pieces outward and upward from the press. Small chips fly faster and higher and tumble with random spin.
- Show a big italic verdict for about 2.5 s, then fade it: "Splat." (melon), "Squeezed." (orange), "Well, that's jam." (fig), "Crushed." (pineapple). Include a stat line: "Gave up at N bar and N% of its height."

AFTER THE BURST: PLAY MODE
- Picking: ray/triangle test against the skinned mesh, with a forgiving screen-space fallback for touch.
- Grabbing pins the grabbed patch (radius ~0.4, only particles of that chunk) to a target on a camera-facing drag plane. Small chips move whole; big pieces stretch and swing like jelly.
- Releasing throws the piece with the pointer's velocity.
- Pieces collide with each other. A particle found inside another chunk's tet is pushed out through that chunk's nearest skin face, with friction. Use a chunk AABB broad phase and a spatial hash of skin tets.
- Pieces stay on stage: side walls, plus an invisible front edge so nothing ends up under the controls or behind the camera.
- The press still works: hold to squash the pieces again (no second fracture); Raise lifts the platen.
- Wet "plop" sounds on landings; a small squelch on grab.
- Cursor: open hand over pieces, closed hand while dragging. Dragging empty space orbits the camera.

UI (editorial, minimal)
- Masthead top-left: "JELLY PRESS" in bold condensed caps, with "PRESS" filled in yellow/black hazard stripes. Subtitle: "Four gummies. One hydraulic press."
- Top-right: Reset and Sound toggle.
- Bottom deck:
  - Caption line with escalating captions while pressing: "Contact." → "It's fine. It's jelly." → "Getting wider." → "That's a pancake now." → "It's making a noise." → "Please."
  - Circular pressure dial (0–400 bar arc, red zone) around a red HOLD button, a Raise button, and a big numeric bar readout.
  - Fruit chips with icons.
- In play mode the caption slot shows "Grab a piece. Throw it." with small "Press again" and "Next jelly" buttons.
- Controls: hold Space or ArrowDown to press, ArrowUp to raise, R to reset, 1–4 to pick a fruit. Wheel zooms; double-click resets the view.
- Camera: low bench-level view; the press frame yaws per fruit so the posts never block the jelly. Framing adapts so the jelly sits between masthead and deck; works on phones (portrait) with a narrower stage.

SOUND (procedural Web Audio, no files)
Hydraulic motor hum that rises with pressure, wet squelches, occasional creaks at high pressure, a valve clunk when the platen stops, a loud burst, soft plops on landing. Unlock on first interaction.

QUALITY BAR
- Smooth 60 fps on a laptop.
- Background warm-up of the other fruits' meshes and shaders so switching is instant.
- Respect prefers-reduced-motion.
- Accessible labels, a gauge with role=meter, focus-visible outlines.
- No console errors. The page never goes blank.

title: Arcane-style Blender animation
text:
Someone shared a prompt for it a while back, but I forgot to post this. 

```
TITLE: "SPARK"

An around 15-second 3D animated shot in the painterly style of the show Arcane (Fortiche).

Made in Blender, or any other tool if superior. Widescreen, no dialogue.

GOAL

The top priority is replicating Arcane's visual and animation style as perfectly as possible, in every way. Someone watching should believe it came from the same studio.

Take as much time and effort as needed. Replicate the technique and look perfectly. Spend as much time as needed, ensuring it's perfect in every way.

SCENE (loose — adapt freely)

A small mechanical creature (not humanoid), something like a brass-and-crystal moth, wakes up on a cluttered inventor's workbench at night. Its crystal core ignites with glowing energy, and it bursts into the air in a swirl of sparks. Change the details, framing, or action if something else shows off the style better. You can animate something else completely different if you want—anything you pick, whatever you can do best—that will also look identical to Arcane.

PROCESS

1. RESEARCH: Before building anything, study Arcane's style in depth. Find references and breakdowns of Fortiche's technique (interviews, making-of material, artist breakdowns). Write down every defining element: textures, shading, line work, color, lighting, frame rate, effects, camera, compositing.

2. STYLE GUIDE: Turn that into a written checklist and a small style frame (a single still image) before animating. Compare it side by side with reference stills and revise until it matches.

3. BUILD: Model, texture, light, and animate following the checklist.

4. REVIEW: Compare frames against Arcane references repeatedly. List every difference you can see and fix it. Repeat until no noticeable differences remain.

STYLE ELEMENTS TO MATCH (at minimum)

- Hand-painted textures with visible brushstrokes on every surface; nothing looks procedural or photographic.

- Stylized, painterly shading with designed light/shadow shapes, not realistic falloff.

- Animation on 2s for characters/objects, with strong poses, snappy timing, anticipation, and smear frames; camera moves smooth on 1s.

- Hand-drawn 2D effects (sparks, energy, smoke, glints, glow) layered over the 3D, animated on 2s with graphic shape language.

- Bold, moody color: warm light vs. saturated glowing accents, rich colored shadows, strong rim light, bloom.

- Painterly compositing: brush-like filtering, grain, subtle texture over the image.

- Cinematic camera: shallow depth of field, purposeful movement, weight on impacts.

SOUND

Detailed, cinematic sound design that matches the action and mood.

Make everything as good as possible: animation, models, textures, effects, lighting, and sound. Use any tools or programs needed. You may study references online and imitate techniques, and copy things, but do not directly use assets you did not create. Keep the whole shot in one consistent style so the 3D, painted textures, and 2D effects feel like a single hand-crafted image.

Do not use memory or previous chats.

You can use any other tools, programs, plugins, literally anything. Use anything at your disposal.

You can use different processes than outlined in this, or animate something else than described, but it should absolutely look as close as possible to the TV show Arcane. Make it perfect in every way and identical.
```

title: Interactive 3D stained-glass hibiscus flower
text:
Create a beautiful, interactive 3D browser artwork of a single stained-glass hibiscus flower.

Use the attached leaf as a reference for material delicacy, intricate veins, translucent colours and restrained presentation. Create an original flower composition.

The flower is the entire experience. It fills most of the viewport against a quiet, near-black charcoal background.

FLOWER

Create five broad, organically shaped petals with gently ruffled edges, subtle asymmetry and graceful curvature. Arrange them into a convincing three-dimensional hibiscus, with natural overlap and a clearly visible centre.

Each petal is made from thin, luminous stained glass. Blend ruby pink, coral, pale peach and honey amber within the glass, with delicate marbling and fine branching veins radiating from its base.

Use extremely thin antique-gold seams and a finely beveled outer edge. Preserve the delicacy of the glass. Include a slender projecting central column with tiny golden anthers, a gracefully curved stem and two small translucent green leaves.

MATERIAL AND LIGHT

The glass must have visible thickness, coloured light transmission, subtle surface irregularities and crisp reflections that change with the viewing angle.

Overlapping petals should remain readable. Balance illumination so the colours stay luminous and the veins remain visible throughout rotation. Avoid large white reflections that erase the detail.

Use soft studio lighting with a warm backlight and a restrained rim light. Avoid excessive bloom, neon colour and heavy black outlines.

MOVEMENT AND INTERACTION

Start immediately with a flattering three-quarter view. Rotate slowly and smoothly so viewers can inspect the curved petals, thin edges and reverse side.

Allow dragging to orbit, scrolling to zoom, and a small pause control. Keep the flower fully framed during automatic rotation.

DELIVERY

Build actual 3D geometry rendered in the browser. Generate the geometry and textures in code.

Deliver a working preview and a downloadable, self-contained stained-glass-flower.html with all dependencies embedded.

Run the result, inspect a full rotation, and fix missing surfaces, transparency problems, clipping or washed-out lighting before finishing. Prioritize the quality of the flower over interface decoration.

title: Cinematic product launch film
text:
PROMPT:
You are an elite creative director, motion designer, product filmmaker, frontend engineer, and cinematic storyteller.

Your task is to CREATE A COMPLETE, POLISHED, PRODUCTION-READY GTM LAUNCH VIDEO FOR:

# CLAUDE SONNET 5.5

This should NOT feel like a generic AI explainer, SaaS promo, Canva presentation, or slideshow.

It should feel like a **premium cinematic technology launch film** produced by a world-class studio.

Think:

* Apple product launch film
* high-end AI research visualization
* cinematic title sequence
* sophisticated motion graphics
* premium brand campaign
* futuristic but restrained
* extremely polished
* visually mesmerizing
* editorial typography
* dramatic pacing
* exceptional sound-design thinking

The viewer should finish the video thinking:

**“This is not just a faster model. This is a fundamentally more capable everyday AI system.”**

---

# 1. CORE MESSAGE

The central narrative:

**Claude Sonnet 5.5 takes the intelligence of the Claude 5.5 generation and makes it faster, more efficient, and more practical for everyday work.**

The story should revolve around three ideas:

**INTELLIGENCE**
**SPEED**
**EFFICIENCY**

Then demonstrate what those mean in the real world:

**Code.**
**Reasoning.**
**Computer use.**
**Visual understanding.**
**Knowledge work.**
**Design.**
**Collaboration.**

Do NOT dump features onto the screen.

Instead, make the viewer EXPERIENCE the capabilities.

---

# 2. LENGTH

Create a cinematic film approximately:

**75–100 seconds**

The pacing should feel intentional.

First 10 seconds:
HOOK.

10–25 seconds:
INTRODUCE SONNET 5.5.

25–65 seconds:
CAPABILITY JOURNEY.

65–80 seconds:
SPEED + COST.

80–95 seconds:
POSITIONING + ENDING.

Do not make every section the same length.

Use pauses and negative space.

Let important statements breathe.

---

# 3. OPENING — THE HOOK

Do NOT begin with:

“Introducing Claude Sonnet 5.5”

That is boring.

Begin with a visual metaphor.

Black screen.

Almost total silence.

A tiny point of light appears.

It begins processing.

The point becomes thousands of rapidly moving particles.

The particles form fragments of:

code,
documents,
charts,
UI,
terminal commands,
images,
graphs,
text.

Everything moves extremely fast.

Then—

**silence.**

Everything freezes.

A single sentence appears:

> “What happens when intelligence gets faster?”

Pause.

Then:

# CLAUDE SONNET 5.5

Minimal.

Beautiful.

Large typography.

Subtle motion.

No cheesy effects.

---

# 4. PRODUCT POSITIONING

Introduce Sonnet 5.5 as:

**A faster, lower-cost complement to Claude Opus 5.5.**

Visually establish the Claude 5.5 family:

OPUS 5.5
SONNET 5.5
HAIKU 5.5

But Sonnet should become the visual focus.

Communicate that:

Opus 5.5 → complex work requiring sustained judgment

Sonnet 5.5 → well-scoped everyday tasks, fixing bugs, creating polished documents, slides and spreadsheets

Haiku 5.5 → high-volume, cost-sensitive applications

Do not spend too much time explaining this.

Use elegant visual hierarchy instead.

Source: Anthropic describes Sonnet 5.5 as the second model in the Claude 5.5 family and positions it as a faster, lower-cost complement to Opus 5.5.

---

# 5. THE BIG PERFORMANCE REVEAL

Create a dramatic data visualization sequence.

Start with:

SONNET 5

Then introduce:

SONNET 5.5

Show Terminal-Bench 4.0:

**10.3% → 70.6%**

Do not simply display a bar chart.

Make the number physically transform.

10.3%

The number fractures.

Explodes into particles.

Reassembles as:

70.6%

Then cut directly into visual representations of an agent working inside a terminal.

Terminal commands appearing.

Files changing.

Tests running.

Code being inspected.

Errors appearing.

Claude fixing them.

The system keeps moving.

Voiceover / typography:

**“From 10.3% to 70.6% on Terminal-Bench 4.0.”**

Then:

**“Agentic coding performance, dramatically upgraded.”**

Important:
Do not claim Sonnet 5.5 is universally superior to every model.

The source explicitly notes that benchmark scores capture only one facet of capability and that Opus 5.5 remains stronger for complex, open-ended work requiring sustained judgment.

---

# 6. CODING SEQUENCE

This should be one of the hero sequences.

Visual language:

A developer's environment.

Dark terminal.

Code.

Git diff.

Architecture diagrams.

Test results.

Logs.

Multiple windows.

Instead of showing static screenshots, create the feeling of an AI actually working.

Show:

READ

UNDERSTAND

PLAN

EDIT

RUN

TEST

FIX

SHIP

These words appear briefly as kinetic typography.

Then accelerate everything.

The interface begins moving faster.

The camera pushes through the screen.

We transition from terminal → code → architecture → finished application.

On-screen statement:

**“Understand the codebase.
Make the change.
Check the work.”**

Mention that early testers reported Sonnet 5.5 understood codebases quickly and often batched tool calls into fewer steps, reducing cost.

---

# 7. KNOWLEDGE WORK

Transition away from code.

A large pile of information appears:

PDFs

spreadsheets

earnings reports

transcripts

charts

documents

slides

The information overwhelms the screen.

Then Sonnet cuts through the noise.

Everything gets organized.

Information flows into:

ANALYZE

SYNTHESIZE

STRUCTURE

CREATE

The output becomes a beautifully designed presentation.

Show a polished operating-review deck being assembled.

Use the Anthropic example:

A public company's quarterly earnings materials + call transcripts + slide template

→

10-slide operating review.

The source says two experts judged one internal test's first draft ready to send as-is. Present this as an example, not a universal guarantee.

---

# 8. VISUAL UNDERSTANDING

Create an elegant sequence involving charts and images.

Start with a complicated chart.

Camera moves toward it.

The chart breaks apart into visual components.

Sonnet identifies relationships.

Numbers transform into explanations.

The visualization becomes understandable.

Use:

**“See the information.”**

Then:

**“Understand the information.”**

Then:

**“Act on it.”**

Reference the published Chartography score:

**61.6%**

versus

**15.6%**

for Sonnet 5.

Also show:

**80.1% OSWorld**

and the broader computer-use story.

Keep benchmark visuals tasteful.

No giant dashboard.

No spreadsheet aesthetic.

---

# 9. LONG-HORIZON / UNEXPECTED CAPABILITY MOMENT

This should be one of the film's most memorable moments.

Introduce:

**Pokémon Red**

But do it cinematically.

Old-school pixel aesthetic appears.

The camera flies into the game world.

A screenshot becomes the environment.

Sonnet interprets what it sees.

Moves.

Adapts.

Continues.

Then pull back from the pixel world into modern AI visuals.

Typography:

**“The first Sonnet model to beat Pokémon Red using only screenshots.”**

This is directly supported by Anthropic's launch page.

---

# 10. SPEED

Now change the energy of the entire film.

Everything becomes faster.

Cursor.

Terminal.

Documents.

Animations.

Responses.

Tool calls.

Words.

Then everything stops.

Huge typography:

# 30%+

A second line:

**FASTER OUTPUTS**

Then:

**Sonnet 5.5 generates outputs more than 30% faster than Sonnet 5.**

This is Anthropic's published positioning.

Use visual motion to communicate speed instead of relying on narration.

---

# 11. COST / EFFICIENCY

This should feel like the “surprise” section.

Show two parallel paths.

SONNET 5

Longer path
More tokens
More steps
Higher task cost

SONNET 5.5

Shorter path
Fewer tokens
Fewer steps
Lower task cost

Then merge the two paths into a single number:

**UP TO 30% LESS PER TASK**

The pricing should appear separately:

INPUT

**$2 / 1M tokens**

OUTPUT

**$10 / 1M tokens**

CACHE READS

**$0.20 / 1M tokens**

CACHE WRITES

**$2.50 / 1M tokens**

Do not imply the list price itself was reduced versus Sonnet 5.

The key point is task efficiency.

## Anthropic states the token prices are the same as Sonnet 5, while Sonnet 5.5 typically requires fewer tokens per task and costs up to 30% less per task in testing.

# 12. EFFORT LEVEL

Create a beautiful visual metaphor for effort.

A single Claude interface.

A slider moves:

LOW → MEDIUM → HIGH

At LOW:

FAST

At HIGH:

DEEPER REASONING

Communicate:

**Choose how much effort Claude spends.**

Show the tradeoff:

Speed ↔ Cost ↔ Quality

Anthropic notes that lower effort produces faster, lower-token responses, while higher effort allows longer reasoning and more checking.

Keep this section under 6 seconds.

---

# 13. COLLABORATION

Show a person working with Claude.

Not “human versus AI.”

Instead:

human → AI → human → AI

Rapid iteration.

A rough idea becomes:

code

document

spreadsheet

presentation

design

finished product

Use the message:

**“Better collaboration.
Faster iteration.”**

Anthropic says early testers described Sonnet 5.5 as a better collaboration partner than Sonnet 5, with speed supporting rapid iteration on less complex tasks.

---

# 14. SAFETY

Do NOT turn this into a scary cybersecurity montage.

Keep it elegant.

Show the system approaching a boundary.

A glowing perimeter appears.

Certain high-risk paths are blocked.

Routine work continues uninterrupted.

Typography:

**CAPABLE**

then:

**CONTROLLED**

Then:

**BUILT WITH SAFEGUARDS FOR HIGH-RISK USE**

Communicate that Sonnet 5.5 launches with cyber safeguards and fallbacks similar to those developed for more capable models.

Do not overstate this.

## Routine software development and most life-sciences work are described by Anthropic as unaffected by these safeguards.

# 15. FINAL SEQUENCE

Return to the original point of light.

But now it is enormous.

It contains everything we saw:

code

documents

charts

images

interfaces

terminal

research

design

All orbiting around one point.

The system contracts into a single elegant symbol.

Silence.

Then:

# CLAUDE SONNET 5.5

Underneath:

**Faster.
More capable.
More efficient.**

Then one final line:

**Built for the work between the big breakthroughs.**

Hold.

Fade to black.

Anthropic logo / Claude wordmark treatment.

End.

---

# 16. VISUAL DIRECTION

The visual quality is critical.

Use:

* cinematic depth
* volumetric light
* subtle particles
* glass interfaces
* realistic screen reflections
* macro details
* sophisticated typography
* smooth camera movement
* 3D space
* depth of field
* subtle grain
* elegant transitions
* premium UI animation
* kinetic typography
* data visualizations
* procedural motion
* intentional negative space

Avoid:

* cheesy AI imagery
* robots
* glowing brains
* generic humanoid AI
* stock footage
* cliché “future city” visuals
* excessive neon
* overused holograms
* template-style transitions
* random particles everywhere
* corporate PowerPoint aesthetics
* excessive text

The visual language should feel **intelligent, restrained, premium and modern.**

---

# 17. COLOR / BRAND

Use a restrained Anthropic-inspired palette.

Primarily:

deep blacks
warm whites
soft neutrals
subtle Claude orange accents

Orange should be used strategically.

Do not turn the entire video orange.

Typography should be editorial and premium.

Use extremely large type for important statements.

Use small precise typography for benchmark data.

---

# 18. SOUND DESIGN

Treat sound as a major part of the experience.

Create a conceptual soundscape that evolves with the intelligence of the system.

Beginning:

near silence

low-frequency ambience

tiny digital clicks

Middle:

keyboard sounds

terminal activity

subtle system pulses

data movement

rising tension

Speed section:

rapid rhythmic elements

compressed transients

increasing tempo

Final reveal:

everything drops away

single tonal hit

silence

then the final title.

The audio should feel like a film, not background music.

---

# 19. EDITING LANGUAGE

Use:

hard cuts where impact is needed

slow cinematic transitions where context matters

match cuts

particle transformations

camera push-ins

screen-to-world transitions

typographic wipes

data morphing

light-based transitions

motion blur

depth transitions

Do NOT over-transition.

Every transition should communicate a conceptual connection.

---

# 20. BENCHMARKS TO FEATURE

Prioritize the benchmarks visually instead of showing every benchmark.

Use:

Terminal-Bench 4.0
70.6%

Sonnet 5:
10.3%

FrontierCode:
46.2% Max

CursorBench:
55.5%

GDPval-AA:
1844

AA-Briefcase:
1811

Humanity's Last Exam:
64.5% with tools

OSWorld:
80.1% partial

Chartography:
61.6% no tools

These figures come from Anthropic's published benchmark table.

Do not misleadingly imply that one benchmark proves overall intelligence.

---

# 21. ACCURACY RULE

This is extremely important.

Do NOT invent:

benchmarks

customers

quotes

performance numbers

capabilities

pricing

features

comparisons

scientific claims

Do not make unsupported claims like:

“best model in the world”

“beats every model”

“AGI”

“human-level”

“revolutionary”

“the smartest AI ever”

unless explicitly supported by the provided source.

Use the supplied Anthropic source as the factual source of truth.

---

# 22. PRODUCTION QUALITY

Do NOT simply produce a storyboard.

Actually build the complete experience.

If this is being implemented as code:

1. Inspect the existing project.
2. Determine the best technology for cinematic motion.
3. Build reusable animation primitives.
4. Build the timeline as modular scenes.
5. Keep typography perfectly synchronized.
6. Make every animation deterministic.
7. Optimize rendering performance.
8. Avoid unnecessarily heavy assets.
9. Ensure the result runs smoothly.
10. Make the entire film feel authored rather than procedurally random.

The final result should feel like an actual professional launch film.

---

# 23. RESPONSIVENESS / EXPORT

Design the composition primarily for:

**1920 × 1080**

16:9 cinematic master.

But structure the scene system so it can later be adapted to:

9:16

1:1

without rewriting the entire animation.

---

# 24. IMPORTANT CREATIVE PRINCIPLE

Do not explain AI.

**SHOW AI WORKING.**

Instead of saying:

“Sonnet 5.5 is good at coding.”

Show:

problem → codebase → reasoning → changes → tests → working result.

Instead of:

“Sonnet 5.5 is good at knowledge work.”

Show:

chaotic information → understanding → synthesis → polished deliverable.

Instead of:

“Sonnet is faster.”

Show the entire world accelerating.

Make the audience FEEL the improvement.

---

# 25. NARRATION

Use extremely sparse narration.

The film should work even with the sound off.

Narration should feel like a premium technology documentary.

Short sentences.

Confident.

No marketing fluff.

Example style:

“What happens when intelligence gets faster?”

“Code.”

“Reasoning.”

“Understanding.”

“Creation.”

“Then everything moves faster.”

“Same model family.”

“Less waiting.”

“Fewer tokens.”

“More work done.”

“Claude Sonnet 5.5.”

Do NOT narrate every fact.

Let visuals carry the story.

---

# 26. FINAL EXPERIENCE

The finished result should have:

**A killer first 5 seconds.**

**A memorable middle.**

**A visually spectacular climax.**

**A clean final brand lockup.**

It should be good enough to publish as:

* an Anthropic-style launch film
* X/Twitter launch content
* a website hero video
* Product Hunt launch material
* developer marketing
* conference screens
* YouTube

The viewer should understand three things by the end:

### 1.

**Sonnet 5.5 is substantially more capable than Sonnet 5 in many evaluated tasks.**

### 2.

**It is significantly faster and more efficient.**

### 3.

**It is designed for practical, everyday professional work.**

Build the experience around those three ideas.

Do not make this feel like an advertisement.

Make it feel like **the arrival of a new piece of technology.**

title: Watermelon rubber band test: Opus 5.5 vs GPT-6 Astra
text:
PROMPT:  
Create "The Watermelon Test": a single-file interactive 3D toy in HTML. A striped watermelon sits on a warm beige floor; each tap wraps another rubber band around it, the fruit squeezes into an hourglass, and at some point it bursts. Deliver the full working HTML, not a mockup or code fragment.  STAGE AND LOOK - WebGL via Three.js (bundled inline or pinned from a CDN). No image or audio files. Google Fonts are the only external resource. - Warm studio look: page background is a soft radial gradient from #f4f0e8 (centre) to #e6dfd3 (edges). Transparent canvas over it. Floor is a shadow-catcher only, plus a soft contact-shadow blob under the fruit. One key light from above-right with soft PCF shadows, a warm fill light, a hemisphere light, and a subtle room environment for reflections. Neutral tone mapping so the greens stay clean. - Camera pitched about 23 degrees down, 28 degree FOV. Size the scene so the fruit is about 55% of the width on a portrait phone and about 40% of the height on desktop.  TYPOGRAPHY - Title "THE WATERMELON TEST" in an extra-wide bold grotesque, all caps, tracked (Archivo at 125% width). Subtitle "How much pressure can it take?" in a light italic serif (Newsreader). Small mono labels (JetBrains Mono, wide letter-spacing). Big italic display serif for the end screen (Instrument Serif). Ink #1d1a16, accent red #d2404c. Top-left title, top-right RESET and SOUND buttons with small line icons, bottom-centre HUD.  THE WATERMELON - Egg-shaped surface of revolution about 2 units long, max radius 0.74, right end slightly narrower. Rebuild its vertices and normals on the CPU every frame from a radius profile, so it can pinch. - Procedural rind shader driven by each vertex's rest position, so stripes stay glued to the fruit while it deforms: about 15 wavy dark-green stripes (#265c33 range) on pale, slightly mottled green (#aed087 range), soft stripe edges, fine grain as a bump, stripes converging into a dark pole at each end, waxy clearcoat. - On load it drops from above with a bounce and a squash, then rests. Dragging rotates it freely with inertia (trackball style). Mouse and touch.  RUBBER BANDS - Tap on the fruit adds one band at the tapped position along its long axis; taps elsewhere do nothing. Ignore taps that were drags. Also Space or Enter adds a band. Hover cursor changes over the fruit. Each tap shows a short expanding ring at the pointer (tan outline). - Bands are thin flat ribbons (width about 0.04 to 0.056) that hug the deformed surface, each tilted 1.5 to 12 degrees in a random direction so they cross. A new band starts about 1.5x too large and snaps onto the fruit with a spring overshoot. - Bands slide along the surface and stack into a bundle around their centroid. Bundle width about (0.22 + 0.0058 x N) in rest units. Each band sits at a slightly different radial layer. - Colour goes from tan (#d9a66a) toward cream (#f6e9cc) as pressure rises, strongest in the middle of the bundle, with random variation so you see both. - Squeeze depth D = 0.60 x (N/65)^1.15 pinches the fruit around the bundle (waist about half the end diameter near 53 bands), with the ends bulging slightly. Every tap adds a small spring kick. Above about 40 bands add a faint tremble.  HUD - "BANDS:" with the count (red once above 0), a caption that changes with a quick fade, and a thin progress line that fills N/65 and turns red at 40 or more. - Captions: 0 "Tap the watermelon to add pressure", 1+ "Everything seems fine.", 13+ "Probably still fine.", 28+ "Bro is under pressure.", 40+ "This feels irresponsible.", 49+ "Maybe stop."  BURST - Each round picks a random burst count between 50 and 62. On the last band: 0.34 s of violent tension (shake, bands whiten), then it bursts. Hide the fruit, shake the camera, and spawn rigid-body debris:   - 7 jagged curved rind shells (striped green outside, pale green-to-white edge, flesh inside fading from white at the rim to coral pink),   - 15 faceted low-poly red flesh chunks of varied size, flat shaded,   - about 26 flat glossy black seeds,   - the rubber bands as curly strands and loose loops,   - about 130 small pink droplets that turn into flat translucent pink splat decals on the floor when they land. - Debris physics: gravity, contact points against the floor with impulse and friction, restitution, damping, sleeping when still. Keep pieces inside the visible floor area, with some cropped at the screen edges. - After about 1.9 s fade in a centred overlay: huge italic "Well…", a small mono line "53 BANDS." with the number in red, and a black "DO IT AGAIN" button. Hide the HUD. RESET and DO IT AGAIN start a new round with a new random threshold.  SOUND (procedural Web Audio, no files) - Create the audio context only after the first user gesture. SOUND button toggles it (on by default), icon shows muted state. - Band snap: a short filtered noise click, a triangle "twang" dropping in pitch (pitch rises with pressure), and a dull low thump; small random variation each time. - A slow, quiet creak now and then once past about 30 bands. - Burst: sub thump, noise crack, wet splats, and a flurry of band snaps. Soft thuds when debris lands, rate limited. - Limit simultaneous voices and disconnect every node when it ends.  QUALITY - Works on desktop and phone (portrait and landscape), pixel ratio capped at 2, no horizontal scroll, side gutters at least 16px. Skip geometry rebuilds when nothing is moving. Fallback message if WebGL is unavailable. Visible focus states and aria labels on the buttons and canvas. Real content only, no placeholders.

title: Zelda Style 3D Scene
text:
Claude Opus 5.5 is absurdly good at 3D.

I reran one of my recent 3D experiments with Claude Opus 5.5.

Same prompt, same references, same real-world scene I had previously built with GPT-6 Astra.

The result was much better than I expected.

Put simply, for this specific use case, Claude Opus 5.5 was a clear win for me.

The biggest differences for me were instruction following and taste.

With the same references, Opus 5.5 got much closer to the Zelda Breath of the Wild-style look I was aiming for.

The layout felt more intentional.

It picked better camera angles.

Asset placement made more sense.

And I spent much less time fixing basic mistakes.

In my Astra version, I had to repeatedly correct things like tree roots not touching the ground, rough geometry being used where proper assets already existed, or objects being placed in ways that just looked wrong.

Opus 5.5 got much more of this right on its own.

The interesting part for me is that I have almost zero real 3D skills.

I mostly give references, look at the result, explain what feels wrong, and keep iterating.

With better instruction following and visual judgment, that loop becomes dramatically easier.

Still plenty to improve, especially indoors.

Next test is whether I can recreate the interior of the house with the same level of quality.

title: Interactive Black Hole Lensing Lab
text:
I asked Opus 5.5 to explain gravitational lensing by building an interactive black hole lab

One prompt for the first version, then a dynamic workflow to polish it for three rounds while I slept. This is what I woke up to: 5h 28m end to end, $90 at API prices

https://blackhole.voxyz.ai

Drag the black hole and the sky behind it bends into arcs, closing into a full ring when everything lines up

Each round ran 3 agents. Two reviewers each picked 9 to 10 issues and ranked them P0, P1, P2. The third one fixed them.
Round 1: 3D materials and lighting + UI and type
Round 2: camera motion and interaction + science-communication design
Round 3: a design director deciding whether it ships + visual QA and performance

Every P0 got fixed, the rest only if worth it. When the two reviewers disagreed, it picked one and wrote down why. It backed up before each round, checked screenshots after, and rolled back anything it couldn't fix.
