title: Far Cry 3 clone game (polished)
text:
PROMT PART 2. (first promt in previous post) 

 CLOSING THE GAP TO THE REFERENCE (Stages 6–11)

Stages 1–5 are done: the world, controller, outpost, water, sky, vegetation, hands, weapons, inventory, weather, time of day, audio and menus all work, and the layout already matches the reference. What's missing is image quality. Right now the frame looks like clean low-poly under a milky haze. The reference looks like a saturated, high-contrast, gritty, lived-in photograph. Stages 6–11 close that gap.

Global rules for Stages 6–11:
- Every new effect sits behind a quality flag. Low must stay fast.
- Don't break earlier stages: time of day, weather, rain, wetness and lightning must all still combine correctly. At the end of each stage, check Noon/Clear and Sunset/Storm once.
- Keep existing APIs compatible: getWaterHeight(x,z), addRipple(x,z,strength), setSkyState({...}), shared globals (wind, wetness, rain, time) and the effects event bus.
- Rebuild the standalone bundle after every change and do one console-error check. No test loops.
- Run each stage in a fresh session. Do only that stage.

────────────────────────
STAGE 6 — Light, atmosphere, color grading, dappled shadows (reasoning: High)
Goal: remove the milky haze and get a punchy tropical-noon frame with lace-like leaf shadows. This stage is the cheapest and has the biggest impact.

1. Haze/fog: cut daytime fog density and height sharply. Fog only lies low at the foot of the mountains and far out over the water. Aerial perspective is blue (#9cc3dc → #cfe6f5), never white. Mountains read in 3 depth layers, with more blue on each layer further back.
2. Sky: zenith ~#4f9fe0 fading to a #cfe6f5 horizon. Cumulus clouds get crisp, sunlit white tops, blue-grey undersides and a silver lining near the sun. Denser clouds, less smeared vapor.
3. Sun and ambient: stronger sun; darker, cooler ambient/hemisphere light so shadows go deep (shadowed areas at ~15–20% of lit brightness); warm bounce light from the sand.
4. Grading: an S-curve for contrast, saturation ~×1.25, slightly lower exposure, warm highlights and cool turquoise shadows. Add a contrast-adaptive sharpening pass after FXAA. Raise the bloom threshold so it never washes the frame out. God rays only through foliage, not across the whole screen. Make sure eye adaptation doesn't brighten the image back up.
5. Dappled shadows: add 1–2 palms over the shelter, with one trunk and its fronds framing the top-left of the starting view like the reference. Leaves cast alpha-tested shadows (custom depth/distance materials using the leaf mask). Also add an animated light cookie that projects leaf dapples inside the shelter and sways with the wind. Tighten the shadow frustum/cascade near the player so shadows on the table stay crisp.
6. Ambient occlusion: stronger SSAO where surfaces meet (table/deck, crates, legs, props on the table), plus small contact-shadow decals under objects.
7. First-person hands: warmer skin, a bit more fill light from the sand, and scale/position closer to the reference (large, low in frame).
Acceptance: the starting frame next to the reference has comparable contrast and saturation, a deep blue sky, and visible leaf dapples on the deck and table.

────────────────────────
STAGE 7 — FLAGSHIP WATER (reasoning: Max)
Goal: water is the star of the game, at modern AAA quality — something you'd watch for minutes. Rewrite the water module in depth, not as patches, while keeping the CPU height query (getWaterHeight) exactly in sync with the GPU surface.

7.1 Wave model
- Large swell: 6–8 Gerstner harmonics using the correct deep-water dispersion relation. The CPU height query evaluates the same harmonics (iterative inverse displacement).
- Fine surface: GPU FFT ocean spectrum (Phillips/JONSWAP) with ping-pong render targets, 128²–256², in 2–3 cascades at different scales. Output displacement, normals and a Jacobian map for foam. Low quality: 1 cascade at 64² or baked tileable normals.
- No visible tiling: non-multiple cascade sizes plus rotation. In the distance, filter normals (Toksvig/LEAN-style) instead of letting them shimmer.
- Shallow water: waves shoal (grow steeper and shorter as depth drops) and refract toward the shore along the seabed gradient. Inside the lagoon it's calm and almost mirror-like; beyond the reef it's livelier.

7.2 Optics
- Per-channel RGB Beer–Lambert absorption over the real underwater ray length (from the scene depth buffer), plus in-scattering (#1fb0b8 / #16739e). Result: 0–0.5 m of water is nearly colorless, 1–3 m is vivid turquoise (#46d6c8), 6 m and deeper is deep blue, with a sharp turquoise-to-blue edge at the reef drop-off like the reference.
- Screen-space refraction offset by the normal and scaled by depth. Use a depth test so objects above the surface don't leak into the refraction. Add subtle chromatic dispersion.
- Reflections: screen-space reflections (High) with a sky/PMREM fallback, plus a half-resolution planar reflection over the near lagoon (High) so the pier, boat and palms reflect properly. Schlick Fresnel with F0 = 0.02: clear up close, mirror-like at grazing angles.
- Sun: a tight GGX highlight plus stochastic micro-facet glitter sparkling on wave crests. A proper sun glitter path at sunset, a moon path at night.
- Subsurface scattering: backlit wave crests glow turquoise.
- The sky and clouds in reflections come from the same sky function, and clouds move in the reflection too.

7.3 Seabed, caustics, reef
- Animated caustics (layered Voronoi or a baked caustic texture with perspective warp), RGB chromatic split, intensity by depth. Project them onto everything underwater: sand, rocks, pier piles, boat hull, the player's legs. Caustics fade in shadow (sample the shadow map).
- Reef: 40–80 instanced coral/rock clusters on the lagoon floor (the dark patches in the reference), swaying seagrass, sand ripples on the bottom (normal map), scattered shells. The seabed gets its own darker wet material.
- Underwater light shafts when looking up from below the surface.

7.4 Shore and foam
- Swash: a thin sheet of water runs up the sand and drains back. It leaves a dark wet band that dries with a delay, and a bubbly foam line rides on its leading edge.
- Foam: a real procedural bubble/foam texture, not raw noise. It spawns on crests (from the FFT Jacobian), along the shoreline, and around rocks, piles and the boat (from depth difference). It persists and decays over time (an accumulation buffer on High).
- Rings of foam and small ripples around piles and rocks standing in the water.

7.5 Interactivity
- addRipple feeds a real height-field wave simulation: a 256² ping-pong grid centered on the player that scrolls with them. Stone splashes, bullet impacts, raindrops and the player's footsteps in water create rings that reflect and interfere physically.
- Wake/Kelvin-style bow waves from the player wading.
- Buoyancy: the boat, fallen crates, shells and stones bob using the height query plus the surface normal. The boat tugs at its mooring lines. Fix the boat: hull above the waterline, clearly visible next to the pier in the starting frame.
- Underwater mode (camera below the surface): water-colored underwater fog, distortion, caustic light shafts, muffled audio (emit an 'underwater' event for the audio system), and a correct half-in/half-out waterline split across the screen.

7.6 Weather and time hooks
- Expose every new parameter through water.setParams({...}), driven by the weather/time compositor: wind drives the spectrum (flat calm when clear → whitecaps in a storm), rain adds droplet rings to the height field plus surface roughness, night gives a moon path, sunset a golden path.

7.7 Performance
- High: FFT with 2 cascades at 256², planar reflection + SSR, height field at 256². Low: 1 cascade at 64² (or baked normals), no planar reflection/SSR, height field at 128². Target: water under ~4 ms per frame on a mid-range GPU at High.
Acceptance: the starting frame shows crystal-clear turquoise shallows with a visible reef and caustics, a crisp drop-off into deep blue, a living swash line on the beach, and the pier and boat reflected. A thrown stone produces physically believable interfering rings.

────────────────────────
STAGE 8 — Terrain: karst mountains, rocks, beach, jungle (reasoning: High)
1. Karst mountains: ridged-multifractal displacement on top of the current shapes, sheer vertical walls, ledges and erosion gullies. A slope-based shader: steep areas are grey limestone with vertical streaks; ledges and gentle slopes are green canopy (a crown-shaped noise with occlusion between crowns). Thousands of cheap instanced canopy billboards on the slopes (one draw call). The sea arch and rock islet use the same materials.
2. Boulders: noise-deformed rocks with sharp ridged facets, grouped in clusters of 3–7, half-buried in sand or water, moss on top, and a dark wet band at the waterline. Triplanar texturing.
3. Jungle: broadleaf trees with clumped card-based crowns; palms of different ages and leans; dense undergrowth on the right-hand slope (ferns, bushes, banana/monstera) at 3–4× the current density with LODs; vines between trees; grass along the beach edge. No more "lawn": dark soil and leaf litter under the trees.
4. Beach: wind ripples (normal map), a wet band synced with the Stage 7 swash, pebbles, driftwood, fallen palm fronds, coconuts; a gradual transition from sand to soil to jungle, with grass.
5. Move the hut and the watchtower 20–30% closer into the starting frame if it doesn't break collisions or paths.

────────────────────────
STAGE 9 — Next-level procedural materials (reasoning: High)
All generators produce albedo/normal/roughness(/AO) maps at 1024² (512² on Low), cached.
1. Old weathered wood: stretched-noise grain, knots, cracks, a different tone and UV offset per plank, dark seams, grime in the corners, sun bleaching, worn light edges (from curvature). No striped "zebra" look. Used for the deck, table, pier, crates and posts.
2. Metal: paint → chipping → rust, driven by curvature/noise masks, plus rust streaks and scratches (barrel, ammo can, lantern). The mug gets chipped enamel.
3. Fabric: canvas with visible weave, stains and faded folds. Flags in faded rust-brown (#a8352a → rust), with torn alpha edges and a dirty skull.
4. Leopard pelt: correct rosette pattern plus fur shells (4–6 layers, High only) or a dense normal map, with a jagged hide edge.
5. Rope: twisted-fiber normals, thicker, frayed ends.
6. Rock and sand: triplanar mapping, moss by normal direction; grainy sand with tiny crystal glints in the sun.
If hand-made tileable PBR texture sets exist locally, use them instead of the matching generator (and embed them in the standalone bundle).

────────────────────────
STAGE 10 — Foreground props + custom models (reasoning: Medium)
1. Load any local .glb models from the models folder through the existing loader, keeping the procedural fallback. For each model: real-world scale in meters, grounding on its surface, colliders, shadows, wetness injection, and the Stage 3 interactions (inspecting the lantern/mug/map; the crate lid opens if the model has a separate lid part, otherwise keep the procedural lid).
2. Table: make the props larger and lay them out like the reference — the AK diagonally across the whole table, the knife on the front edge, the map under the knife, the mug, the ammo can, the lantern on the right, the bottle.
3. Left side: the cot (tube frame, sagging canvas, a plump pillow), the pelt hanging over its edge, a backpack and a crate next to the cot, a rusty barrel.
4. A torn flag hanging from the canopy at the top right, like the reference; rope lashings on the posts.
5. The boat moored at the pier (buoyancy from Stage 7), a crate on the pier, mooring ropes to the piles.
6. Hut and watchtower: corrugated tin roof, canvas awning, barrels, crates.

────────────────────────
STAGE 11 — Performance + final match against the reference (reasoning: Medium)
1. An FPS/frame-time overlay (F3) with a per-pass breakdown. Budget: ≥60 FPS on High on a mid-range discrete GPU, ≥30 FPS on Low on a modern iGPU.
2. Optimize: instancing, LODs, distance culling, half-resolution for the expensive passes, cached and compressed textures, proper disposal.
3. Take one screenshot from the starting view next to the reference and do a final palette tune. Check every time-of-day × weather combination.
4. Rebuild the bundle, do one console check, update the status log.

title: Epic chronicle film: A History of Chinese Civilization
text:
Make an epic chronicle film, "A History of Chinese Civilization". You can write code to render frame by frame, then composite with ffmpeg.
Use the soundtrack as a clock: pentatonic modes, with instruments evolving from bone flute and bianzhong bells all the way to orchestra, BPM speeding up with the eras, and all cuts landing on the beat.
Alternate two art styles: line drawings on xuan paper and mud-gold on a dark ground; each volume gets one main colour and a set of patterns that evolve with the era (painted pottery pattern → taotie pattern → cloud-vapour pattern → scrolling-grass pattern → interlocking-branch pattern → meander pattern).
Each shot has one large calligraphy keyword that appears phrase by phrase, accompanied by a line drawing. Full-film HUD: a vermilion seal with the volume number at the top left, dynasty names in vertical text on the right, and a scroll-style timeline ruler with a year counter at the bottom.
Volume transitions are impact transitions, with a vermilion seal stamped down and a heavy drum and bell strike. First set the beat grid and the shot list, then render.
Maps are schematic only, and no real modern or contemporary figures are drawn. Verify the dates before delivery.

title: 55-second brand film template with archival footage
text:
<inputs>
Ask me for: a brand name, its logo (SVG or high-res PNG), one line of what it becomes in 5 years (not today's features), one coined word the film should teach (e.g. "signal"), a public-domain archival clip of the old way of doing it (http://archive.org Prelinger), an archived web page from ~2000 where people asked for things (Wayback Machine), a royalty-free song ~100-120 BPM with a real drop (Mixkit, free for commercial use), and a free ElevenLabs key for the narrator (premade voices only).
</inputs>

<direction>
An a16z x Content Rewards brand film, ~55s. It sells one feeling and one idea, never features. Real archival and real web pages, never stock footage, never product screens, never fake UI. One hero object: a 3D button with the logo embossed into it, the ONLY saturated colour in the film. Everything else white, silver, cream and archival black. Small white captions that light up word by word on the narrator's timestamps. Film texture: fresh grain every frame, halation on bright edges, soft vignette, warm lifted blacks. The brand appears at the end, never before.
Banned: stock footage, dashboards, chat UIs, feature tours, cards without real profile pictures, wobbly "worm" graph lines, random glitches, any hold longer than 1.5s, purple, rainbow gradients, orange on anything but the button.
</direction>

<structure>
Cold open (0-8s): the archival clip plays on a glowing old CRT TV with its real dialogue, captions word by word.
The past (8-17s): push into the real 2000 web page, a cursor lands on one real "wanted" post, old pages strobe one per frame, a counter ticks EVERY frame up to today's scale. Narrator: "People have always asked the internet for what they need." / "Today, there are five hundred million posts a day."
Bridge (17-30s): a galaxy of real old asks. One ask snaps to a white outline with a chip of the coined word ("We call that a signal."). Archival of people doing it by hand on the TV. Cut on each word: "Door by door. Call by call. Scroll by scroll." The narrator never stops talking between acts.
Button (30s): the button rises out of black, rim light first, colourless. "[Brand] finds the signals." A flat grey line: "this is how you find customers by hand". Hard cut to a button macro, the colour comes alive, the music drop lands on this exact frame. "and this... is with [Brand]": a steep lit curve, counters changing every frame, a glowing sine with a comet head the camera chases, then platform strikes (X, Reddit, LinkedIn, YouTube, Instagram, TikTok) each with its own counter, then the galaxy again with glowing platform logos: "Every signal on the internet." Hyperspace.
End: the tagline word by word, then "[Brand] is live.", ONE cream frame on the kick, then logo + URL in silence.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML file, 1920x1080. Everything is computed from time inside seek(t): no CSS transitions, no timers, no Math.random (seeded hash), no state between frames.
2. Button: three.js MeshPhysicalMaterial (clearcoat 1, roughness ~0.4), ACES filmic, cool + warm rim spots, room env map. Emboss the real logo by displacing a dense disc with a blurred mask of the logo, folded into the rim so corners don't show. Brushed-metal base.
3. Counters: linear on the film's global clock, so they keep running through cutaways. Tabular numerals, fixed unit label.
4. Captions: <=7 words, one idea per shot, hand-placed line breaks, one text layer on screen at a time. Grey to white over 0.2s on the word timestamps (ElevenLabs /with-timestamps).
5. Glitch = 1-2 frames, only on a real cut, always with a click. Readable things stay on screen >= 8 clean frames.
6. Render with Playwright per frame (Chromium with --use-angle=swiftshader so WebGL renders headless), finish in numpy: fresh grain per frame, halation, vignette ~0.65x at the corners, 1px chroma fringe with EDGE-CLAMPED shifts. Pipe PNGs into ffmpeg, h264, 24fps.
7. Mix: narrator 10-15dB over the music, duck -18dB while speaking, hits on the exact action frame, -14 LUFS.
</build>

<gotchas>
np.roll wraps pixels and draws coloured lines on the frame edges, so clamp instead. A 10-pattern grain bank loops visibly, generate fresh grain every frame. Measure text only after fonts load or the widths are wrong. Headless Chromium with --disable-gpu renders WebGL blank. Counters that step every 3 frames look fake. If the narrator goes quiet between acts the film feels broken, so write a bridge line for every act change.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for the inputs, then show me the script with timings and 6 stills (cold open, past, bridge, button reveal, macro on the drop, end card) before you render the full film. After every render, send me one 2fps contact sheet and fix what I call trash.
</start>

title: Prompt para Película de Palabra Hablada Cinética
text:
Create a 20.00-second kinetic spoken-word film titled “BUILD THE FLOOR.” Treat this as an original miniature speech staged entirely through typography. Every line changes the architecture of the frame. The final declaration must stand on something the earlier words physically constructed. Deliver one self-contained HTML file, 1080×1080, targeting 60fps, using SVG and/or Canvas. Embed all required assets.

ART DIRECTION
Background #102820. Paper #F4E9D5. Structural accent #F2B544. A literary editorial world with the scale and confidence of a public monument. Use a high-contrast serif for the speech, a heavy grotesque for load-bearing words, and a restrained monospace for small timing marks. No distressed protest-poster clichés, megaphones, flags, crowds, microphones, or stock footage.

ORIGINAL SPEECH — EXACT WORDS, EXACT ORDER
“We were told to wait.”
“So we learned the weight of waiting.”
“Then one voice made room.”
“Then another.”
“Now the floor belongs to us.”

Do not attribute these words to any real person. No extra slogans. The complete speech must be understandable without audio.

CENTRAL VISUAL RULE
Words have assigned architectural roles. WAIT is a lintel. WAITING is a suspended load. VOICE is a support. ROOM is an opening. FLOOR is a platform. These roles must emerge from the actual letterforms, not from separate illustrations placed behind text.

STORYBOARD
0.00–3.00 “We were told to wait.” The sentence occupies a narrow horizontal opening beneath a massive WAIT. The opening slowly compresses while the sentence remains readable. The pressure comes from the layout, not camera shake.
3.00–6.50 “So we learned the weight of waiting.” Reveal the sentence in spoken phrase groups. WAITING lowers on two fine vertical rules. Those rules become suspension cables. A baseline bends under the visual load using a controlled vector deformation.
6.50–10.00 “Then one voice made room.” VOICE enters vertically and rotates into a structural support. It lifts one end of the baseline. The counter of the O in ROOM becomes an aperture. The next composition is revealed through that aperture.
10.00–12.50 “Then another.” A second support arrives. The tilted structure levels. This is the first moment of perfect horizontal alignment in the film. Use a brief stillness to make the change feel earned.
12.50–16.00 “Now the floor belongs to us.” Earlier structural words assemble into a platform. The final sentence settles onto it. US receives emphasis through shared alignment and scale, never through a separate flashy effect.
16.00–18.00 Hold the complete declaration. A slight release of tension travels through the supporting rules. No new text. No restless decorative motion.
18.00–20.00 The camera tracks beneath the completed platform. Its underside fills the frame and becomes the opening WAIT lintel. Under full occlusion, return hidden elements to their initial positions. Reveal the exact opening composition.

CHOREOGRAPHY
Do not force the speech onto a dance beat. Use a cue sheet based on phrases, pauses, and emphasis. Phrase reveals should follow reading order. Allow at least one 400ms moment of absolute stillness. Use critically damped motion for settling loads. Use controlled elastic deformation for the baseline only. Make the changes in available space carry the emotional progression.

TYPE IMPLEMENTATION
Use actual glyph paths for structural words. Preserve counters and legibility during deformation. For transitions between unrelated words, use occlusion or matched structural edges; do not interpolate arbitrary path points. Keep the currently spoken phrase readable before it becomes architecture.

ENGINEERING
Implement window.seek(t) as a deterministic scene renderer. No accumulated physics, autonomous CSS transitions, or changing random values. Use time-remapping curves and analytic transforms. Use a 20-second periodic timeline with render(0)=render(20). Provide fixed-step access at n/60 for 1200 export frames. Audio is optional and off by default; no browser speech synthesis or autoplay dependency.

QUALITY GATE
Inspect eight representative frames. Check that the speech reads in the correct order. Check that structural transformations never destroy a line before the audience can read it. Check the final platform is visibly assembled from earlier elements. Return the complete HTML implementation.

title: Far Cry 3-style playable game prototype in Three.js
text:
PROMT:

Create a visually stunning, highly atmospheric, interactive first-person 3D game set in a small tropical lagoon with a jungle survival outpost.
The game should capture the feeling of standing alone on a beautiful tropical island, similar in atmosphere and environmental design to Far Cry 3, with modern graphics, cinematic lighting, advanced shaders, and detailed environmental interactions.
I WILL PROVIDE REFERENCE IMAGES. Use the uploaded images as the primary visual references for the environment, composition, color palette, vegetation, outpost design, lighting, and overall atmosphere. Recreate the visual mood and environmental character of the references as closely as possible.
The result should be a playable, polished first-person experience, not a static scene or a simple tech demo.
1. WORLD AND ENVIRONMENT
Build a SMALL but extremely detailed tropical lagoon.
Do not create a massive open world. Prioritize visual fidelity, environmental density, atmospheric quality, and interactivity over map size.
The scene must include:

A beautiful tropical beach with sand, small rocks, driftwood, and scattered vegetation.
A stunning turquoise ocean with realistic waves and water transparency.
Shallow coastal water transitioning naturally into deeper blue water.
Dense tropical jungle surrounding the lagoon.
Palm trees, tropical bushes, vines, ferns, tall grass, and exotic plants.
Large moss-covered rocks and weathered coastal cliffs.
A small survival outpost located directly beside the beach, partially surrounded by jungle.
Natural pathways connecting the beach, outpost, and jungle.
Small environmental details that make the location feel authentic and lived-in.
The lagoon should feel isolated, peaceful, mysterious, and slightly dangerous.
The environmental aesthetic should be strongly inspired by Far Cry 3's tropical island atmosphere, but with the graphical quality and lighting of a modern high-end game.
2. THE OUTPOST
Create a small jungle survival outpost, NOT a large military base.
It should resemble a tiny improvised shelter, wooden shack, or canvas tent built by someone surviving on a tropical island.
The outpost should feel handmade, worn, and realistic.
Include:

A small improvised wooden shelter or tent.
A simple wooden table.
A small sleeping cot or military-style bed.
An AK-47 lying somewhere inside the outpost.
A survival knife resting on the table or near the bed.
Animal skins and hides hanging from the shelter or lying on the furniture.
A wooden supply crate that can be opened.
Small storage containers.
Old backpacks and survival equipment.
Ropes, fabric, wooden planks, and improvised construction elements.
Subtle environmental storytelling through scattered personal belongings.
Everything should feel physically placed in the environment rather than randomly generated.
Make the shelter visually interesting through layered materials, shadows, ambient occlusion, fabric simulation, and carefully placed props.
3. FIRST-PERSON CHARACTER
The player controls a character from a FIRST-PERSON perspective.
The player's hands and forearms MUST be visible.
Create high-quality first-person animations:

Idle breathing.
Natural hand movement.
Walking and running animations.
Looking around.
Picking up objects.
Holding a weapon.
Throwing stones.
Using a knife.
Interacting with the environment.
The camera should have subtle, natural movement.
Avoid excessive camera shaking.
Hands must feel connected to the player's actions. They should not look like floating objects or static models.
4. STONE THROWING MECHANIC
One of the most important features is the ability to pick up and throw small stones into the ocean.
The player should be able to:

Look at a small stone on the beach.
Pick it up.
See the stone in their hand.
Aim toward the ocean.
Throw the stone using a natural first-person animation.
The stone must have realistic projectile physics.
When the stone hits the ocean, create:

A visible water splash.
Expanding circular ripples.
Small water droplets.
Appropriate splash sound.
Realistic interaction between the projectile and water surface.
Stone throwing should feel satisfying and physically believable.
Allow the player to throw multiple stones without restarting the game.
5. AK-47 INTERACTION
Place an AK-47 inside the outpost.
The player must be able to approach the weapon and pick it up.
When equipped:

Display the AK-47 in a proper first-person weapon position.
Show both hands holding the weapon.
Implement realistic weapon sway.
Implement a shooting animation.
Add muzzle flash.
Add recoil.
Add shell casing ejection.
Add realistic gunshot audio.
Add environmental bullet impacts.
Add an optional reload animation.
The player should be able to shoot at rocks, trees, wooden objects, and other environmental surfaces.
Bullets should create appropriate visual and audio effects depending on the material they hit.
There is no need to create enemy AI or a combat campaign. Focus on making the weapon interaction feel polished and satisfying.
6. KNIFE INTERACTION
Create an interactive survival knife inside the shelter.
The player can pick it up and equip it.
Implement:

First-person knife holding animation.
Idle knife animation.
Knife swing animation.
Slash animation.
Appropriate sound effects.
Natural hand and wrist movement.
The knife should feel like a proper usable first-person tool, not a static object attached to the camera.
7. INTERACTIVE OBJECTS
Make the environment feel alive and interactive.
The player should be able to interact with selected objects.
Important interactions include:
Supply crate
The player can approach a wooden crate, interact with it, and open its lid.
The lid should animate naturally.
Plants
The player can approach specific tropical plants and harvest them.
Create a small first-person harvesting animation.
After harvesting, the plant should disappear from its original location or visibly lose its harvested part.
The collected plant must be added to the player's inventory.
Inventory
Create a simple but visually polished inventory interface.
Collected plants and other pickup items should appear in the inventory with their name, icon, and quantity.
The inventory must actually work and retain collected items during gameplay.
Other objects
Allow selected small objects around the outpost to be picked up or examined when appropriate.
Use subtle interaction prompts rather than oversized UI elements.
8. WEATHER SYSTEM
Implement a functional dynamic weather system.
The player should be able to switch between:

Clear tropical weather.
Cloudy weather.
Tropical rain.
Heavy tropical rain.
Rain must affect the entire environment visually.
When rain begins:

Rain particles appear.
Rain hits the ocean and creates small surface disturbances.
Sand and rocks become darker.
Leaves and wooden surfaces become wet.
Wet materials become more reflective.
Puddles appear where appropriate.
Atmospheric fog increases.
Rain audio becomes audible.
Ocean and jungle ambience change naturally.
Use wetness shaders and physically based material transitions.
The rain should feel like an actual tropical storm, not simply particles falling in front of the camera.
9. TIME OF DAY SYSTEM
Add a dynamic time-of-day system.
Allow the player to switch between:

Early morning.
Bright tropical noon.
Golden hour / sunset.
Night.
Each time of day must produce a noticeably different visual atmosphere.
Morning should include soft lighting and atmospheric mist.
Noon should feature strong tropical sunlight, vibrant turquoise water, and deep jungle shadows.
Sunset should have warm orange light, beautiful reflections on the ocean, and cinematic shadows.
Night should have moonlight, dark jungle silhouettes, subtle ambient lighting, and a peaceful tropical atmosphere.
Weather and time of day must work together.
For example, the player should be able to experience heavy rain at sunset or a cloudy nighttime lagoon.
10. GRAPHICS AND SHADERS — EXTREMELY IMPORTANT
VISUAL QUALITY IS ONE OF THE MAIN PRIORITIES.
Make the game look like a modern, high-quality tropical exploration game.
Use as many appropriate advanced graphical techniques as possible while maintaining playable performance.
Prioritize:

Physically Based Rendering (PBR).
Realistic water shaders.
Water refraction.
Screen-space or equivalent reflections.
Realistic ocean foam.
Shoreline water interaction.
Subsurface scattering for vegetation.
Detailed foliage shaders.
Wind-driven vegetation animation.
Soft dynamic shadows.
High-quality ambient occlusion.
Cinematic global illumination where supported.
Volumetric lighting.
Atmospheric fog.
Sun shafts passing through palm leaves.
Realistic wetness shaders.
Beautiful sky and cloud rendering.
High-quality tone mapping and color grading.
Subtle bloom.
Natural exposure adaptation.
High-quality material textures.
Realistic surface roughness and normal mapping.
Make the ocean and vegetation particularly impressive.
The water should look mesmerizing, with vibrant tropical colors, natural wave movement, and beautiful sunlight reflections.
Leaves and palm trees should move naturally in the wind.
The jungle must feel lush, dense, and visually rich.
Avoid flat lighting, generic low-poly graphics, cartoon-like materials, and empty environments.
Do not sacrifice the entire frame rate just to enable expensive effects. Use optimized techniques appropriate for the chosen engine.
11. SOUND DESIGN
Create immersive tropical environmental audio.
Include:

Ocean waves.
Water moving along the shoreline.
Wind passing through palm leaves.
Jungle birds.
Tropical insects.
Distant wildlife.
Footsteps on sand.
Footsteps on wood.
Stone throwing and water splashes.
Weapon handling.
AK-47 gunshots.
Knife swings.
Crate opening.
Rain hitting leaves, sand, wood, and water.
Use spatial audio and environmental sound variations where possible.
The lagoon should feel alive even when the player does nothing.
12. CONTROLS
Implement intuitive first-person controls.
WASD — Move.
Mouse — Look around.
Shift — Sprint.
Space — Jump.
E — Interact / pick up objects.
Left Mouse Button — Shoot, swing knife, or throw a held stone.
R — Reload the AK-47.
1 — Equip AK-47.
2 — Equip knife.
3 — Equip stone, if available.
I — Open inventory.
T — Change weather.
N — Change time of day.
ESC — Pause / settings.
Provide a small, elegant interface for changing weather and time of day.
Do not clutter the screen with unnecessary HUD elements.
13. VISUAL ATMOSPHERE AND ART DIRECTION
The entire experience should capture this feeling:
You are alone in a hidden tropical lagoon.
The ocean is crystal clear.
The jungle is dense and full of life.
A small improvised shelter stands beside the beach.
Your AK-47 rests near your sleeping cot.
A knife and survival equipment lie on the wooden table.
Animal skins hang from the structure.
Sunlight passes through palm trees and reflects from the ocean.
You can pick up a stone and throw it into the sea, watching the splash and ripples disappear into the waves.
You can explore the shelter, pick up your weapon, examine objects, gather tropical plants, and watch the weather change.
The scene should be beautiful enough that the player wants to stand still and admire the environment.
The visual identity should combine:
Far Cry 3 tropical island atmosphere + modern cinematic graphics + realistic water rendering + dense, detailed jungle + immersive first-person interactions.
14. IMPORTANT DEVELOPMENT REQUIREMENTS
This must be a WORKING, PLAYABLE EXPERIENCE.
Do not simply create a beautiful static 3D render.
Implement the actual gameplay systems described above.
Prioritize a small, complete, polished environment rather than a large unfinished game.
All important mechanics should work:

First-person movement.
Visible animated hands.
Pickable and throwable stones.
Functional water splash effects.
Equippable and shootable AK-47.
Equippable and usable knife.
Opening supply crates.
Harvesting plants.
Functional inventory.
Dynamic rain.
Dynamic time of day.
Advanced environmental shaders.
Do not replace the requested systems with decorative placeholders.
If development limitations require prioritization, complete the core mechanics first, then add graphical polish.
15. REFERENCE IMAGES
I WILL UPLOAD REFERENCE IMAGES AFTER THIS PROMPT.
These images are extremely important.
Analyze them carefully and use them as the main visual guide.
Pay particular attention to:

Lagoon shape and composition.
Position of the ocean relative to the beach.
Tropical vegetation density.
Structure and scale of the outpost.
Color palette.
Lighting.
Water appearance.
Atmosphere.
Environmental details.
The final game should feel like a playable recreation of the location and mood shown in my reference images.
Do not blindly generate a generic tropical island.
Use the references to create a distinctive, carefully art-directed, immersive lagoon environment.

title: Cute creatures explain how LLMs work
text:
Create a 40-second animated video explaining how Large Language Models (LLMs) work.

Every frame must be generated from code. No stock footage. No video generators. No image editors.

The video must feature cute animated creatures that help explain the process. Make it fun, watchable, and technically accurate.

TECHNICAL REQUIREMENTS
Use Remotion (React/TypeScript) for the animation

Draw all visuals in SVG and Canvas
Use an open-source TTS voice for narration
Synthesize a light, playful score in Python
Export as MP4, 1080x1080 (square for X)
40 seconds total
VIDEO STRUCTURE

0-5s: Hook
Black screen. A small glowing dot appears in the center.

Text types out: "Ever wonder how AI actually thinks?"
The dot expands into a cute, simple creature, like a tiny round blob with big eyes. It blinks and looks around.

5-12s: Tokens (The Input)
The creature receives a sentence: "The cat sat on the..."

The sentence breaks apart into small glowing puzzle pieces, these are tokens.
Each token floats toward the creature, who catches them one by one.
Narration: "First, your words get broken into tokens, small pieces of language."
Cute detail: each token has a tiny face and waves as it flies in.

12-20s: Embeddings (The Map)
The creature holds the tokens and they transform into colorful little gems.

The gems arrange themselves into a 3D map, a colorful cloud of dots.
Similar gems cluster together. "Cat" gems are near "dog" gems. "King" gems are near "queen" gems.
Narration: "Each token becomes a point in a giant map of meaning."
Cute detail: the creature walks around the map, pointing at clusters like a tour guide.

20-28s: Attention (The Thinking)
The creature stops. Multiple tiny creatures appear around it, each one is an "attention head."

They all look at different parts of the map at once.
Lines of light connect the important tokens to each other. "The" connects to "cat." "Sat" connects to "on."
Narration: "The model pays attention to what matters, connecting the dots between words."
Cute detail: the attention creatures nod at each other as they find connections.

28-35s: Prediction (The Output)
The main creature now stands in front of a giant scoreboard.

Hundreds of possible next words appear as floating bubbles: "mat" (biggest), "floor" (small), "moon" (tiny).
The creature reaches up and picks the biggest bubble "mat."
Narration: "Then it predicts the next word and the one after that, and the one after that."
Cute detail: the creature looks proud as it picks the right word.

35-40s: The Kicker
The creature takes the new word and feeds it back into the loop.

The screen fills with a chain of words forming a sentence: "The cat sat on the mat."
The creature smiles, waves at the camera.
Text fades in: "That's how LLMs work. One word at a time."
Narration: "One token at a time. That's the whole trick."
VISUAL STYLE
Dark background (deep navy or charcoal) with soft glowing accents

Cute, simple creature design, round, big eyes, minimal detail, expressive

Tokens and gems have soft glowing edges

Colors: warm gold, soft blue, gentle pink, mint green
Lines and connections drawn in soft neon
Typography: clean sans-serif, white or light gray
Everything should feel warm, playful, and technically clear
AUDIO
TTS voiceover: warm, friendly, slightly curious tone
Script:"Ever wonder how AI actually thinks?"
"First, your words get broken into tokens, small pieces of language."
"Each token becomes a point in a giant map of meaning."
"The model pays attention to what matters, connecting the dots between words."
"Then it predicts the next word, and the one after that, and the one after that."
"One token at a time. That's the whole trick."

Background score: light, playful electronic tune with a soft bounce

Sound effects: soft pops when tokens appear, gentle chimes when connections form

OUTPUT
Export as MP4, 1080x1080
Include the code so it can be re-run with new explanations
Make it easy to add new creatures or scenes later
Build a cute, fast, visually engaging 40-second video that explains LLMs clearly and makes people smile while they learn.

title: Apple Liquid Glass style UI motion showcase
text:
PROMPT:

<role>
You are a senior UI motion designer and creative technologist. You build UI animations in code, frame-accurate, and render them to video yourself.
</role>

<inputs>
Style: Apple Liquid Glass. Reference platforms: iOS 26, iPadOS 26, macOS Tahoe 26.

Format: 1440x1440, 60fps, seamless loop.

Song: "Digital Clouds" by Alejandro Magaña (A. M.), from Mixkit, free under the Mixkit License. If the file is not attached, ask me for it and nothing else.

Tempo: about 120 BPM, 8 bars, and something happens on every beat. Measure the real tempo from the file. If it differs from 120, keep the beat map in beats and derive every time from the measured grid.

Palette: light mode system materials.
- Labels: #1D1D1F. Secondary labels: #6E6E73. Opaque surfaces: white.
- One accent, #0A84FF, used only for on, active and selected states.
- The Dynamic Island is the only pure-black element.

Canvas: a macOS Tahoe style wallpaper.
- Large, soft color fields: deep blue #1B3A8C, teal #2BB3B1, violet #7B5CFF, and a warm peach highlight #FFB38A.
- Slow parallax drift: 12px per bar at most.
- Saturated enough that the glass visibly refracts it, calm enough to sit behind text.

Font: SF Pro Display for 20px and above, SF Pro Text below 20px, if installed locally. Otherwise use Inter from Fontsource: 600 for titles, 500 for labels, 400 for body. Use -1% tracking at display sizes and tabular numbers for any number that changes.

Icons: one SF Symbols-like set drawn as SVG, medium weight matched to the adjacent text, one consistent optical size per state. Symbols needed: play, pause, speaker with 3 waves, house, heart, chart bars, person, magnifier, note, checkmark.

Pointer: an iPadOS adaptive pointer.
- A 22px translucent gray circle (#8E8E93 at 45%).
- It snaps (magnetism) into any control it hovers and becomes that control's highlight shape.
- It becomes an I-beam in text fields.
- It shrinks 10% on press.
</inputs>

<direction>
Apple keynote and WWDC Liquid Glass session-level UI motion. One element, never cut. Every state is the same element morphing its size, corner radius, material and color, while its content swaps with a short blur. The pointer drives every change with real clicks, holds and drags.

Material:
- Liquid Glass is a lens, not frosted plastic. It refracts the wallpaper, and the bending is strongest at the rim.
- Light frosting and a 10–16% white tint.
- A 1px specular rim lit from the top-left, with a fainter counter-highlight bottom-right. The highlight shifts as the element moves.
- A soft contact shadow: 0 10 30 at 12% black.
- Glass never sits on glass. Content on glass uses vibrant or solid fills.
- Corners are concentric: inner radius = outer radius − padding.
- When glass shapes split or merge, they join like droplets (smooth union), never crossfade.

Motion language:
- Apple-like springs everywhere:
  - Morphs: response 0.45, damping 0.86.
  - Presses: response 0.25, damping 0.72.
  - Pointer snap: response 0.3, damping 0.9.
- Overshoot is at most 3%.
- On press, glass lifts and swells (scale 1.06–1.12, brighter rim). It never shrinks.
- A toggle knob on hold turns into a clear, enlarged glass lens that stretches in its direction of travel.
- The tab bar selection is a glass droplet that magnifies the icons under it while dragged.
- Sliders thicken when grabbed and rubber-band past their limits.

Camera:
- Each state fills about 60% of the frame, and the wallpaper is always visible around the glass.
- Camera moves use response 0.6, damping 1.0.
- The wallpaper scales at 70% of the camera zoom for depth.

The last frame is the first frame, pointer position and velocity included.

Banned: bouncy or elastic easing, overshoot over 3%, particle bursts, neon glows, colored gradients on UI chrome (the glass specular rim is the only gradient), heavy drop shadows, glass on glass, mismatched corner radii, mismatched icon weights, emoji, crossfades between states, dead time longer than half a beat, anything that looks like a template or a Dribbble clone.
</direction>

<structure>
120 BPM, 8 bars, 32 beats. Beat map, one line per beat:

1. A glass capsule button "Continue" floats on the wallpaper. The pointer glides in.
2. The pointer snaps into the button and becomes its highlight.
3. Click: the glass lifts and swells, the rim brightens.
4. The capsule contracts into a circle and becomes a spinning activity ring.
5. The ring completes, filling in accent.
6. It morphs into a checkmark that draws itself.
7. The circle stretches into a black Dynamic Island, compact: album art on the left, a live waveform on the right.
8. Click: the island expands into Now Playing ("Digital Clouds", "A. M.", progress 0:42 / 1:41).
9. Click play: the play icon morphs into pause, with a path morph rather than a swap.
10. Grab the progress bar: it thickens, and the time labels shift out of the way.
11. Scrub forward with direct manipulation. The time counts in tabular numbers.
12. Release: the bar springs thin, and playback continues from the new position.
13. The island dissolves into a glass volume slider with a speaker icon.
14. Drag up: the fill follows the pointer, and the speaker waves appear one by one.
15. Drag past max: the whole slider rubber-bands and stretches, leading edge first.
16. Release: it springs back to its length at 100%.
17. The slider morphs into a toggle (track plus knob), off. Its label is "Focus".
18. Hold: the knob turns into a clear, enlarged glass lens that shows the track through it.
19. Flip on the beat: the lens stretches in its travel direction, and the track fills with accent.
20. The knob detaches as a droplet and becomes the selection lens of a floating glass tab bar with 4 tabs: Home, Health, Activity, Profile.
21. Drag the lens across the tabs. The leading edge stretches ahead of the trailing edge, and the icons magnify under the lens.
22. The lens settles on "Activity", and its icon turns accent.
23. The tab bar grows upward into a glass widget card titled "Activity", with concentric radii.
24. A 7-day bar chart (M T W T F S S) rises in a left-to-right stagger.
25. Hover Thursday: a glass tooltip bubble shows "8,412 steps", anchored to the bar.
26. Hover Friday: the tooltip slides over and counts to "11,036 steps".
27. ⌘Space: the card collapses into a Tahoe Spotlight bar with a magnifier icon.
28. Type "ne": the results list filters (New Note, Network, News), and rows spring in and out.
29. Type "w": "New Note" rises to the top as a selected accent row.
30. Enter: the row presses and lifts.
31. The Spotlight bar drops into a glass notification banner from the top: a Notes icon, "Note created", "now".
32. The banner contracts back into the "Continue" capsule. The pointer returns to its frame-1 position and velocity.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML file at 1440x1440. Everything is computed from time inside seek(t): no CSS transitions, no timers, no state carried between frames.

2. Springs are closed-form damped step responses with Apple parameters: ω = 2π/response, ζ = dampingFraction.
   - A value that is retargeted many times is the sum of one spring per retarget, so it stays a pure function of time.
   - Releases start from the current value and the current velocity.

3. Asymmetric edges: the tab lens, the toggle knob and the slider stretch each have their leading edge on response 0.28 and their trailing edge on response 0.42.

4. Drags are direct manipulation.
   - While held, the value is a function of pointer position, with rubber-banding past limits: offset = limit + (1 − 1/(x·0.55/d + 1))·d.
   - On release it springs back from wherever it was.

5. Glass is rendered in a WebGL2 pass, not with CSS backdrop-filter:
   - The wallpaper is drawn to a texture with a precomputed blurred mip chain.
   - Every glass shape is a rounded-rect SDF. Merging and splitting use smooth-min with k = 24px.
   - Refraction offsets the sample along the SDF gradient. The offset is strongest within 14px of the edge and scaled by lens thickness.
   - Frost is a mip-level bias.
   - Chromatic aberration is at most 1px, at the rim only.
   - The specular rim comes from the SDF normal against a top-left light.
   - The Dynamic Island is an opaque SDF in the same pass.
   - Text, icons, charts and the pointer are crisp SVG/DOM layers above the canvas, under the same camera matrix.

6. Content swaps inside a morphing container:
   - Exit takes 120ms: blur 6px, scale 0.96, fade.
   - Enter starts 60ms later with its own spring.
   - Exit and enter text never overlap.

7. Audio:
   - Analyze the song with numpy (onset envelope plus autocorrelation) for the beat grid, and start on a measured downbeat.
   - Synthesize Apple-subtle UI sounds with numpy: soft taps for clicks, ticks for scrub detents, a low detent at max volume, a keyboard click per typed letter, and a gentle two-note chime for the notification.
   - Place each sound on its measured peak, mixed about 18dB under the track.

8. Render with Playwright at 1440x1440 with 4 subframes per frame (240fps).
   - Blend to 60fps with ffmpeg: tmix=frames=4, select='not(mod(n\,4))', setpts=N/60/TB.
   - Encode H.264 yuv420p, crf 16, with AAC 192k and faststart.

9. Before the full render, render one still per beat (32) as a contact sheet. Fix anything off the grid, cramped, illegible over the wallpaper, or with non-concentric radii.
</build>

<gotchas>
- The glass and the DOM layers must share one camera matrix per frame, or the content drifts off its glass.
- Glass over a bright wallpaper patch kills legibility. Add an adaptive dim under the text based on sampled wallpaper luminance, rather than a heavier tint.
- The Dynamic Island is never glass.
- Icons crossing a morph keep their optical size. Scale the container, not the glyphs.
- The tooltip stays anchored to its bar through the camera move, not to the screen.
- Typed characters in Spotlight enter with the pointer's I-beam; the caret blinks on half-beats.
- Never put will-change on anything the camera scales, or text renders blurry.
- Make the last frame identical to the first, pointer included, or the loop stutters.
</gotchas>

<start>
If the song file is missing, ask for it. Then measure the BPM and the downbeat, and show me the beat map as a table (beat, time, state, pointer action, sound), snapped to the measured grid, before writing any code. Wait for my OK.
</start>

title: Brush-painted short film about hidden emotions
text: Create a complete 30-second 2D animated short film in p5.js. The ATTACHED VIDEO is the strict visual reference. Do not reinterpret its visual style. Do not modernize it. Do not transform it into generative art, vector animation, abstract motion graphics, collage, watercolor, paper cutout, cyberpunk, neon graphics, particle art, or clean digital illustration. The objective is for the final animation to feel as if it belongs to the exact same animated world as the reference video. ABSOLUTE VISUAL PRIORITY The most important requirement is: EVERY FRAME MUST LOOK PAINTED FRAME-BY-FRAME WITH A ROUGH PHYSICAL BRUSH. The reference does NOT look like clean digital illustration. It looks like moving paint. Every surface must visibly contain brush strokes. The brush strokes must remain visible in: skies walls skin silhouettes floors shadows clouds clothing light flames landscapes Never cover the image with smooth digital gradients. Never create large perfectly flat computer-generated fills. The paint itself is part of the image. THE ACTUAL PAINTERLY LANGUAGE Reproduce the following characteristics extremely closely. BRUSHWORK Use hundreds of short, directional, overlapping brush strokes. The strokes should feel like they were made with: a dry bristle brush opaque paint rough digital gouache / oil-like paint visible pressure imperfect edges The painting is NOT delicate watercolor. The paint is relatively opaque and dense. Individual brush marks are clearly visible. Backgrounds should contain visible waves of short strokes following the form of the environment. For example: A night sky is not a smooth navy rectangle. It is constructed from many overlapping navy, ultramarine and violet strokes. A brown wall is not a flat brown surface. It contains hundreds of curved brown and ochre marks. A human silhouette is not a clean polygon. It consists of rough overlapping brush masses. BRUSH DIRECTION Brush direction is extremely important. Do not scatter texture randomly. The strokes must describe the shape. Sky: mostly broad horizontal or gently curved strokes. Walls: large irregular swirling strokes. Ground: horizontal scraped strokes. Human torso: strokes following shoulders, chest and spine. Arms: strokes following the direction of the limbs. Flames: vertical upward strokes. Light beams: long vertical cream / yellow / orange strokes. This gives the entire animation the sensation of a moving painting. TEMPORAL PAINT INSTABILITY The painting itself must subtly change over time. Do NOT freeze the texture. At approximately 12–15 visual frames per second, slightly alter: silhouette edges brush positions paint density small color patches highlight shapes shadow shapes The movement should feel like each frame has been repainted. This is essential. However: do NOT create ugly random jitter. The forms remain coherent. The PAINT changes. The OBJECT does not randomly teleport. Think: frame-by-frame painted animation. EXACT COLOR WORLD The entire film must stay inside an extremely restrained palette. DARKS deep navy blue almost-black indigo ultramarine dark desaturated violet extremely dark brown MIDTONES muddy earth brown burnt umber muted ochre dusty violet dark teal-blue LIGHT cream ivory warm pale yellow PRIMARY EMISSIVE COLOR amber gold burnt orange yellow-orange hot cream-white The dominant visual opposition is: DEEP BLUE / BROWN DARKNESS versus INCANDESCENT ORANGE-GOLD LIGHT Do not introduce green neon. Do not introduce magenta neon. Do not introduce cyan sci-fi lighting. Do not create a rainbow palette. LIGHT STYLE Light in the reference is powerful but still PAINTED. The light source may contain: cream-white core → pale yellow → golden yellow → orange → brown-orange halo But its boundary must never look like a perfect digital radial gradient. The edge should be broken. Uneven. Brushy. Fragments of paint should escape from the luminous area. Strong light may overexpose parts of a character into cream or yellow. Nearby surfaces may receive rough orange brush highlights. Use glow, but hide the digital perfection of the glow beneath irregular painted layers. THE LIGHT BEAM When using a beam of light, reproduce the exact visual logic of the reference: A thick, almost white-yellow painted center. Orange-yellow irregular edges. Small broken fragments around the contour. Slight temporal deformation. A soft warm halo surrounding it. The beam may bend abruptly rather than behaving like realistic light. It should look like a giant painted stroke of light entering the world. NOT: laser sci-fi energy volumetric 3D beam hologram HUMAN CHARACTERS Human characters must follow the same rendering logic as the reference. There are two important visual families. DARK HUMAN FIGURES Dark people are painted almost entirely in: navy indigo black-blue Their bodies are simplified but recognizably human. Edges are rough. Anatomy is suggested with large brush masses. Do not draw individual fingers unless necessary. Do not create clean facial features. Faces are mostly dark. When eyes are visible: use two tiny bright cream/white glowing dots. The eyes should create a slightly uncanny, poetic presence. Do NOT make giant cartoon eyes. LUMINOUS HUMAN FIGURES Some characters may become almost entirely orange-gold. Their bodies appear made from light and paint. Use: orange body mass yellow highlights cream highlights small luminous imperfections Parts of the body may disappear into light. Small glowing flecks may exist inside or around the silhouette. Again: do not make these flecks into a conventional particle system. They are tiny PAINT MARKS. CHARACTER EDGES Never use crisp anti-aliased vector edges. Edges should look created by repeated brush contact. Produce: tiny protrusions missing paint rough angular sections occasional duplicated edge strokes small warm rim lights Dark characters illuminated by orange light should receive a thin, irregular orange-painted rim. Not a clean outline. CHARACTER ANIMATION The body animation should feel naturally observed. Use believable human weight. Characters should: lean hesitate reach pull collapse turn bend look upward hold tension Do NOT animate characters as simple stick figures. Use a skeletal system internally if needed, but render over it with large deformable painted masses. The rig must remain invisible. The visible result should look hand-painted. For fast actions: allow individual painted frames to stretch. Use rough smear poses. A hand may become a long brush mark for 1–2 frames. An arm may momentarily distort. The animation must prioritize expressive movement over perfect anatomy. BACKGROUNDS Backgrounds must be simple in geometry but extremely rich in painted texture. Typical structures: large dark painted skies horizontal mountain bands brown cavern-like interiors flat theatrical floors dark voids simple walls simple windows large horizons Do not fill backgrounds with tiny realistic details. The reference creates richness using PAINT, not objects. A wall may contain only one brown color family but hundreds of directional brush marks. COMPOSITION Use graphic, readable compositions. Often: one strong horizontal line one central vertical light one clearly readable human silhouette large areas of darkness Do not overpopulate every frame. Allow negative space. The visual hierarchy must remain immediate. CAMERA Use mostly: static compositions slow push-ins slow pull-backs gentle pans small reframing movements Occasionally use one sudden motion for an emotional transition. Avoid constant 3D camera movement. Avoid orbit cameras. Avoid cinematic drone-like movement. The visual power comes from: paint composition light body language not virtual camera tricks. NO COMPUTER-GRAPHICS LOOK ABSOLUTELY FORBIDDEN: perfect vector paths clean SVG appearance perfect Bezier silhouettes perfect circles everywhere smooth Illustrator gradients slick motion-graphics easing everywhere 3D objects glossy reflections PBR materials neon cyberpunk holographic effects lens flare packs generic particle emitters glitter clouds starfield screensavers fractal visuals HUD interfaces corporate animation flat-design illustration paper collage cut-paper characters chalkboard aesthetic watercolor wash aesthetic anime cartoon character design The final result should look like animated PAINT. STORY THEME Human beings often try to hide their emotions. But emotions continue to move through us. The short film follows one dark-blue human figure whose inner emotional light gradually escapes from their body. No text. No narration. No labels such as: FEAR ANGER SADNESS Everything is communicated visually. 00:00–00:05 SOMETHING ARRIVES Deep navy painted night. Large horizontal fields of rough dark-blue brushwork. A tiny human figure stands alone near the bottom center. The character is painted dark indigo. Almost invisible. Only two tiny pale eyes are visible. Hold the composition. Then: from outside the frame, a gigantic cream-yellow-orange painted beam enters diagonally from above. It suddenly bends downward. Exactly like a massive brush stroke changing direction. It hits the ground several meters in front of the person. A violent warm light spreads across the painted ground. Small orange paint marks appear around the impact point. The person protects their face with one arm. The warm light creates a rough orange rim around their silhouette. Camera slowly approaches. Inside the impact point: something humanoid begins forming. 00:05–00:09 THE EMOTION TAKES A BODY The orange light rises. Inside the beam appears a glowing orange human figure. Its body is incomplete. Parts flicker between: orange paint yellow paint cream-white light The dark-blue person approaches. The orange person mirrors their posture. Dark human raises an arm. Orange human raises an arm. Dark human leans forward. Orange human leans forward. But with a slight delay. The dark human gradually realizes: this luminous figure is part of them. The beam disappears upward. The orange figure remains. 00:09–00:12 INSIDE Cut abruptly to an extreme close-up of the dark person's back and torso. The background becomes dirty pale cream. Render the body with thick brown-orange and dark brush strokes. A thin vertical line of orange light appears along the spine. It travels downward. The surrounding painted muscles receive moving amber highlights. The light reaches the center of the torso. A brilliant orange-white glow appears. For a moment: the body seems transparent through paint. Inside are several tiny orange flame-like shapes. They are alive. Not realistic flames. Small painted emotional creatures. Some hide. Some tremble. Some jump. Some stare outward. Cut. 00:12–00:16 WE TRY TO CONTROL THEM Large brown painted room. Visible swirling brown brushwork covers the walls. A long pale painted platform crosses the image horizontally. Several dark navy human figures surround it. Their tiny white eyes are visible. Above the table: many small orange flame-like emotional forms float through the room. One person uses a long rough pole ending in a pale painted hoop. They attempt to catch one emotion. Another person reaches toward another. Another tries to push them away. The emotions move unpredictably. Some are tiny. Some suddenly grow. A giant orange emotion briefly enters from above. Everyone freezes. Then it rushes upward out of frame. This scene should feel strange, serious and slightly absurd. Exactly the tonal balance of the reference. 00:16–00:19 FEAR Night again. Simple theatrical landscape. Dark brown lower half. Deep blue-purple painted sky. A row of small cream-orange lights forms a horizontal border. The luminous orange human hangs slightly above the ground. Thin almost invisible lines appear attached above their shoulders and arms. The figure behaves as though being pulled by forces outside their control. A dark-blue person watches from the foreground. The orange human tries to walk. Their leg moves forward. The invisible line pulls them backward. They struggle. Their body flickers. Several tiny warm marks fall from their chest. One reaches the ground. It continues glowing. 00:19–00:22 ANGER Interior view. The dark person extends one arm forcefully. From the hand: not a laser. A thick orange-white painted streak explodes horizontally. The stroke consists of several overlapping rough brush marks. It moves across the image. As it passes: small orange flame-creatures appear. More. More. Too many. The room becomes brighter. The dark person's orange rim becomes stronger. Their gesture initially appears powerful. Then the painted stroke begins bending back toward them. The emotion they released returns. The person's posture changes from attack to surprise. Cut just before impact. 00:22–00:25 TRYING TO UNDERSTAND Top-down view. Brown painted desk. Several dirty cream sheets. The papers must still be PAINTED, not photorealistic paper textures. On them: rough black handwritten marks small arrows tiny red marks primitive diagrams human-like shapes Central page: a large irregular black circle. Several red arrows point toward the circle. The circle must look painted. Not geometrically perfect. A dark-blue painted hand enters. It touches the black center. The circle transforms into a dark opening. Camera enters the opening. 00:25–00:28 WE ARE NOT ALONE Transition into a deep teal-blue painted void. The orange human is suspended vertically in the center. Around them: many pale blue-white human bodies. All are painted using the same rough brush treatment. No clean outlines. Some curl inward. Some reach. Some fall. Some sit. Some appear exhausted. Some float. Very thin vertical lines extend upward from several figures. The composition feels like human beings suspended inside an enormous emotional space. The orange person reaches toward one white-blue person. A thin hand-painted orange arc connects their hands. A small orange point appears inside the other person's chest. Then another connection. Then another. Warmth begins spreading between people. Not through particles. Through painted lines and glowing marks. 00:28–00:30 EMOTIONS MOVE BETWEEN US Very dark final landscape. Two small orange points exist far apart. Each belongs to a human silhouette. One orange point moves away from the first chest. It travels through darkness as one rough glowing brush mark. It enters the chest of the second person. Both silhouettes now have warm orange rims. The environment remains dark. No triumphant sunrise. No happy ending cliché. Only two humans. Two small lights. Large dark painted space. Hold for approximately one second. Cut to black. EMOTIONAL TONE The film should feel: mysterious human melancholic strange warm slightly unsettling intimate poetic Never sentimental. Never cute. Never epic superhero cinema. P5.JS RENDERING STRATEGY Do NOT solve the visual style by applying one texture overlay to normal vector graphics. The actual primitives themselves must look painted. Create a custom brush renderer. A brush stroke can be constructed from: an irregular center path multiple semi-opaque deposits varying width small edge fragments slight hue variation rough alpha mask Create reusable systems such as: PaintStroke PaintedShape PaintedHuman PaintedGlow PaintedFlame PaintedBackground PaintedLightBeam PAINTED BACKGROUND TECHNIQUE Instead of: background(20, 30, 70); construct the visible field from many strokes. For example conceptually: base dark fill 150–400 large brush marks using neighboring colors: navy dark violet ultramarine near-black blue Their opacity should overlap. Their direction should follow the environment. Do this for every major surface. HUMAN RENDERING TECHNIQUE Internally animate a skeleton. But render each limb as several irregular painted polygons / brush masses. A forearm should not be: line() or a perfect capsule. Build it from rough overlapping shapes. Slightly regenerate its contour on the handmade animation frame. Use the skeleton only as hidden construction. DUAL FRAME RATE Render the browser smoothly at approximately 60 FPS. But update the PAINTED DRAWING state around: 12 FPS or 15 FPS. For example: handPaintFrame = floor(time * 12) Use this state to control: brush contour variation paint marks small silhouette changes flame shape changes highlight irregularities Camera interpolation can remain smooth. This contrast is extremely important. GLOW Use digital blur internally if necessary. But always place irregular painted marks over and around it. A glow alone must never reveal a perfect Photoshop-like halo. Bright areas must contain visible paint structure. IMPORTANT FINAL CHECK Before accepting any scene, ask: “Could this frame plausibly be a frame from the attached reference animation?” If the answer is no: change it. If it looks like p5.js generative art: change it. If it looks like vector motion design: change it. If it looks like particles with bloom: change it. If it looks like watercolor: change it. If it looks like paper collage: change it. If it looks too clean: change it. If the brush strokes are not immediately visible: change it. FINAL TARGET The viewer should primarily perceive: PAINT MOVING. Not code. Not particles. Not vectors. Not shaders. Not procedural graphics. A dark, expressive animated painting made of rough brush strokes, deep blue silhouettes, brown and violet painted environments, uncanny tiny pale eyes, and violent warm orange light. The attached video is the authority for: palette brush density edge roughness character rendering light behavior background rendering contrast composition movement visual rhythm Match that visual language as closely as possible throughout the full 30 seconds.
