title: One single continuous 20-second shot, 16:9 landscape, 1080p.
text:
One single continuous 20-second shot, 16:9 landscape, 1080p. NO cuts, NO edits, NO transitions, NO fades, NO title card, NO slow-motion. One unbroken handheld-gimbal camera that moves with the action the entire time. Photoreal supernatural school drama.

STORY
A quiet girl is cornered by four classmates in an old shrine courtyard behind her school. They tear out the pressed-flower pages she has been collecting in her journal and shove her down. Her hurt turns to resolve, and the wind itself answers her. She defeats the four one at a time with acrobatic moves that create visible gusts, calls her flying pages back out of the air, and walks away with them.

REFERENCES
@image1 = the heroine. One girl shown in two views (full body and face close-up); both views are the SAME person. Keep her exact face, dark teal-black layered shoulder-length hair with side-swept bangs, silver hairclip, brown eyes, small beauty mark, slim build.
@image2 = four antagonists, mapped left to right: A = tall, long straight black hair, center part (the leader); B = chestnut bob with blunt bangs; C = high black ponytail with white scrunchie; D = wavy dark-brown hair past the shoulders. Keep each face and hairstyle independent and consistent; never swap identities.
All five wear the reference uniform exactly: navy double-button blazer with white lapel trim, white shirt, red ribbon tie, plaid pleated knee-length skirt, black tights, brown loafers. No other clothing. Do NOT show the white studio backgrounds, lineup poses or split-screen layouts from the references. All five people are the same real-world scale.

NO DISAPPEARING (CRITICAL)
Exactly five real people exist in this scene from the first frame to the last frame: the heroine, A, B, C and D. NOBODY vanishes, fades, dissolves, turns into leaves or dust, teleports, gets blown out of the scene, or is swallowed by the wind. Wind never removes a person from the shot. When the camera moves away from a character and returns, she is still exactly where she was left. Every defeated girl stays physically on the ground in her defeated position, visible, solid and breathing, until the very last frame. Nobody walks or runs out of the courtyard. The count of people stays at five at all times.

SETTING
An old shrine courtyard behind a high school, late-afternoon golden light, soft overcast sky. Gravel and stone-slab ground, two moss-covered stone lanterns, a small wooden shrine gate (torii) in the background, a large ginkgo tree dropping yellow leaves. A low wooden bench on the left. Everything is flat and open, no stairs, no drops, no water. The wind is NOT a storm: it is a controlled, localized swirl of a limited number of yellow ginkgo leaves, light gravel dust and moving hair. The leaves stay thin and sparse, never form a thick cloud or wall, and never cover a person's body or face. Wind is transparent: no glowing beams, no neon, no smoke, no animal shapes, no tornado.

PROPS
One small hand-bound journal with a green cloth cover. Exactly five thin washi-paper pages, each holding a pressed flower (a pink cosmos, a blue hydrangea, a red maple leaf, a tiny forget-me-not, a white camellia), are torn out together. The journal is dropped near the heroine's feet and stays there until she picks it up. The five pages float in the air at the left side of the courtyard during the fight and never act as weapons. Two school bags rest against the shrine wall from the start and are never touched.

CAMERA, ONE CONTINUOUS MOVE
The camera starts in a tight handheld medium shot on the heroine's face, drifts around her, then follows each action in a smooth flowing path at eye level and side three-quarter angles, mostly medium to medium-full so every acrobatic move is fully visible. It never cuts. It sweeps from character to character with whip-pan-style swings that settle on the next target. After each defeat, the camera glides briefly across the fallen girl so the audience sees she is still there. At the climax the camera does one 100-degree orbit around the heroine at normal speed. In the final seconds the camera slowly pulls back to a medium-wide view that shows all five people.

PERFORMANCE TIMELINE (all in one take)

0–4s: Camera starts close on the heroine, holding her green journal against her chest. A (long black hair) snatches it, holds it out of reach and says in a mocking voice, in English: "This is trash." She tears five pressed-flower pages out in one handful and flings them into the air while the others laugh. Camera pans with the pages fluttering, then returns.

4–7s: She turns to chase the pages. B (chestnut bob) steps in and shoves her; she stumbles, drops to one knee and one palm, the journal falls near her. A few loose ginkgo leaves skitter across the gravel. Camera pushes in on her wet eyes and tight jaw. Laughter fades. Hold the hurt for a beat. A, B, C and D are all visible standing nearby.

7–9s: She says quietly and firmly, in English: "Stop it already." Her hair lifts, a few leaves begin to circle, and the five pages stop and hover on the left. The four step back, uneasy, all clearly visible. B moves in first.

9–12s: DEFEAT 1, B. The heroine pushes off her palm into a single handspring into a side cartwheel. Her spinning legs pull the air into one narrow gust that travels sideways across the gravel into B's chest. B is thrown off balance, slides, and ends seated against the left stone lantern base. She stays there, visible, for the rest of the video.

12–16s: DEFEAT 2, C. The camera glances at B still seated, then whips to C, who charges from the right. The heroine drops into a low crouch and slides on the gravel into one long circular leg sweep. The sweep sends a flat current of leaves and dust along the ground into C's ankles. C's feet slip and she falls forward onto her hands and knees at the right edge. She stays there, visible.

16–20s: DEFEAT 3, D. D rushes in with both hands out. The heroine springs up, performs one standing back handspring into a backflip. As she rotates, her heels drag a wide, flat wall of air in front of her that hits D at torso height. D is pushed back two steps and sits down hard on the wooden bench. She stays seated, visible. Nobody collides with anyone else.

DEFEAT POSITIONS (never reset)
B: seated at the left stone lantern. C: hands and knees at the right edge. D: seated on the bench. A: seated alone near the torii gate. All four stay conscious, remain in the courtyard, never rejoin the fight and are never hit by another person's attack.

RULES FOR THE POWERS
Every technique follows: acrobatic movement, wind forms, wind travels, wind makes contact, reaction. The heroine's feet never touch anyone. Each gust fades after its own hit. Only the targeted person is affected; the others may flinch. No blades of air, no blood, no injuries, no one hits their head. One execution per move: no repeated flips, no extra spins.

AUDIO
Natural courtyard ambience, distant cicadas, rustling leaves, gravel scrapes, shoes, paper tearing, mocking laughter, breathing, cloth movement, wind whooshes, bodies landing on gravel. Only TWO spoken lines in the whole video, both in clear natural English with accurate lip sync: A says "This is trash." and the heroine says "Stop it already." No other dialogue. No music, no narrator, no subtitles, no on-screen text.

LOOK
Natural daylight color with warm golden tones, fine film grain, soft halation, real skin texture, no plastic faces, no HDR glow, no vignette, no letterboxing. Side-on, athletic stunt framing; clothing moves naturally with the acrobatics, never framed as spectacle.

AVOID
Anyone disappearing, fading, dissolving, teleporting or leaving the courtyard; a storm, tornado or thick leaf cloud; cuts, split-screens, studio backgrounds, duplicated heroine, extra characters, group takedowns, changed uniforms, mint or green hair on anyone, sliding planted feet

title: Plush Crab
text:
PROMPT 
Create a self-contained interactive WebGPU page "Plush Crab" in the existing Material Studies plush series
(No. 020, fig. 20), matching the series' editorial layout: serif masthead, specimen control panel, live
readouts, collapsible "Inside the experiment" notes, English UI, works on mobile, graceful no-WebGPU fallback.

THE TOY: a cute plush crab sitting on a studio table. A wide, puffy domed shell with a flat seat and a soft
brow; two eyes on short stalks, each a fuzzy eyeball with a round white felt patch and a glossy safety eye;
an embroidered smile and soft blush cheeks; pale spots scattered over the top of the shell; a paler
underside; stitched seams where legs are sewn on. Real-time shell-texture fur (many shells, alpha-to-coverage,
MSAA) that lags behind jiggles and can be combed. Palettes: Coral (default), Sand, Blue (with red claw tips).

BODY: one SDF meshed with surface nets, simulated as an XPBD soft body (hex lattice, shape matching +
tetrahedral volume) under gravity and friction; it breathes, rights itself, can be grabbed, squashed,
lifted and thrown, and lands softly.

LEGS AND CLAWS: eight walking legs and two arms are rods with a plastic "wire" inside — posed toward
blended targets (sit, stand, hide, wave, hang), and bent legs keep the new shape until "Straighten".
Each arm ends in a chunky claw with two fat fingers that hang from the arm tip in the claw's own frame;
opening and closing is a single angle. Legs get pale joint bands and toes; claw fingers get dark tips.

BEHAVIOUR: "Scuttle" walks sideways (keeps its side to the goal) with an alternating gait and footholds;
"Snip snip" raises both claws and snaps them a beat apart (count snips in a readout); "Hide" pulls the legs in
and covers its eyes with the claws, then peeks out; "Wave claws" raises them high. With the Finger tool it
scuttles toward a held-out finger, turns to face it, reaches with its claws and gives a gentle pinch (toast);
poking the shell makes it hide. Held up in the air, legs dangle and paddle. Idle: small scuttles, snips, waves.

CONTROLS: tools Hand / Finger / Comb; sliders Stuffing, Pile, Wire; buttons Scuttle, Snip snip, Hide,
Wave claws, Straighten, Smooth fur, Reset; ¼ speed, Mesh, Pause. Readouts: Mass, Volume (% of rest),
Steps, Snips. Single HTML file, no external models or textures.

title: Night Monster
text: The humanoid face in the mirror, monster, woman, hands, facial close-ups, and bathroom all adopt the same distinct AAA computer-generated fantasy game CG aesthetic; the woman must also possess the sculpted facial volumes, strand-bundled hair, and unified material shading of a polished game character, preventing her from looking like a live-action actor while only the monster is CG. Not live-action footage, cosplay, standard gameplay, 2D animation, or cel-shaded. The image natively fills the entire widescreen; no text, subtitles, titles, logos, or watermarks throughout. Environment: late night in an old, cramped bathroom with low ceilings, yellowed and cracked white square tiled walls, and dark weathered floor tiles; an old rectangular mirror hangs on the wall above the sink, its edges marked by black oxidation spots; below the mirror is a white ceramic sink and a narrow countertop. The only noticeable practical light source is a white candle placed on the right side of the sink counter, its flame flickering continuously, casting warm amber light from below onto the subjects and throwing thick but readable elongated shadows; a light mist lingers in the air after a bath. Maintain desaturated brown, dark gold, and monster reddish-brown palette without cold blue neon or modern lighting. Exactly two independent subjects: A is an adult female approximately thirty years old, fair skin, medium build, wet dark brown long hair draped over her shoulders, wearing a dark grey long-sleeve pajama top and dark trousers, unarmed. She stands before the sink facing the mirror, shoulders stiff with terror, hands braced on the sink rim, wide-eyed, breathing rapidly. B is the same giant, slender humanoid monster: initially disguised as A's reflection in the mirror—sharing an identical face, wet hair, and pajamas, but smiling while A is not, with the mouth corners barely wider than normal and eyes slightly more open, expression quiet, stiff, and unnatural, not a cartoonish grin. Once peeled open, the interior reveals a deformed elongated face of interwoven dark red and fleshy-pink muscle bundles, sunken nasal cavities, staring round eyes, fine ivory teeth, and an abnormally stretched oral cavity with multiple rows of teeth aligned longitudinally down the oral cavity and deep into the lower jaw; the mouth is a tall, narrow vertical slit whose height greatly exceeds its width when open, not a round hole or skull-like; the head, neck, and torso maintain continuous anatomical structure, not several distinct heads. The entire body consists of sculpted reddish-brown and fleshy-pink biological tissue with defined contours across shoulder blades, spine, ribs, elongated arms, and thighs, with restrained wet highlights, not a human painted red. Limbs are extremely long, hands thick with slender fingers, standard two arms and two legs; no armor, weapons, horns, wings, or visible genitalia. When crawling out of the mirror and crouching, it remains significantly taller than A, forced to bend knees and hips and lower its back under the low ceiling; scale disparity is communicated through the woman, sink, candle, and mirror together. The humanoid reflection and subsequent red behemoth represent the continuous state of B shedding its disguise, with no third subject added. 0.00–0.60s: Begin directly with a tight frontal close-up of the mirror reflection, face filling the frame from forehead to chin with mirror oxidation spots faintly visible at the borders; wet hair clings to the face, illuminated from below by candlelight, background blurred. Reflection stares straight into the camera with that stiff, unnervingly subtle smile; camera nearly static with a minimal slow push-in, without first establishing an empty bathroom. 0.60–3.10s: Retain the full-frame frontal close-up; one hand of the reflection grasps the top hairline while the other pinches the lower edge of the chin; hands only grip the perimeter, never obscuring the central face, eyes, or mouth. Upper hand pulls upward, lower hand pulls downward, peeling the humanoid face open along a straight vertical midline. Fingers gain purchase, outer layer tightens, then pale skin splits down the center revealing the continuous red monster face beneath; fine moist connective fibers stretch across the fissure. Fingers consistently hold the same outer layer without introducing a separate face or flashing into a monster. Movement is slow, continuous, showing tensile resistance; camera does not cut away from the reveal. 3.10–4.90s: Continue the close-up; the peeled halves remain attached at the sides of the head without falling off, each human eye still open and staring directly into the camera; the elongated red monster face pushes forward between them into full view, displaying both remaining human eyes alongside the monster face. It parts the tall, narrow vertical slit revealing rows of fine teeth and stretched jaw anatomy, uttering a low, non-verbal hiss; moist fibers tauten and slacken between the face halves and red flesh. Maintain visceral body-horror reveal without fire, lightning, transformation beams, or duplicated heads. 4.90–7.20s: Hard cut to a frontal close-up of woman A from the mirror's perspective at a slightly low angle. She freezes at the sink, eyes wide, brow furrowed, mouth slightly parted in terror, chin trembling, head pulling back slightly; wet hair and pajama collar sharp, one side lit by candlelight while the other falls into shadow. Continuous breathing and micro-reactions without speaking. 7.20–10.90s: Maintaining A's framing, two massive reddish-brown monster hands reach out from the mirror into frame: the mirror surface ripples and yields like liquid black mercury as arms push through. One hand presses onto her forehead and hairline while the other cradles her jaw, long fingers depressing the lower lip. Clear contact between palms, forehead, and jaw is established before opposing force gradually forces her head backward and mouth open wider. Her eyes remain locked on the creature in the mirror, throat straining, hands gripping the sink rim tightly; contact remains clear without covering her eyes or clipping through cheeks. Her face remains identical, only opening wider under supernatural pressure without mutating. 10.90–13.40s: Hard cut to a low-angle side wide shot establishing bathroom geometry: A stands at the left before the sink, head forced back; mirror and sink on the right wall. B has crawled more than halfway out of the undulating liquid mirror: long arms stretch left holding her forehead and jaw; torso hunched over the sink, one long leg stepping out with foot planted on the counter rim, other leg trailing in the rippling glass, knees bent and back arched under the low ceiling. Candle sits secure on the counter's right beside the monster's foot. B tilts head back, opening the narrow vertical slit to maximum revealing multiple tooth tiers, releasing a raspy, piercing non-verbal screech vibrating through throat and chest, making the candle flame flutter violently. 13.40–17.00s: Continuing the side wide shot, B keeps mouth agape after the screech, lowering head and neck toward the front-left, aligning its elongated face toward A's unnaturally opened mouth; the stabilizing hand on her forehead and supporting hand on her jaw sustain the posture as the monster's head begins continuous descent into her mouth opening. A remains braced at the sink, torso arched back, hands gripping the edge, neck taut. B's head and neck make contact and gradually enter, keeping massive back and hindquarters outside; does not engulf A into the monster's mouth, no inverted orientation, no transparent mesh clipping. 17.00–20.00s: Persisting wide shot, B's shoulders push forward-left, neck and head increasingly obscured within A's oral cavity, massive arched back shifting weight as the second leg steps out onto the counter, mirror surface behind settling back to calm reflection of the dim room. Both hands firmly hold forehead and jaw without extraneous limbs; A trembles with weakening knees but remains upright, pajamas creasing under tension. Candle remains standing, flame wavering, shadows of creature and woman shifting slowly against the tiles. Ends at 20 seconds amidst ongoing intrusion with bulk and legs still outside, without concluding full penetration, escape, transformation, or death. Rhythm & Cinematography: Slow-burn supernatural horror reveal without devolving into chase or melee. Preserves shot progression: reflection close-up peel — woman's reaction close-up — hands emerging to manipulate jaw — side wide shot showing massive scale crawling out, screeching, and descending. Driven by continuous deformation and reaction, settling into a sustained wide shot for full spatial dynamics; avoids orbit shots, abrupt zooms, unrelated reaction cutaways, or jumpscare black frames. Slowness derives from calculated force and approach, without artificial ultra-slow motion, speed ramping, or freezes. Consistent warm amber grade, candle lighting direction, and spatial continuity. Continuity: Exactly two subjects; A remains adult female, wet brown hair, dark grey pajamas at the same sink; B has two arms and two legs, with the peeled reflection face identical in material and anatomy to the emerged giant body. Mirror remains unbroken without glass shards. Intact anatomy throughout, clear hand placement, entry trajectory strictly monster head into woman's mouth. Emphasizes bio-mechanical forms, dread reactions, and progressive uncanny action without gore splatters, flying viscera, or dismemberment. Strictly prohibits background music: no score, soundtrack, melodic themes, rhythmic percussion, choir, songs, musical drones, or tonal ambience at any point. Only synchronized diegetic audio native to the physical scene: slow sink drip, faint candle crackle, subtle tile resonance, fabric friction, woman's breath and strained gasps, monster's low breathing, wet tearing sound of parting tissue, low liquid resonance of distorted mirror, skin contact sounds, the raspy piercing screech from 10.90–13.40s, and deep creaks of strained joints. No dialogue, voiceover, intelligible speech, or subtitles; no musical cues or rhythmic pulses filling silence. Any presence of background music fails evaluation. music=0; no_music=1; strict_no_music=1; audio=diegetic_only; Native full-bleed frame without letterboxing, rounded corners, text, subtitles, titles, logos, UI, or watermarks.

title: Interactive 3D Coral Reef Diorama Simulation
text:
Build "Coral Reef", a playable miniature-diorama world: a glass aquarium block of tropical sea where the player brings a bleached coral reef back to life, as ONE self-contained HTML file.

It must be **beautiful above everything**, like a premium animated film: a jewel-like aquarium with crystal-clear water, dancing light, saturated coral colours and lively, characterful fish. Great animation on everything that moves: nothing pops, snaps or teleports; things grow, ease, overshoot a little and settle. Calm and satisfying to play, spectacular to watch.

## Tech

* three.js r170 with WebGPURenderer (automatic WebGL2 fallback). Load it with an importmap from jsDelivr: map "three", "three/webgpu" and "three/tsl" to `three@0.170.0/build/three.webgpu.min.js`, and "three/addons/" to `three@0.170.0/examples/jsm/`.
* Use TSL node materials, OrbitControls from the addons, and a subtle BloomNode pass (strength ~0.4, threshold ~1.5) so only emissive things glow (fluorescent coral at night, glowing plankton, sun glints, the octopus' startled flash).
* No external assets. Every texture is drawn on a canvas or generated as pixel data at startup. Every sound is synthesized with WebAudio. The only network requests are three.js from jsDelivr and the Fredoka font from Google Fonts; if the font fails to load, fall back to a system rounded sans-serif without breaking anything.
* Start the HTML with `<!doctype html>` and `<meta charset="utf-8">`.
* It must run inside a sandboxed iframe (`sandbox="allow-scripts allow-pointer-lock"`, no `allow-same-origin`). There, `localStorage` and cookies throw a SecurityError: wrap every storage access in `try/catch` and keep values in memory instead. Do not use `alert`, pop-ups or top-level navigation.
* Neutral tone mapping, soft 2048 shadow map (1024 on phones).
* Known three r170 pitfalls, avoid them:
   * the scene background is drawn after transparent objects, so draw the sky/backdrop as a mesh (or give transparent sky objects `depthWrite: true`), or they disappear;
   * never `.clone()` a CanvasTexture (the clone uploads black); create separate textures or use DataTexture;
   * never let a helper overwrite a shared temp vector that its caller is still using.
* The simulation runs on a fixed 60 Hz timestep and is frame-rate independent. At low frame rates, drop simulation time instead of exploding.
* A quality scaler lowers the pixel ratio, then particle counts, when frames get slow.
* Respect prefers-reduced-motion: softer shake, slower camera moves.

## Priorities

Build in this order and finish each tier properly before the next. A polished tier 1 beats a broken everything.

1. **Must be excellent:** the aquarium block (water volume, caustics, light shafts, surface), the fish school that follows the finger, coral regrowing colour, feeding, the demo mode.
2. **Must work:** the octopus, turtle, shark pass, clownfish and anemone, coral planting, day/night with fluorescence, the reef-alive meter and milestones, sound, the card UI, camera.
3. **Polish:** storm and murky water, the shipwreck and treasure, crabs and seahorse, bubbles tool, glowing plankton trails.

Never ship a feature half-working: if a tier-3 feature can't be done well, leave it out cleanly.

## The diorama

* A 10×7×10 glass aquarium block on a dark wooden stand, with thin white glass edges, soft studio backdrop (deep teal gradient), soft contact shadow.
* **Water:** the whole block is water. The surface is a live wave heightfield (ripples from the finger and from feeding), seen from above and from below (total internal reflection: a silvery mirror from underneath). Volumetric look: blue-green depth fog, **animated caustics** on the sand and on every creature, and **god rays** from the surface that sway.
* **Sea floor:** white sand with ripples, rocks, a sloping reef shelf, seagrass meadow that sways, a sunken shipwreck half-buried at the back.
* **Coral:** procedurally generated branching coral (L-system or recursive cones), table coral, fan coral (sheets that sway), brain coral (sphere with a groove pattern), soft coral that pulses, anemones with swaying tentacles. Each coral has a **health** value: **bleached** corals are white-grey and still; healthy corals are saturated (orange, pink, purple, yellow, teal) and gently move. Health changes animate slowly, colour flowing from the base to the tips.

## Life

* **Fish school (boids):** 150–300 small fish (instanced) with separation, alignment, cohesion and obstacle avoidance (coral, glass, floor). **They follow the pointer** gently when it moves slowly through the water, **scatter** from fast swipes and from the shark, and form a tight **bait ball** when the shark passes. Iridescent silver-blue with a tail wiggle.
* **Reef fish:** a few species with personalities (yellow tangs, striped damselfish, a parrotfish that nibbles coral and leaves tiny sand puffs), each with its own home coral.
* **Clownfish pair** living in an anemone: they dart out to the finger and back, nuzzle into the tentacles.
* **Octopus:** crawls over rocks with curling arms, **changes colour and texture to match what it sits on** (sand, coral, rock), flashes white when poked and **squirts a cloud of ink** then jets away.
* **Sea turtle:** glides through slowly on a loop, sometimes rests on the sand.
* **Reef shark:** passes every ~45 s (or with the Shark button), unhurried; the school balls up and small fish hide in coral.
* **Crabs** scuttle on the sand; a **seahorse** hides in the seagrass (tail curled around a blade).

## Tools (card, keys 1–5)

* **Hand:** move slowly through the water and the school follows; swipe fast to scatter; tap the surface for a ripple; tap a creature to poke it.
* **Feed:** tap to sprinkle food flakes at the surface; they drift down with wobble; fish dart to them (a feeding frenzy with little bites); fed fish make the corals near them healthier.
* **Coral:** tap the reef to plant a new coral fragment (cycle type with repeated taps); it grows over ~10 s with a growth animation.
* **Clean:** brush over bleached coral to remove algae and kick-start recovery (sparkle particles).
* **Bubbles:** place an air stone; a column of bubbles rises and wobbles to the surface (the turtle likes to swim through it).

## Simulation

* Coral health rises with nearby fish activity, feeding and cleaning, and falls slowly in a storm or if the water is murky. Recovery spreads to neighbouring corals.
* **Day / night slider:** at night the light dims to deep blue, corals **fluoresce** (green, pink, orange emissive), plankton glows when disturbed (the finger leaves a sparkling trail), the octopus hunts, the fish sleep in the coral.
* **Storm slider:** surface waves grow, light flickers, sand gets stirred up (murky water) and settles again over time.

## Goal and milestones

* **Reef alive** meter (0–100%): average coral health plus how many species are present. The reef starts **bleached and grey** with few fish; it ends vivid, crowded and moving.
* At 100%: a celebration: every coral blooms bright, a manta ray glides overhead, and the treasure chest in the shipwreck creaks open with a golden glow.

Milestones (toasts, once each): "First feeding", "School follows you", "First coral bloom", "Octopus ink!", "Shark pass", "Night glow", "Turtle visit", "Reef alive".

## Easter egg

When the reef reaches 100% at night, a **whale's eye** slowly slides past the back glass, blinks once, and is gone. Toast: "Something big was watching." Never hint at it in the UI.

## Interface

A light, playful UI that never covers the world. On phones the card becomes a compact bottom sheet.

* Top left:
   * small caps "POKEABLE · WORLD";
   * a big chunky rounded heading on two lines, "Coral" / "Reef", in Fredoka from Google Fonts, dark ink by day and light at night, with a tiny bubble rising from the "o";
   * caption "Bring the reef back to life.".
* Top right: a live status dot with "WEBGPU · LIVE" (or "WEBGL2 · LIVE"), a speaker pill button (ON / MUTED), and "PAUSED" when paused.
* Right card "Reef": about 240 px wide, off-white, 20 px corners, soft shadow, no hairlines, coral-pink (#f2667a) accent, collapsible to a small pill. Contents:
   * a big animated "Reef alive" % with a bar, and species icons (fish, clownfish, octopus, turtle, seahorse) that light up when seen
   * tool picker: Hand, Feed, Coral, Clean, Bubbles, each with a drawn icon and its key number
   * event buttons: Shark, Feeding time
   * sliders with monospace value chips: Time of day, Storm, School size, Sound (master volume)
   * switches: Fish (on), Caustics (on), Slow motion (¼ speed), Cinema
   * buttons Reset and New (random seed), a dark full-width Pause/Resume pill, and the world's number ("No. 0001").
* Bottom left: a one-line hint that changes with the tool:
   * Hand: "Move slowly. The fish will follow you."
   * Feed: "Tap the surface to feed."
   * Coral: "Tap the reef to plant coral."
   * Clean: "Brush the white coral back to life."
   * Bubbles: "Place an air stone."
* Bottom right: a collapsible "How it works" panel, 5–6 plain lines on the boids school, coral health and recovery, caustics and light, day and night fluorescence, the camera controls, and synthesized sound.
* Toasts at the top centre for milestones and events.
* Keys: 1–5 tools, K shark, F feeding time, Space pause, R reset, N new, M mute, S slow motion, C cinema, 0 reset view, Esc stop follow / exit cinema.

## Camera

* OrbitControls with damping and zoom to cursor, within sensible limits.
* Double-click the turtle, the octopus or the shark to follow it; Esc or 0 stops.
* Camera bar (floating pill, bottom right of the scene area): zoom −, a zoom % readout, zoom +, rotate left, rotate right, reset; button moves tween smoothly.
* The default framing fits the whole world into the free area, accounting for the card and title.
* **Cinema (`C`):** hides all UI and slowly orbits the camera.

## Sound

* WebAudio only. Create the AudioContext on the first gesture and never before.
* Master gain feeds a compressor, so rapid actions never clip. Limit voices (about 16) and wrap every call in try/catch so a failing audio call never breaks the world.
* Loops: soft underwater ambience (low filtered noise with slow swells), gentle bubbling, storm rumble with the Storm slider, a dreamy pad at night.
* One-shots: swishes for the school turning, nibble ticks when fish eat, plop for food flakes, a bubbly burst for ink, a deep slow whoosh for the shark, crackle of a coral blooming, a soft chime for each milestone, a deep whale call for the Easter egg.

## Demo mode (required)

If the URL has `?demo=1` (or `#demo`), auto-play a deterministic 4.0 s loop:

* Rules:
   * Hide all UI and the cursor; never create an AudioContext.
   * Fixed quality, default seed, the reef already half alive (some bleached corals, a healthy school), default camera, no OrbitControls.
   * Drive the simulation from real elapsed time with the fixed timestep, and restart from the identical state every 4.0 s.
   * Start moving within 1 s of load, and stay readable at 15 fps.
* Timeline:
   * 0.0–1.2 s: the school sweeps through the frame in an S-curve following an invisible finger; light rays sway.
   * 1.2–2.2 s: food flakes drift down; the school bursts into a feeding frenzy.
   * 2.2–3.2 s: a bleached coral in front recovers: colour flows from the base to the tips; the octopus flashes colour on a rock.
   * 3.2–4.0 s: the turtle glides through; the school regroups.

## Before you finish, check

* The school follows the slow finger, scatters from fast swipes and balls up for the shark, never passing through coral, floor or glass.
* Feeding, planting, cleaning and coral recovery all work and spread.
* Octopus colour matching and ink; turtle, shark, clownfish, crabs, seahorse.
* Day/night fluorescence and plankton trails; storm and murky water settling.
* Reaching 100%: the celebration and the Easter egg at night.
* Every tool, slider, switch, button and key; follow mode; Cinema; pause and resume; resizing to phone width.
* Sound behaviour.
* It works inside `<iframe sandbox="allow-scripts allow-pointer-lock">` with no errors (storage blocked).
* `?demo=1` matches the timeline.
* No console or WebGPU validation errors, and it stays smooth on a mid-range laptop.

Put the school that follows your finger and the reef regaining colour first. It should be the calmest, most alive thing on the screen.

title: Pirate Jelly Interactive WebGPU Diorama
text:
Create a self-contained interactive WebGPU/WGSL page "Pirate Jelly" — part of a "Material Studies" series of jelly dioramas. Single HTML file, no external models, textures, fonts or libraries; everything procedural. English UI.

LOOK & LAYOUT
- A square block of translucent jelly sea (≈5.2 × 5.2 units) standing on a paper-studio floor; the camera looks in at the front corner at ~27°. The block's cut faces show candy strata (chocolate bedrock, caramel clay, a shell band, vanilla sand); the sea surface and walls refract and tint what's behind them, with caustics on the sea floor, light shafts, a tinted caustic shadow on the floor, foam lace on the shoreline and a bright meniscus on the cut edges.
- A small tropical island toward the back: sandy beach, a cove facing the viewer, a mossy jungle hump with ~9 gummy palms (ringed caramel trunks, translucent fronds that flutter), lumpy gummy bushes with flowers, ferns, beach grass, rocks around the shore.
- SKULL ROCK at the island's west tip, standing in the shallows: a cartoon skull sculpted as a signed-distance field (cranium, cheekbones, jaws, deep eye sockets, heart-shaped nose, crack on the crown, rock strata and noise, moss on top, a wet band at the waterline), meshed with surface nets; two rows of separate box teeth set into a carved grin. At night its eye sockets glow like a candle-lit cave.
- A PIRATE SHIP riding at anchor in front of the island, seen at three-quarters from the stern: black hull with an ochre gunport strake, red bottom, gunports with cannons, raised quarterdeck with lit stern windows and a stern lantern, three masts (square courses and topsails on fore and main, a gaff sail on the mizzen, a jib to the bowsprit), shrouds and stays, and a Jolly Roger (skull and crossed bones drawn procedurally in the shader) streaming aft. Her anchor chain runs from the bow down through the jelly to an anchor lying on the sea floor.
- The camp on the cove beach: a campfire (stone ring, teepee of logs with glowing ends, embers, a tripod with a pot, two seating logs), an iron-bound treasure chest under a leaning palm with a hinged lid and a heap of gold and gems inside, a shovel in a sand heap, barrels, a crate, a pyramid of round shot, a rum bottle, a rowing boat pulled up with its bow on the sand, and an "X" scored in the sand.
- On the sea floor: the bow half of an old wreck lying on its side with ribs showing and its broken mast beside it, swaying kelp, a few doubloons, bubbles caught in the jelly.

SIMULATION
- Linear shallow-water waves on a staggered grid with a little surface tension (springy jelly); the block can be tipped and the sea sloshes and the jelly wobbles (shear + squash).
- The ship floats on 10 buoyancy points (heave, pitch, roll), is pushed by a gently veering offshore breeze, held by an elastic anchor rode at the bow, and weathervanes into the wind. Her displaced volume is handed back to the sea, so she makes a wake.
- Rigid bodies: cannonballs (dense, fly in a clean arc, punch a crater, sink and roll on the floor), barrels (float on their side), doubloons (flutter down and settle flat). All interact with the sea (buoyancy, drag, splashes, bubbles), the terrain, the skull, the props, the palm trunks and the ship's hull.
- One particle system: fire flames (additive), embers, woodsmoke, muzzle flash, white gunsmoke, sea spray, sand puffs, gold glints over the open chest, fireflies at night.

INTERACTION
- Tap the ship → fire the next gun on the side facing the viewer (ball, flash, smoke, recoil heel). Drag the ship → tow her against the rode; release → she drifts back to her anchor.
- Tap the chest → lid swings open/shut with a bounce; gold glitters. Tap the fire → it roars and throws sparks. Tap the X → three doubloons pop out of the sand.
- Drag across the water to make waves; drag a side of the block to tip it; pick up and throw balls/barrels/coins; drag a palm to bend it; drag empty space or right-drag to orbit; wheel/pinch to zoom.

TIME OF DAY
- A slider from Noon → Afternoon → Golden hour → Sunset → Dusk → Night → Midnight. The sun lowers and warms, the backdrop turns peach, then the moon takes over (dim blue), stars appear on the backdrop, the page UI switches to a dark theme, and the campfire becomes the main light: a flickering point light that warms the sand, palms, sails and gold, reflects in the water, and lights the smoke from below. Stern windows and lantern glow.

UI (editorial, like the series)
- Top-left masthead: eyebrow "MATERIAL STUDIES", big italic serif title "Pirate / Jelly.", a short line of copy.
- Status pill (WebGPU · Live / Paused / Unavailable).
- Right glass panel: "The cove" — buttons Fire a gun / Doubloons / Barrel, a liveliness meter, tally Shots · Afloat · Sunk; "Flavour" — Turquoise, Rum (amber), Kraken (violet) jelly palettes; sliders Firmness, Wave damping, Time of day; Reset / Pause / Reset view.
- Bottom-left "How to play" line plus small instructions. Space fires a gun.
- Mobile: the panel becomes a bottom sheet; touch orbit and pinch zoom.
- Fallback card when WebGPU (or an adapter) isn't available. Respect prefers-reduced-motion.

title: Time
text:
A middle-aged clockmaker is repairing an antique pocket watch in his old-fashioned workshop at night when he discovers a mysterious clock that controls time.

He carefully turns its brass winding crown backward, causing a nearby pendulum to slow down, falling dust to become suspended in the air, and the second hands of surrounding clocks to stop moving.

He turns the crown forward, and everything resumes its natural motion. Fascinated, he turns it backward again, gradually freezing time throughout the workshop while he remains able to move.

The video ends with a cinematic close-up of the mysterious clock as its second hand continues ticking in an otherwise motionless room.

Photorealistic cinematic fantasy, realistic mechanical gear interactions, believable pendulum physics, natural gravity and inertia, consistent character appearance, realistic brass reflections, warm workshop lighting, physically accurate shadows, natural human movement, smooth camera tracking, realistic depth of field, and continuous object trajectories throughout. The supernatural time-control effect is the only exception to real-world physics.

title: Seamless Morphing UI Motion Design
text:
<inputs>
Ask me for: 4 photos (a mountain valley at sunrise, a top-down drone shot of a roundabout, a latte being poured from above, the sun over the sea at golden hour), one accent color (mine is violet #A898FF), and a royalty-free song around 118 BPM with a drop (e.g. Pixabay, free for commercial use).
</inputs>

<direction>
Apple-level motion. One object, never cut: every state is born out of the one before it, a knob opens like a lens into a photo, a card shrinks into the sun, a row in a list grows into a full photo. Night #0A0A0C to day #F2F0EB and back, ink #0E0E10 UI, real photos for the big moments, frosted liquid glass for small panels, one clean font (Geist, Geist Mono for times). Every morph uses one curve, cubic-bezier(.45,0,.15,1), springs only for pop-ins. Text rises through a mask, never fades. The camera zooms so each state fills about 60% of the frame and creeps in through every hold. The last frame is the first frame, so it loops.
Banned: crossfades, cuts, grey mush between colors, clip-art icons, glows, bouncy easing, dead time, anything that looks like a template.
</direction>

<structure>
118 BPM, 47 beats, the drop lands on the first release.
6:30 alarm pill → slide to stop, the sunrise shows through behind the knob → release on the drop, the knob irises into the sunrise card → a glass droplet rises into a weather panel, 14° counts to 18° → the card shrinks into the sun → the sun floods the screen into day → its core becomes a violet location dot → an aerial map unfolds around it → the route draws, the dot drives, "8 min" counts to "Arrived", it bounces on the pin → the pin irises into a latte photo → "Pay $4.20" grows out of the card → tap → loader → check → the card folds into the check → the check stretches into a Focus toggle → it opens into today's schedule, a line sweeps 9:00 to 18:00 → the 18:00 row grows into a sunset → the card closes on the sun, the sun turns into the moon → night floods back → the moon becomes the 6:30 pill.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML canvas, square 1440x1440. Every frame is computed from time inside seek(t): no CSS transitions, no timers, no state carried between frames.
2. One shape grammar: pill 640x120 → card 620x780 radius 64 → circle 240 → map 760 square → portrait 560x780 → check 96 → pill 560x130 → schedule 620x520 → card 620x780 → moon 200 → pill 300x96.
3. Reveals are circular clips: the photo is drawn at its final position inside a circle that grows from the exact point it is born from. Floods grow by the square root of progress so the area changes evenly.
4. Liquid glass: blur a copy of the frame under the panel, magnify its inner edge 1.08x, add a white tint, a top highlight and a 2px white rim.
5. Camera zoom per state: 2.3 alarm, 1.2 cards, 2.5 sun and moon, 1.18 map, 2.1 check, 1.7 toggle, 1.35 schedule, gliding on the same curve.
6. Analyze the song with numpy for the beat grid and land the drop on the release. Every event gets its own real sound, placed by its measured peak.
7. Render with Playwright: 8 subframes per frame, blended for motion blur at 60fps. Render a sheet of stills first and fix anything cramped or cheap looking.
</build>

<gotchas>
A photo that irises open must already sit where it will end up, or it slides when the clip finishes. Text inside a growing card needs its own timing or it vanishes before anyone reads it. Never let the card underneath peek out around a growing photo. Make the last frame identical to the first or the loop stutters.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for the inputs, then show me the state list on the beat grid before you write any code.
</start>

title: Interactive WebGPU Plush Hammerhead Shark
text:
Build a single-file interactive WebGPU page called "Plush Hammerhead".

Page: an editorial layout with a big two-line title "Plush / Hammerhead.", a warm studio-grey background, a control panel on the right, live readouts and collapsible technical notes. English UI.

The toy: a plush hammerhead shark. It has a wide, flat hammer-shaped head (cephalofoil) whose ends sweep back a little, with a shallow notch at the middle of the front edge. A glass eye sits on each tip of the hammer, looking out sideways. It has a tall sickle-shaped dorsal fin, two pectoral fins and a tail with a long upper lobe and a small lower one. A cream belly panel is sewn on below a seam along each flank, with embroidered gill lines. A smiling mouth is cut in under the hammer, lined with felt and set with soft white felt teeth; its lower jaw swings open on a hinge.

Simulation:
- Body, hammer and fins are one signed distance field filled with a soft-body XPBD lattice: shape-matched hexahedral cells and tetrahedral volume preservation. It is skinned to a high-res surface-nets mesh.
- It swims with a travelling S-wave that bends the cells' rest shapes side to side, more toward the tail, and steers by turning its head, the body curving into each turn.
- Fur is drawn as alpha-to-coverage shells over minky pile. The pile lags behind each jiggle on a spring and can be combed.

Behaviour:
- It circles its space.
- Scan: it sweeps its hammer side to side over the floor the way real hammerheads hunt. It also does this on its own now and then, and a little while hunting.
- Feed drops in a felt fish: it turns, closes in faster, opens wide and snaps it up.
- Dash is a burst of fast tail beats; Chomp opens the mouth and snaps it shut.
- Grab it by the tail and it thrashes; let go and it shoots off.
- Boop the middle of the hammer with the finger and it wriggles and blushes.

Tools: Hand, Finger, Comb.

Controls:
- Buttons: Feed, Dash, Scan, Chomp, Smooth fur, Reset, Pause.
- Toggles: Circle, quarter speed, Mesh.
- Sliders: Stuffing, Pile, Tail beat.
- Three fabrics: Bronze, Lagoon, Sunset.

title: Nobel Prize Neutrino Astronomy Scientific Explainer Motion Graphics
text:
You are a world-class cinematic Motion Design Director, After Effects Art Director, 3D Scientific Visualization Director, and VFX Director.

I want to create a high-end scientific music animation about the Nobel Prize in Physics based on the SRT lyrics I provide.

SRT is the only basis for timing.

Do not assume, modify, or generate timelines on your own.
Do not output fixed timecodes.
Do not mechanically map one lyric line to one shot.

You must autonomously design shot durations, editing rhythm, camera changes, and visual climaxes based on actual lyric onset times, pauses, repetitions, rhythm, and musical structure in the SRT.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
[1. Final Visual Goal]
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

What I want is not an ordinary popular science animation.
Not a PPT.
Not an infographic.
Not children's science.
Not a simple 3D model display.
Not an AI tech template.

What I want is:
Cinematic AE Motion Design
+ Top-tier 3D VFX
+ Apple TV+ science documentary texture
+ High-end tech keynote visual aesthetic
+ IMAX science documentary scale
+ Modern music MV rhythm
+ Houdini / Cinema 4D / After Effects level visual effects

Overall feeling:
Stunning, Mysterious, Premium, Modern, Grand, Precise, Cinematic, Futuristic, Scientific.

The visual should make the audience think:
"This is not an ordinary YouTube explainer, this is a cinematic science visual blockbuster."

But the spectacle must be grounded in scientific logic.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
[2. Core Narrative]
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

The entire animation must revolve around a complete visual story:

Distant universe generates neutrinos
↓
Neutrinos barely interact with ordinary matter
↓
They can penetrate massive celestial bodies and even Earth
↓
This also makes them extremely difficult to detect
↓
Scientists bury massive numbers of optical detectors deep in Antarctic ice
↓
Forming the IceCube Neutrino Observatory
↓
A rare neutrino interacts with an atom in the ice
↓
Producing a charged particle
↓
The charged particle produces Cherenkov light in ice
↓
Detectors record photon arrival positions and times
↓
Massive data forms a spatial trajectory
↓
Tracing the neutrino's incoming direction from trajectory and time data
↓
Ultimately tracing back to high-energy celestial objects in the distant universe
↓
Humanity gains a new way to observe the universe

The whole video must let general audiences understand this logic. Not just look scientific, but be truly comprehensible.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
[3. Most Important Visual Concept]
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Establish a single core visual DNA across the entire piece:
"The blue neutrino trajectory."

Do not design the neutrino as an ordinary glowing ball.
It should be: ultra-thin, high-speed, mysterious, almost invisible, with a subtle blue-white glow, like a ghost trajectory from the depths of the universe.

This trajectory runs through the entire video:
passing through nebulae, supernovae, near black holes, through Earth, through human bodies, entering Antarctica, traversing 2 km of ice, and leaving an observable blue trace in IceCube.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
[4. Visual Style]
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Primary colors: Pure black, Deep space blue, Deep gray, Ice blue, Silver white.
Sole primary accent color: Electric Blue / Cherenkov Blue.

Prohibited: Cheap rainbow gradients, cyberpunk purple/pink, excessive RGB, overt neon, cheap glow, game UI, tech templates, heavy HUDs, meaningless complex numbers, PPT charts.

Must have abundant black negative space to keep light, particles, and ice as visual focal points.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
[5. Cinematic Cinematography]
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Avoid static shots. Use cinematic visual language: Extreme Wide Shot, Macro Shot, Extreme Macro, Deep Space Fly Through, Orbital Camera, Long Lens, Dolly In/Out, Tracking Shot, Crash Zoom, Whip Pan, Parallax, Volumetric Camera, Micro-to-Macro, Continuous Camera Movement.

Emphasize scale transitions across: Universe → Galaxy → Star → Earth → Antarctica → Ice Sheet → Detector → Atom → Particle.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
[6. Cosmic Section]
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Space scenes must serve the concept that neutrinos originate from extreme environments: supernovae, black hole accretion disks, relativistic jets, AGNs, gravitational lensing, spacetime curvature.

Extract a fine blue neutrino trajectory from an immense cosmic event and follow it with the camera.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
[7. Neutrino Penetrating Earth]
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Camera rapidly approaches Earth from space. Earth turns semi-transparent, revealing crust, mantle, outer core, inner core. Neutrino passes straight through with volumetric light and realistic layering, exiting the opposite side.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
[8. Why Difficult to Detect]
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Contrast visually: photons hit/reflect/absorb; other particles interact; neutrinos pass right through. Repeat, leaving darkness and a faint blue point.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
[9. Antarctic Ice Sheet]
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Cinematic ice dive from space down into Antarctica's ice depth, showing real refraction, scattering, crystal structure, cracks, air bubbles, and volumetric light, plunging into total darkness before IceCube detectors light up one by one.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
[10. IceCube as a Visual Icon]
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Design as an architectural, temple-like, futuristic 3D detector grid spanning kilometers with strong scale contrasts.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
[11. The Most Important Scientific VFX]
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Neutrino enters ice; camera dives to extreme macro (ice → molecule → atom → nucleus). Neutrino interacts → charged particle created → travels faster than light in ice → Cherenkov blue light cone forms, illuminating surrounding ice crystals and triggering IceCube sensors.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
[12. Blue Light and Detectors]
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Detectors light up sequentially according to physical arrival times, producing faint blue halos as camera flies through.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
[13. Abstracting Principles into Visuals]
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Show Cherenkov light detection, recording 3D coordinates and arrival timestamps, organically synthesizing the reconstructed particle trajectory.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
[14. Timing-Difference Localization]
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Visualize wavefronts, timestamps, and 3D paths merging into a directional arrow extending back through ice, Earth, and space pointing to the distant cosmic origin (SOURCE RECONSTRUCTION).

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
[15. Final Cosmic Scale]
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Camera pulls back from IceCube → Antarctica → Earth → Moon orbit → Solar System → Milky Way → deep cosmos, connecting the tiny blue point to the vast universe.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
[16. Final Visual Climax]
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Black void with blue neutrino trajectory branching into LIGHT, GRAVITATIONAL WAVES, NEUTRINOS. First two fade, highlighting NEUTRINOS, concluding with "A NEW WINDOW TO THE UNIVERSE".

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
[17. Motion Design]
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Utilize particle systems, point clouds, volumetric light, depth of field, motion blur, procedural animation, physics-based motion with inertia and easing.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
[18. SRT-Driven Timing]
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

I will provide an SRT file as the sole time reference. Automatically determine shot durations, transitions, and pacing based on lyrics.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
[19. Visual Rhythm]
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Verse: mysterious, restrained.
Pre-chorus: accelerating particles and camera motion.
Chorus: grand, explosive blue light, massive detector grid.
Science section: precise macro clarity.
Final chorus: cosmic scale release.
Outro: absolute silence, black void, single vanishing blue trajectory.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
[20. Typography]
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Cinematic modern sans-serif title design, emphasizing keywords (NEUTRINO, ICECUBE, 2 KM, CHERENKOV LIGHT, TIME, POSITION, DIRECTION, SOURCE) in white and ice blue with ample negative space.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
[21. Scientific Accuracy]
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Preserve scientific rigor: do not claim neutrinos are massless; do not depict neutrinos as ordinary photons; Cherenkov radiation comes from secondary charged particles traveling through ice.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
[22. Aesthetic Standards & Final Deliverables]
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

title: Interactive WebGPU Plush Cow Material Study
text:
Build a single-file WebGPU "material study" page called "Plush Cow" in the same studio style as my previous plush toys (plush goat / crab / shark / penguin): editorial layout, large italic serif title "Plush / Cow.", kicker "Material Studies / No. 029", live status chip, specimen panel with tools and sliders, stats row (Mass, Volume, Steps, Moos), collapsible "Inside the experiment" notes. UI in English, works on mobile (no horizontal scroll).

The toy: a round stuffed Holstein cow (inspired by the cartoon cow that runs on its udder) who stands and runs on the four teats of her big pink udder — the splayed teats are her only legs. Body = one smooth SDF (round barrel body, big head, wide hot-pink muzzle, rounded udder with a crease, four teats ending in felt pads, a rope tail with a black shaggy tuft) meshed with surface nets. Black Holstein spots with wobbly edges (one around an eye), glossy button eyes, stubby cream felt horns, embroidered oval nostrils and a smile, pink blush, and two cloth ears sewn on sticking straight out at the sides (white outside, pink inside) that flap like wings.

Physics: XPBD soft body on a hex lattice (shape-matched cells + tetrahedral volume preservation, volume readout ~100%), skinned to the mesh. Posture-driven locomotion: teat nodes are feet with footing targets, swing lift and a lead point; trot in diagonal pairs (front-left + back-right, then the others). Behaviours: Trot (wanders), Gallop (bouncy laps), Hop (airborne, ears beat like wings), Moo (WebAudio low sawtooth "mmm-OOO" through an opening/closing lowpass, ears flick up, slow head toss), Topple (falls on her side and rocks back up), Smooth fur, Reset. Booping her nose with the finger makes her moo.

Fur: real-time shell fur with per-vertex pile (soft coat, short head, velvety pink muzzle and udder, long tail tuft and forelock), combable with the Comb tool. Tools: Hand (grab & squash, pull ears), Finger (poke / she follows it), Comb. Sliders: Stuffing, Pile (mm), Table friction (felt ↔️ ice). Palettes: Holstein, Jersey, Strawberry. 60 fps.

title: Meteor Time-Freeze Cinematic Sequence Prompt Orchestrated by Opus 5.5
text:
[Identity Lock | Woman]
Adult female, ~28, straight black hair, fair skin, dark brown eyes; knee-length bright red wool coat, black jeans, black ankle boots; red coat is the dominant color; continuous single actor, no face-swapping or outfit changes.

[Identity Lock | Man]
Adult male, ~30, short dark brown hair, light stubble, light olive skin; navy jacket, grey hoodie, dark jeans; holding two white paper coffee cups without logos; continuous single actor, no face-swapping or outfit changes.

[Space]
Fixed geography: ~15m wide two-lane urban street flanked by storefronts; warm-lit cafe on left with glass door facing street; glass bus stop on right facing cafe; street extends to horizon; meteor streaks from top right to horizon, exploding outside city; dust wall surges towards camera; he exits cafe on left, she waits at bus stop on right, meeting in street center without screen direction inversion; ~10 pedestrians.

[First Frame]
24mm low-angle wide shot looking down street; quiet night street, shop lights, streetlamps, dark sky; top-right sky glows bright orange-white.

[Timeline / SHOT 1]
0.0–4.0s | 24mm low wide upward tilt: 0.0–1.5s sky lights up brighter than day, cast shadows swing rapidly; 1.5–3.0s pedestrians gaze up as massive burning meteor streaks across top-right sky towards horizon; 3.0–4.0s meteor glare reflects on cafe door glass, creating first match cut.

[Timeline / SHOT 2]
4.0–9.0s | Match cut from glare, 35mm handheld outside cafe: 4.0–5.5s he pushes door open holding two coffees, looks up and halts; 5.5–7.0s he sees her across the street at the bus stop, eyes meet; 7.0–8.0s both sprint into street; 8.0–9.0s massive white explosion at horizon washes out screen, creating second match cut.

[Timeline / SHOT 3]
9.0–15.0s | Match cut from whiteout, 35mm elevated street view: 9.0–11.0s whiteout fades to mushroom cloud and orange fireball; 11.0–13.5s shockwave blasts storefront windows successively towards camera, alarms blare, dust wall rolls forward; both sprint towards street center; 13.5–15.0s nearest window shatters toward lens, creating third match cut.

[Timeline / SHOT 4]
15.0–19.0s | Match cut from flying glass, 50mm eye-level profile, both in street center: 15.0–17.0s reaching out, he drops both coffees, liquid spills, glass whirls, dust wall 20m away, wind pulls hair; 17.0s time abruptly freezes completely; 17.0–19.0s absolute standstill except she slowly blinks, creating fourth match cut.

[Timeline / SHOT 5]
19.0–25.0s | Match cut from blink, 35mm handheld over her right shoulder: 19.0–20.5s realizing she can move, she looks around; 20.5–23.5s steps forward through suspended shards, gently deflects a floating glass shard which stays in place; passes frozen coffee spill, frozen pigeon, frozen pedestrians, frozen fiery dust wall; 23.5–25.0s approaches him and reaches out, creating fifth match cut.

[Timeline / SHOT 6]
25.0–30.0s | Match cut from reaching hand, 50mm close profile: 25.0–26.5s fingertips touch his frozen cheek; 26.5–28.0s he blinks, inhales, looks at her and unfreezes, clasping her hand; 28.0–30.0s adjacent suspended glass shard vibrates and drops; both watch it fall; scene cuts mid-fall.

[Physics]
Meteor illumination realistically shifts street shadows; shockwave shatters glass sequentially outward; dust wall is volumetric fire/dust; time freeze is total for all background elements with zero motion blur or drift; deflected shard stays at new position; gravity resumes on moving subjects; only final shard vibrates and drops.

[Cinematography]
6 sequential camera setups; 5 match cuts matched to ending elements (reflection, flash, shard, blink, hand); camera static during freeze except Shot 5 tracking; no slow motion, no hero low-angles.

[Lighting/Color]
Opens cold blue with warm shop light; switches to harsh orange-white under meteor; orange-red explosion lighting; frozen world back-lit by fire inside dust wall; red coat remains focal point.

[Audio]
Shot 1 quiet traffic to escalating roar; Shot 2 doorbell, footsteps, distant impact; Shot 3 blast roar, shattering windows, alarms; Shot 4 wind/glass noise abruptly cuts to dead silence at 17s; Shot 5 quiet footsteps on glass and soft breath; Shot 6 sharp inhale and gentle glass hum.

[Locks]
Strictly 6 shots, 5 match cuts; zero spoken dialogue; continuous outfits and character identities without fusion; exact anatomical consistency; live-action film realism; video cuts while the shard falls.

title: First-Person 3D Procedural Arms and Dynamic Grip Rigging in Three.js
text:
TASK: Build production-grade first-person arms ("Hands 2.0") for a Three.js browser game, then fix them until every pose actually holds the object it should hold. Do the whole thing yourself with scripts, from generating the model to the in-game checks. I already did this once. Below is what works and the traps I fell into, so you don't repeat them.

━━━ PART 1 — THE MODEL (Blender + MPFB2, fully scripted) ━━━

1. Don't patch AI-generated "statue" arms (Meshy etc.). Chaotic topology with no edge loops at the joints and fingers baked into a pose will crease at every bend. Without clavicle and twist bones the wrist twists like a candy wrapper. Gluing separate generated parts together only adds seams to the same bad mesh. Start over with a real humanoid generator.

2. Use Blender (headless: `blender --background --python tools/hands/*.py`) + MPFB2 (MakeHuman, CC0) and its official asset packs. Put every step in a script so it can be rebuilt:
   - build_body.py: macro params (male, ~30 y/o, wiry and lean: muscle ~0.66, weight ~0.3) plus local arm targets.
   - build_arms.py: game skeleton with clavicle → shoulder → upperarm01/02 → lowerarm01/02 (twist bones!) → wrist → metacarpals → 3 phalanges per finger. Keep skin only from the elbow down and apply subdiv 1. Make the sleeve a separate mesh on the same bones, with real geometry for the rolled cuff. Accessories (watch, bracelet) are parented to forearm/wrist bones; watch hands are bones too.
   - build_tex.py: UVs, then bake veins, tendons and knuckles into geometry and normals. Author every detail in bone-local 3D space so it survives re-UVs, then bake in Cycles.
   - https://t.co/3ocKmFbTLm → pack script → hands_v2.glb. Budget ~25–40k tris for both arms incl. sleeves (they're huge on screen), 1–2 skin materials + sleeve + accessories. Textures 2048² on High, 1024² on Low, plus a tiling micro-normal for pores.
   - Generate a full body with pants, boots and the same shirt, and save it as a .blend for a future "player body" stage. Don't put it in the game yet.

3. Look: tanned back of hand and forearm, paler palm and inner side. Scars, calluses, short nails with natural cuticles. Flannel sleeves rolled just below the elbow, with a visible inside-out lining on the roll. Tactical watch on the left wrist, cord bracelet on the right.

4. Check skin weights on stress poses before you export: fist, pinch, spread fingers, 90° supination. Fix weights in a script, not by hand.

5. HARD STOP #1: render review shots in Blender (neutral light and warm daylight): front, back, palms, fist, pinch, cylinder grip, spread fingers, sleeve close-up, two plaid colour variants. Wait for my verbal OK. Iterate. Don't integrate anything into the game until I say yes.

6. glTF only gives you standard material slots, so use them as carriers. Example: MR = (R AO, G roughness, B subsurface thickness), emissive = masks (R hair, G dirt accumulation order), clearcoatNormal = pore tile. Document the mapping and read it back in the runtime.

━━━ PART 2 — SHADERS (MeshStandard/Physical + onBeforeCompile) ━━━

- Skin: wrap lighting, back-lit translucency in thin areas (fingers, webbing, knuckles go red against the sun), pore detail normal, micro-sheen, tan gradient by mask.
- Hair: 4 fur shells in ONE instanced draw, only on hairy triangles, visible on the silhouette against the sun. Disabled on Low.
- Dynamic state:
  · wet = max(world wetness, rain when not under a roof), with two layers of droplets. The sleeve goes darker when wet.
  · dirt builds up from game events (gather, pickup, log, fish_land, climb_out…), fingers and palms first through the mask, and washes off in water or rain.
- Arm lighting mirrors the world: shade under roofs, lamp light, lightning.
- Precompile every arm shader behind the loading screen. https://t.co/nXMh9v1zBi.programs.length must not grow during gameplay.
- Budget: the arm overlay may cost at most ~0.3 ms more GPU than before on High. Measure with a timer query before and after, not by feel.

━━━ PART 3 — THE ARM SYSTEM (data, not code) ━━━

Goal: a new item or action (axe, bow, paddle, steering wheel) should be a data entry plus a clip, never new logic.

1. Rig wrapper: bone map, wrist twist spread over the twist bones (e.g. 0.3 / 0.8 on lowerarm01/02). No candy-wrapper wrists.
2. Two-bone IK (shoulder–elbow–wrist) with pole vectors (elbows down and out) and joint limits.
3. grips.js: for each item, per hand: `at / axis / back / r / diag / gap / slide / fingers / thumb` in item space. One hand owns the item, the other IKs to its socket.
4. Fingers are always a joint table `[[mcp, pip, dip, spread, twist] × 5]` (absolute bend) and blend between poses. Autogrip closes the fingers until they touch the handle.
5. Animation layers, in this order: base pose → clip keyframes → IK → procedural (breath, bob, mouse-turn inertia, sway, recoil, fatigue tremor) → additive reactions. Smooth transitions between states.
6. Clips: JSON keyframes in code, plus importing .glb animations (with empty hand_R/hand_L) for future Blender-made actions. Clip events (strike frame, bow release) go onto the effects bus.
7. In-game pose editor (Shift+H, game keeps running, cursor free): sliders for item offset and rotation, sockets, every finger joint, elbow pole, shoulders, layer speeds. Show changes live. "Copy" puts JSON on the clipboard to paste into grips.js. I need to be able to tune a grip without Blender.
8. Keep the old public API as a facade (hands.anim, reach, lampInHand…) so fishing, boat, lamp, weapons, sleep and the seaplane don't need deep rewrites.
9. Port EVERY existing action: rifle (stance, ADS, fire, reload with mag, dry fire), knife (2 strikes), stone throw, fishing rod (cast, fight, reel, fish in hand), carried log, lamp, reach and pickup, plant gathering, inspect, crate, swimming (breaststroke and crawl), boat tiller, hands down while sleeping, hidden arms in vehicles. Each one must be at least as good as before. Delete the old arm code only after everything is ported (keep a backup).
10. HARD STOP #2: in-game screenshots for my approval (idle, rifle, rod, log, lamp at night, wet after swimming, dirty after firewood, under a roof and in full sun).

━━━ PART 4 — THE FIX PASS (bake this in from day one) ━━━

The first version shipped with these bugs. Every one of them came from old poses written for "stump" arms with no shoulder.

ROOT CAUSE: a real arm has a fixed length (shoulder→wrist ≈ 0.48 m in view space). Old poses put wrists at targets the arm can't reach. The solver then "cheated": it pushed the clavicle out (up to 0.32 m) and clamped the wrist rotation. The hand ended up somewhere else, while finger curls were cached for the ideal hand position, so the fingers squeezed thin air.
  - Rifle, left hand: handguard 0.516 m away with a 0.479 m arm → shoulder pushed out ~0.3 m and the fist still sat 3.8 cm below the handguard.
  - Rifle, right hand: wrist rotation clamped by ~21°, palm not seated on the grip.

FIXES, as SYSTEM features:
1. Shoulder stance as data: per item/pose, `stance: { L:[x,y,z], R:[x,y,z] }` with smooth blending, and the elbow pole moves with the shoulder. Rifle: left shoulder forward and in, right shoulder slightly back (a real shooter's torso rotation). The left elbow stays slightly bent and the clavicle doesn't stretch.
2. Elbow auto-swivel: give each forearm a pronation range (e.g. R −100°…+95°, 0 = thumb up). If the requested pole would over-twist the forearm or bend the wrist past its limit, rotate the elbow around the shoulder–wrist line to the nearest valid angle. The old poses were silently over-twisted (+101° on the rifle, +80° on the knife).
3. Grip by the REAL handle shape. A cylinder radius is wrong: the knife handle was a 2.6 × 4.2 cm oval, not Ø2.5 cm, so the knuckles sank 2–6 mm into it.
   - Handle = elliptical cylinder with end caps (`sec` [along back, across], `span`, `inset`).
   - measureSection(item, socket): take the cross-section automatically by slicing the item mesh around `at` along `axis`.
   - CPU-skin the hand (SkinnedMesh.getVertexPosition, palm and phalanx vertices with weights) and test real skin vertices, not phalanx tips.
   - gripFit, cached and computed at startup: first push the palm out until it leaves the handle. Then close each finger with all joints together until first contact, and after that only the joints past the touching phalanx. If the start pose already intersects, open it up.
   - Fingertip targets: `fingers: {1: {to:[x,y,z]}}` puts the index pad on the trigger.
4. Validator: hands.check(pose) and hands.checkAll(). Run every scenario × both hands + the live rod pose, print a console table, and show it live in the Shift+H editor with a "Check all poses" button. RED if wrist miss > 0.5 cm, rotation clamp > 3°, shoulder push > 0.5 cm, twist over the limit > 3°, or any skin vertex deeper than 1.5 mm inside the handle. Don't call the work done until it's all green (mine ended at 122/122).

DATA FIXES that came from my screenshots:
- Rifle: left hand on the WOODEN handguard, not the metal in front of it. Handguard runs diagonally across the palm, thumb along the left side, forearm coming in from the lower-left corner. Right hand fully on the pistol grip using the grip's real rake (axis (0, 0.95, −0.32), not a guessed 40°), index on the trigger. On reload the hand leads and the mag rides in the hand, and the shoulder dips to follow it. Check sprint, recoil, dry fire, and steering a boat while holding the rifle.
- Log: nobody carries a 44 × 7 cm log with two arms like a crate. One hand, an ordinary hammer grip like a bottle: knuckles up, thumb on top, held about a third from the back end, log pointing forward and up from the thumb side, riding in the fist. The throw is a one-handed wind-up and lunge. The left hand stays free, so the lamp stays in it.
- Swimming: fingers together and slightly cupped (no fan), hands in the bottom third of the frame. Crawl recovery comes in from the side, palm facing out. The sleeve never covers the middle of the screen and the palm never faces the camera.
- Fix every pose the validator flags: stone wind-up and throw, aim, lamp, lamp lowered, climbing, reach.

━━━ RULES ━━━
- Backup before each stage. Measure, don't guess: write every claim down as a number (cm, °, ms, tris, programs).
- No performance regression: grip fit is cached per socket, and the validator only runs in the editor or dev builds.
- Write down what's still unfinished honestly in the report (e.g. "right hand mostly below the frame on the rifle", "pinky sometimes curls without contact").
- DONE = I approved the renders and the screenshots, bends are clean on every grip, fingers wrap handles with zero penetrations, wet and dirt work, every old action works on the new system, a new item is one grips.js entry + one clip, and FPS is unchanged.

title: Rahibe Melek Savaşçı Dönüşümü

title: Ask me for: a short label for the first toggle, one main word, a…
text:
<inputs>
Ask me for: a short label for the first toggle, one main word, a percentage for the graph, text for the final card, one accent color and a track with a clear beat.
</inputs>

<direction>
A 2D motion design film in 16:9. Use a warm off-white canvas, near-black backgrounds, bold type and one vivid orange accent. The orange dot links every scene: it begins in the UI, becomes the dot above a letter, draws a spring graph, expands into a shape and reappears on the end card. A cursor makes the opening click feel real. Keep the movement crisp and controlled, with subtle spring overshoots and no empty pauses.
Banned: stock footage, gradients, glows, particle bursts, arbitrary transitions and movement that doesn't grow from something already on screen.
</direction>

<structure>
Around 15 seconds, with a visual change on every major beat.
Open: a cursor clicks the orange toggle beside "Reduce Motion". The letters bend and shift into place until only "Motion" remains, with the orange dot above the "i".
Spring: the dot leaps away from the word and lands on a graph. Its trajectory draws a spring response, passes the target and settles next to a "+22%" callout.
Shape: the dot races along a line, expands into an orange circle and fills the frame. A black rounded square rotates inside it, then extends into a pill. Everything contracts into one orange dot on black.
Type: words including "SPRINGS", "EASING", "KINETIC TYPE", "3D" and "SOUND" circle the dot. The ring of words spreads into a field of tiny dots.
Reveal: the halftone field expands and turns black, uncovering the final card: "Opus 5.5", "Motion designer." and "0 keyframes".
Return: the orange dot travels back through the halftone, graph and toggle. Make the last frame match the first for a seamless loop.
</structure>

<build>
1. Use one HTML file, 1920x1080 at 60fps. Calculate every visual from time inside seek(t): no CSS transitions, timers or state carried between frames.
2. Use closed-form springs for the toggle, moving dot and graph. Draw the graph with the same spring function that controls the dot.
3. Move the letters individually as "Reduce Motion" becomes "Motion". Keep the orange dot above the "i" until it jumps away.
4. Treat the orange circle, rotating square and pill as states of one shape. Carry its position and momentum through each change.
5. Arrange the words on a circular path, then send their letters outward to transition into the halftone grid.
6. Draw the halftone as a dot grid whose sizes react to the orange dot. Expand it beyond the frame before showing the end card.
7. Align the click, dot landing, graph peak, shape changes and final title with measured beats. Render one frame per beat to check timing before the full export.
</build>

title: Please use Three.js to write a single-file HTML (index.html) to…
text:
Please use Three.js to write a single-file HTML (index.html) to create a "hiking documentary style" 3D scene for screen recording narration videos.

[Basic Requirements]
- Import Three.js via CDN (cdnjs or jsdelivr), no build tools required, runnable directly by double-clicking in a browser.
- Strict 16:9 aspect ratio, designed internally at 1920x1080, centered with aspect ratio maintained and black bars filled when resizing.
- All adjustable parameters (terrain seed, route points, camera speed, etc.) centralized in a CONFIG object at top of file.

[Terrain]
- Use multi-layer noise (Simplex/Perlin, self-implemented) to generate a north-south mountain gorge: high mountains on both sides, valley bottom in the middle with a winding riverbed.
- Color by elevation and slope: deep brown/gray ridges, earthy yellow slopes, light yellow valley, blue-gray riverbed, light snow on peaks.
- Add fog and directional light to create a cold, dry plateau atmosphere.

[Route & Character]
- Define hiking route using a list of (x, z) waypoints in CONFIG, smooth with CatmullRomCurve3 matching terrain height.
- Render route as thick red line (subtle glow), passed section bright red, upcoming section semi-transparent.
- Red low-poly figure (capsule + sphere head + red coat) walking along route at constant speed, adjustable speed, supports pause.
- Support event markers on route (e.g., Assembly point, Last seen), displayed as vertical signs with text or pulsing rings.

[Camera]
- Four modes switchable via keys 1-4 with smooth transitions:
  1. High overhead view (flying forward along route, slightly tilted)
  2. Follow (behind and above character)
  3. Orbit (slow orbit around character)
  4. Free look (drag to rotate, scroll zoom, WASD move)
- Camera speed, height, pitch angle adjustable in CONFIG.

[UI Overlay (HTML/CSS)]
- Columns of member cards on both sides: square avatar (solid color + initial placeholder, customizable via URL), name, role caption.
- Member status: Normal / Deceased (gray card with red border) / Missing (semi-transparent with question mark).
- Centered bottom subtitle bar, white text with black stroke, supports [[keyword]] yellow highlight.
- Top right shows "Episode X" title and progress bar (optional).

[Timeline Driven]
- Describe storyline in CONFIG with a TIMELINE array, each entry containing time (seconds) and action:
  { time: 0,  action: "camera", mode: 1 }
  { time: 3,  action: "subtitle", text: "Then why did you dare to [[join]]?", duration: 4 }
  { time: 8,  action: "walk", from: 0, to: 0.4 }
  { time: 15, action: "status", member: "Hu Yanglin", state: "missing" }
  { time: 20, action: "marker", at: 0.6, text: "Last seen" }
- Playback logic: Space to play/pause, R to reset, auto-trigger events at timestamps.
- Small debug panel top-left, press H to hide for clean recording.

[Sample Content]
- Preset 8 fictional members (Tie Gao - organizer, Qian Niao, Hu Yanglin, Mimi, Members 5-8), ~90s demo timeline covering overhead view, walking, event markers, status changes, ending subtitles.

[Code Requirements]
- Clearly partitioned code with Chinese comments (terrain, route, character, camera, UI, timeline).
- Stable 30fps+ on standard laptops, terrain resolution ~256x256 vertices.
- Explain how to modify route, avatars, and add timeline events after completion.

UI in English, works on mobile.

The toy: a round plush hedgehog — one SDF body (a round bun with a pointed snout, two little round ears, a flat seat) meshed with surface nets, a button nose, glass eyes, four short plush paws (tubes with a bendable wire inside that keep the shape you bend them to).

Physics: XPBD soft body on a hex lattice (shape-matched cells + tetrahedral volume preservation, live volume readout), skinned to the mesh, sitting under gravity on Coulomb friction. It breathes with its flanks, twitches its snout when it sniffs, and slowly rights itself toward the way it last walked. Curling into a ball is a second rest shape found once at load (the body led nose-to-tail and squeezed into a sphere so the stuffing can really take that shape); curling blends every cell's rest shape and every tet's rest volume toward it. Nothing holds the ball upright, so a push makes it roll; when it stops it unrolls and stands up again.

Spines: hundreds of soft felted cones rooted on the skin, rebuilt every frame from the skin's stretch and turn; they lie back toward the tail, stand up when it bristles or curls, lag behind every jolt on a damped spring, part around the finger and fold on the table instead of going through it. Cream root, dark band, pale tip, a short fuzz over each. The face, belly and paws wear minky shell fur that lies back from the nose and takes the comb.

Behaviours: Trundle (walks on its paws in diagonal pairs), Curl up, Roll, Bristle, Smooth fur, Reset. Hand: pick it up — hold it a moment and it curls into a prickly ball in your hand; put it down, squash it, throw it; bend a paw. Finger: it trundles over and sniffs your finger; run the finger through the spines and they part; poke its back and it huffs and rolls up. Comb: brush the minky. Sliders: Stuffing, Pile, Spines. title: Interactive 3D Squishy Toast Memory Foam Simulation
text:
Build "Squishy Toast" - a single self-contained HTML file (three.js from a CDN is the only dependency): an interactive 3D slice of slow-rise memory foam bread you can press, poke, stretch and squash.

The toast
- A real bread silhouette: square body, rounded "muffin top" crown, soft beveled edges
