title: One-file 1440×1440 UI morphing sequence with beat-synced state changes
text:
Ask me for: 8 to 12 UI states I want the shape to become (e.g. button, loader, player, slider, toggle, tabs, chart, command palette, toast), pure black and white or one accent color, and a royalty-free song around 120 BPM (e.g. Mixkit, free for commercial use).
</inputs>

<direction>
Dribbble-level UI motion. One shape, never cut: every state is the same element morphing its size, radius and color while its content swaps with a short blur. A cursor drives every change with real clicks and drags. Light warm-gray canvas, black and white components, one clean UI font (Geist). Springs everywhere, a tiny overshoot at most. The camera zooms so each state fills the frame. The last frame is the first frame, so it loops.
Banned: bouncy easing, particle bursts, glows, gradients on UI chrome, mismatched icon strokes, dead time, anything that looks like a template.
</direction>

<structure>
120 BPM, 7 bars, something happens on every beat.
Button → loader → check → dynamic island → music player with a play/pause morph → scrub the progress bar → it becomes a volume slider that stretches when dragged past max → a toggle flips on the beat → the knob becomes a liquid tab indicator → the tabs open into a chart that draws itself, with a tooltip on hover → it collapses into ⌘K → type to filter → enter → toast → back to the button.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML file, square 1440x1440. Every style is computed from time inside seek(t): no CSS transitions, no timers, no state carried between frames.
2. Springs are closed-form step responses. A value that changes target many times is the sum of one spring per change, so it stays a pure function of time.
3. The tab indicator's two edges ride different springs, so the leading edge stretches ahead of the trailing one. Same trick for the toggle knob.
4. Drags are direct manipulation: while the cursor is held, the value is computed from its position. On release it springs back from wherever it was.
5. Analyze the song with numpy for the beat grid and start on a downbeat. Place every UI sound by its measured peak.
6. Render with Playwright: 4 subframes per frame, blended with ffmpeg tmix for motion blur at 60fps.
7. Render one frame per beat before the full render. Fix anything off the grid, cramped or hard to read.
</build>

<gotchas>
Never put will-change on anything the camera scales or the text renders blurry. Text that swaps inside a morphing container needs its own enter and exit timing or it overlaps. Make the last frame identical to the first, cursor position and speed included, or the loop stutters.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for the inputs, then show me the state list on the beat grid before you write any code.

title: Photoreal SpaceX Falcon 9 launch in a Three.js HTML scene
text:
Create a single self-contained HTML file using Three.js that renders a photoreal industrial **Falcon 9 launch** in daylight. The scene should look like filmed reference of a Cape Canaveral / SLC-40-style pad, not a stylized game trailer.

Constraints

* Load Three.js from a CDN only. No other libraries. No physics engine. No build step.
* Everything lives in one HTML file and runs when opened in a modern browser.
* Fill the entire viewport edge to edge. No margins, borders, blank bars, or unused frame.
* No overlay text, titles, labels, HUD, captions, menus, buttons, or UI.
* Start automatically on page load.
* Optimize for smooth real-time performance. Prefer fewer physically grounded effects over many decorative particle systems.

Visual style

* Photoreal industrial daylight, not stylized, not neon, not “vibrant AAA.”
* Palette: scorched concrete, dirty white metal, soot, steel, sunlit steam, pale blue sky.
* The only intense color should come from the engine plume and its heat light.
* Use `MeshStandardMaterial` / `MeshPhysicalMaterial`, ACES Filmic tone mapping, physically based lights, PCF soft shadows, and light atmospheric fog.
* Hard sunlight, readable shadows, dirty wear on metal and concrete. No toy-like plastic materials.

Falcon 9

* Build a recognizable Falcon 9 Full Thrust / Block 5-class stack as the clear focus: first stage, black interstage, second stage, payload fairing.
* Correct tall proportions. Keep the vehicle large enough to read tank bands, raceway, octaweb, engine bells, folded landing legs, and stowed grid fins.
* Nine Merlin engines in the octaweb. Landing legs and grid fins stay stowed.
* White booster with realistic panel seams, soot, and wear. Not a stack of untextured cylinders.
* Sit the rocket vertically on the pad at the start.

Launch site

* Detailed industrial pad: scorched concrete, blast marks, flame trench / deflector, pipes, platforms, barriers, service equipment, tanks, and a SpaceX-style **strongback / transporter-erector** beside the rocket — not a generic NASA gantry.
* Mechanical arms / umbilicals hold and service the vehicle before release.
* Distant low coastal terrain and structures only. Almost no vegetation in the blast zone. No green park, no colorful hills, no decorative grass next to the engines.
* Water deluge hardware implied by the effect: at ignition the ground cloud is mostly **steam and soot**, not desert dust.

Lighting

* Bright daytime sky, strong sun, high visibility.
* Engine light is a local warm/white source that lights the octaweb, pad, trench, and lower strongback. It must not flood the whole world like a generic point light.

Animation sequence

Drive the motion with simple authored timing and kinematics only. No rigid-body physics library.

1. Short calm pre-launch: faint venting, light steam drift, small warning beacons.
2. Nine engines ignite under hold-down. Tight high-velocity plumes, not campfire flames.
3. Hold-down fire for about 1.5–2 s

title: Interactive translucent gummy-dice playground with soft-body physics
text:
Create “Jelly Dice” — a polished, interactive 3D playground with translucent gummy dice that users can grab, stretch, poke, and roll. Deliver a complete single-file HTML experience using genuine WebGPU.
ART DIRECTION
Make the dice look like premium gummy candy: rounded corners, glossy surfaces, rich translucent colors, small internal bubbles, and clearly readable pips.
Use a warm off-white background, soft studio lighting, and subtle contact shadows. Keep the composition spacious and elegant, with large dice as the main attraction.
The dice should feel heavy, elastic, and substantial — not weightless balloons, rigid plastic, or liquid slime.
GEOMETRY AND MATERIALS
Generate all geometry procedurally. No external models or image files.
Create rounded cubes with slightly pillowy faces and gently rounded pips.
Use conventional dice numbering, with opposite faces adding up to seven.
Keep pips and internal details attached to the deforming geometry.
Use thickness-dependent translucency, color absorption, refraction, soft internal scattering, and smooth highlights.
Thick regions should have deeper color; thin edges should transmit more light.
Avoid blown-out reflections, harsh black outlines, visible seams, and disappearing surfaces.
Provide six saturated color presets: Emerald, Amethyst, Amber, Sapphire, Ruby, and Lime. Default to Emerald. Changing colors must not reset the simulation.
SOFT-BODY PHYSICS
Use a stable volumetric mass-spring or position-based dynamics system with approximate volume preservation.
Each die must deform locally. Do not fake softness by scaling the entire object.
Pulling a corner or face should stretch that area first, while the rest follows elastically.
Grounded dice should resist immediately tipping over when pulled. Their lower surface should have enough friction to create a convincing anchored stretch.
Stronger, sustained pulls should still lift or overturn them naturally.
Separate rigid-body rotation damping from internal deformation damping, so the dice can feel heavy while remaining visibly squishy.
On release, stretched regions should recoil, wobble, and gradually settle.
Landing should briefly compress the die before a restrained rebound.
Include gravity, inertia, floor friction, and collisions between dice.
Prevent excessive overlap, floor penetration, explosive impulses, and endless bouncing.
Use fixed simulation steps, bounded grab forces, and stretch limits for stability.
INTERACTION
Left-click or touch a die to grab it at the exact contact point.
Drag to stretch, lift, or move it.
A quick tap should produce a small local poke and wobble.
Right-drag or drag empty background to orbit the camera.
Support a limited zoom range and a Reset view button.
Keep object dragging separate from camera gestures.
Offer a selector for 1–5 dice, with three selected initially.
Add a Roll the dice button and Space-key shortcut.
Toss dice with varied trajectories and rotations, then let the simulation settle naturally.

title: Interactive 3D snow globe browser scene with snow and weather controls
text:
Create "Snow Globe" — a beautiful, interactive 3D snow
globe that users can shake and watch settle in their
browser. Deliver one complete standalone HTML file using
genuine WebGPU with WGSL shaders.

ART DIRECTION
- A glass sphere on a turned wooden base, large and
  centered, on a warm off-white background with soft
  studio lighting and a subtle ground shadow.
- Inside: a tiny procedural winter village — three or
  four cottages with pitched roofs and softly glowing
  windows, a few layered pine trees, a small footbridge,
  and a snow-covered ground mound.
- The glass should read as real glass: refraction that
  visibly bends the village at the edges, Fresnel
  reflections, a crisp window-shaped highlight, and a
  faint rim caustic on the base.
- Mood: cozy, quiet, a little magical. Keep it elegant
  and uncluttered.

GEOMETRY
- Generate all geometry procedurally. No external models,
  textures, or image files.
- The village must sit fully inside the sphere with
  nothing clipping through the glass.
- Snowflakes are small, soft, slightly varied flakes, not
  uniform dots. Include a toggle for sparse glitter
  flecks that catch the light.

SNOW AND WATER PHYSICS
- Simulate several thousand snow particles on the GPU in
  a compute shader.
- Shaking the globe moves the water: particles swirl in
  vortices, trail behind the motion, and slosh back when
  the shake reverses. Use a simple fluid velocity field
  or curl-noise flow driven by the globe's motion, not
  independent random drift.
- After shaking, flakes slow down, drift, flutter, and
  settle over roughly 10–20 seconds.
- Settled snow accumulates on roofs, tree branches, and
  the ground, and is knocked loose by the next shake.
- Particles must never escape the sphere or pass through
  the village. Use fixed simulation steps and bounded
  velocities so violent shaking stays stable.

INTERACTION
- Click-drag or touch-drag the globe to shake it; faster
  drags produce stronger swirls, and the globe itself
  tilts and springs back.
- On mobile, a "Use motion" button requests device-motion
  permission (required on iOS) and lets the user shake
  the phone.
- Right-drag or two-finger drag orbits the camera, with
  limited zoom. Keep camera gestures separate from
  shaking.

CONTROLS
- Give it a shake (auto-shake button)
- Reset, Reset view, Pause
- Snow amount slider
- Water thickness slider (how slowly flakes fall)
- Glitter toggle
- ¼ speed toggle
- Three scenes: Alpine Night, Cabin Dawn, Northern Lights
  (aurora glow in the sky dome inside the globe).
  Switching scenes must not reset the snow.

INTERFACE
- Top left: small "MATERIAL STUDIES" label, large italic
  serif heading "Snow Globe.", caption "Shake gently.
  Wait patiently. Winter keeps."
- Top right: WebGPU status indicator.
- Right side: compact "THE KEEPSAKE" control panel.
- Bottom left: a short interaction hint.
- Clean sans-serif controls, thin borders, generous
  whitespace. Adapt to mobile without covering the globe

title: Synced launch video remake for a product
text:
TASK: synced remake of REF=[path/to/reference.mp4] for [PRODUCT] = [one line: what it sells + the offer + price]. Played side by side with REF it is visibly frame-locked; played alone nobody can tell it came from REF. KEEP IDENTICAL (measured, not eyeballed): every cut frame, shot length, layout slot, element size + position per frame, entrance/exit frame, easing curve, camera move, typing cadence (chars per frame), cursor path, transition coverage % per frame, luminance per shot (dark where REF is dark), blur on/off per move, audio hit times, music drop frame. SWAP EVERYTHING ELSE: every image, object, word, colour, texture, UI chrome, logo, font. Look = [LOOK, e.g. "page #FDFDFB + sky linear-gradient(180deg,#263F72,#769CC2) with thin white line art at 20–35%, frosted glass (white 30%→14%, backdrop blur 24px saturate 1.3, 1px white rim, shadow 0 18px 50px rgba(10,22,50,.18)), Inter 600, one accent #2F6BFF"]. Images = [my real work frames/clips | CC0/public-domain photos | original characters drawn in code]. BANNED: 3D-modelled props, stock/generated people, copyrighted memes/characters/logos, purple/magenta/orange as brand, blue-on-blue with scanlines, fake camera HUDs, hexagon bokeh, code-synthesized audio.
ACCEPTANCE (all numeric, all reported; nothing ships without the table):
Cuts: 0 frames off REF.

Per shot: motion-energy curve (mean-abs frame diff at 192x108 grey) cross-correlated with REF's over the shot → peak at lag 0 ±1 frame AND corr ≥ 0.80.

Per shot: 10 stacked REF-over-ours frames; key element edges within 1% of frame (19 px x, 11 px y).
Beauty: a fresh critic that sees only REF vs ours at full res answers "is ours at least as beautiful and polished as REF at this frame?" → YES on every storyboard frame.
Not recognisable: the same critic, shown ours alone, cannot name REF's brand or product from any frame.
Smoothness (ours, full film): 0 runs of ≥3 frozen frames (diff < 0.03) mid-scene; < 5 jerky steps (consecutive moving frames whose diff ratio > 2.2); no diff > 25 except at a REF hard cut.
Voice: every line starts within ±40 ms of the frame its first word appears; no word spoken > 150 ms before its word is on screen; each line one continuous take (longest internal silence < 120 ms unless REF has it); speed 0.95–1.05.
Sound: every REF hit within ±15 ms; every small cue ≥ 3 dB above its band at that moment; voice p10 ≥ 9 dB over music+SFX on every line; -14 LUFS ±0.5, true peak ≤ -1.0 dBTP (4x oversampled), limiter active < 2% of samples; every music splice crossfaded (jump ratio at splice ≤ the track's own beat jumps).

title: Interactive 3D sakura jelly tree made of translucent gummy candy
text:
Create “Sakura Jelly” — a beautiful, interactive 3D cherry blossom tree made entirely of translucent gummy candy. Deliver a complete standalone HTML file using genuine WebGPU.

ART DIRECTION

Imagine a miniature sakura tree made for a premium candy exhibition.

Give it a curved trunk, gracefully branching limbs, and an airy canopy of individually modeled blossoms and petals. Use rich cherry pink, raspberry, and soft rose tones, with a translucent amber-pink trunk.

Use a warm off-white background, soft studio lighting, and a subtle ground shadow. Keep the tree large and centered. Avoid washed-out colors, blown-out highlights, and a canopy made of simple opaque spheres.

JELLY MATERIAL

Create glossy, translucent gummy material with:
- Thickness-dependent color absorption.
- Refraction and soft internal light scattering.
- Smooth highlights and delicate rim lighting.
- Richer color in thick branches and greater translucency in thin petals.

Generate geometry and material details procedurally. No external models or image files.

PHYSICS AND INTERACTION

Let users grab the trunk or a branch and pull it sideways. The tree should bend locally and elastically, with smaller branches following with a slight delay.

Keep the base anchored. Use a stable mass-spring or position-based dynamics system with fixed simulation steps, damping, and bounded stretching.

On release, the tree should spring back and gradually settle, with visible secondary motion throughout the canopy. Do not simulate softness by simply rotating or scaling the entire tree.

SHAKING AND FALLING PETALS

This is the main interaction:
- Shaking the tree makes jelly petals detach and fall.
- Stronger shaking releases more petals.
- Detect shaking from changes in motion, not just from holding the mouse.
- Petals should flutter and rotate while falling.
- When they hit the ground, they should squash, bounce softly, wobble, and settle.
- Fallen petals remain translucent and visibly jelly-like.
- Let users grab and move a limited number of fallen petals.

Keep detached petals separate from the canopy so nothing visibly duplicates or teleports. Gradually regrow blossoms, and provide a Reset button.

CAMERA AND CONTROLS

- Left-click or touch the tree to grab and shake it.
- Right-drag or drag empty space to gently orbit the camera.
- Support limited zoom.
- Keep camera gestures separate from grabbing.

Add:
- Shake the tree
- Firmness slider
- Internal damping slider
- Petal amount slider
- Reset
- Pause
- Reset view

Provide three palettes: Cherry, Raspberry, and Peach. Change colors without resetting the simulation.

INTERFACE

Use a minimal editorial layout:
- Small “MATERIAL STUDIES” label.
- Large italic serif heading: “Sakura Jelly.”
- Caption: “A little spring. A little wobble. A very sweet blossom.”
- Compact control panel on the right.
- Bottom hint: “Take hold. Give it a shake. Let spring fall.”

title: Interactive 3D balloon demo with pumping and popping
text:
Build "The Balloon Test": a single-file, mobile-friendly 3D toy in one HTML page (Three.js bundled inline, Web Audio, no external assets except Google Fonts).

Scene: a warm paper studio. On the right, a latex balloon is pulled over the chrome nozzle of a weighted stand. On the left, a floor pump: charcoal barrel, chrome rod, wooden T-handle and a round pressure gauge (0–8 kPa, red zone from 5), joined to the stand by a rubber hose. The camera reframes as the balloon grows, keeps the pump in view and leaves room for the HUD. On tall phones the pump stands further back.

Play: tap anywhere (or Space) to pump. The handle drives down, air moves while it travels, the hose twitches and the gauge needle overshoots slightly and settles. The limit is hidden and random per round. Captions escalate ("The first breath is the hardest.", "Easier now. Watch the needle.", "Getting round.", "That is a lot of balloon.", "The rubber is getting thin.", "Please stop."). Flick (F) taps the skin: a ripple runs over it, and the note rises as it tightens. Water toggle (W), reset (R).

Physics you can read:
- Inflation pressure follows a Gent rubber model. It peaks on the first stroke, falls as the balloon grows, then climbs steeply near the limit, and the gauge shows exactly that.
- Inflation shape: the uninflated balloon is a flat, limp pouch that flops over. Early on, only the neck end inflates while the slack tip still lies on top. Then it becomes a teardrop with a small thick nub at the tip. Near the limit, a weak spot bulges out (an aneurysm).
- It swings about the nozzle (the neck bends, the nozzle does not), with a light idle drift. Water balloons are squatter, heavier and jiggle.

Rendering the latex (the core of the look):
- Draw each wall in two passes, back wall first, then front. A multiply pass filters the background by per-channel Beer–Lambert transmittance from the dye colour, with thickness = rest thickness / area stretch and longer paths at grazing angles. An additive pass adds scattered light, clearcoat reflections and a little translucency glow.
- The result: deep, saturated colour when slack, glassy and tinted when stretched, with a saturated rim and lighter centre. Slack rubber shows wrinkles. The neck has a rolled lip.
- A coloured floor shadow from an analytic ellipsoid: tinted in the middle, dark at the rim. Water balloons add a caustic.
- A printed design glued to the rubber's own coordinates (star, polka dots, smiley, "POP? / HANDLE WITH CARE", hearts or plain). It starts tiny and crumpled, grows with the balloon, and cracks into a mosaic when overstretched. Every balloon also carries "@vib3coded" in the same ink, printed from a separate layer so it stays legible while the motif cracks.
- Water mode: a slightly smaller inner skin with real transmission/refraction.

The pop, in real time (no pause):
- It goes on the final stroke. A ragged tear front runs from the weak spot round the skin in a couple of frames, the rubber bunching along i

title: Interactive translucent jelly dice scene in the browser
text:
Build "Jelly Dice": a single self-contained HTML file (all JS/CSS inline, no build step) with translucent gummy-candy dice that behave like real soft bodies. Render with raw WebGPU (WGSL shaders, no three.js). If WebGPU is unavailable, show a clean fallback card that explains why.

PHYSICS (the heart of it; it must feel like real jelly, not a rigid die with a wobble shader)
- Each die is a rounded cube simulated as a tetrahedral lattice with XPBD: co-rotational shape matching (per cell and per tet) for elasticity, tet volume constraints so it is nearly incompressible, and hard strain limits so it can never stretch without bound. Inverted elements must always recover.
- Floor contact with static and kinetic friction, plus a raised rim around the plate. Die–die contact against each other's rounded box, with friction.
- Separate rigid motion from deformation: rotational resistance on the floor, internal damping that only damps the wobble, never the rigid motion.
- Sleep when calm: settled dice must never jitter. Wake neighbours when an awake die comes close.
- Heavy landings soak up the rebound, so a dropped die squashes and settles instead of bouncing like rubber.

INTERACTION
- Drag a die to stretch it. The grab is compliant and progressive: a gentle pull stretches the jelly while its base clings to the plate, and a firm pull lifts and moves it. Cap the force, and allow no launches or wild spin on release.
- A quick tap pokes: a small squish into the surface, and the whole die rings.
- Drag the empty table to orbit the camera, pinch or scroll to zoom. The camera drifts gently toward where the dice are, never while one is held.
- Roll button (and Space / R): throw 1–5 dice (number picker). When everything settles, read each top face and show the values plus the total. A die resting cocked against another gets a small nudge (twice at most) before the result is read.

LOOK (photographic, like a product shot of real candy)
- Procedural photo studio: warm paper sweep, a big overhead softbox, a back-left strip light and a cool fill card.
- The dice sit on a frosted-glass plate with a bright rolled bevel, satin sheen and fine grain, casting its own soft shadow on the table.
- Candy material: real refraction (bend the ray in, find the exit depth from a back-face pass, look up what is behind), Beer–Lambert absorption by thickness so thin parts are light and the core is deep, thin edges glowing when the key light shines through, and glossy Fresnel skin with a crisp highlight.
- Pips: ivory dots set just under the skin in shallow concave dimples. Pips on the far faces stay visible through the body.
- Dice seen through other dice must refract correctly (depth layers wherever their screen footprints overlap).
- Soft shadows whose penumbra grows with distance; the shadows are tinted with the candy colour and lighter, because the candy is translucent. Contact occlusion from a top-down height map.
- Smooth normals from the deformation Jacobian (cofactor)

title: Naruto runs through nine anime worlds in changing styles
text:
Build a complete, polished browser animation called “One Naruto, Nine Worlds.”

The experience is a moving illustrated gallery: one Naruto runs sideways through nine anime worlds arranged in a 3×3 grid. As he enters each world, his anatomy, face, linework, shading and movement change to match that anime’s visual language.

1. COMPOSITION AND LAYOUT

Create a clean 3×3 gallery in this exact arrangement:

TOP ROW:
Naruto | JoJo’s Bizarre Adventure | One Piece

MIDDLE ROW:
Dragon Ball | One Punch Man | Jujutsu Kaisen

BOTTOM ROW:
Sailor Moon | Pokémon | Attack on Titan

Each panel has its own illustrated environment, a consistent frame and a small, readable title. Use a warm off-white gallery background with narrow, even gutters.

Keep Naruto relatively small: approximately one-third of a panel’s height while running normally. Leave room to appreciate the scenery, silhouettes and movement.

Only ONE Naruto is visible at a time. The other panels contain their environments while awaiting his arrival.

Keep the gallery responsive, preserve the 3×3 arrangement and use the available viewport space efficiently.

2. NARUTO’S IDENTITY

Preserve the recognizable identity across every transformation:
- Blond hair.
- Forehead protector.
- Whisker marks.
- Orange as the main clothing color.
- A recognizable Naruto-inspired outfit.

Adapt the design itself to each world. Change body proportions, facial construction, hair shapes, line weight, shadow shapes and motion.

If a reference sheet is attached, use it to guide the individual styles and composition. Build actual animation around those designs.

3. NINE DISTINCT VISUAL DIRECTIONS

NARUTO
A warm Hidden Leaf Village environment with tiled rooftops, trees and distant rocky scenery. Use classic shōnen proportions, expressive eyes and clean cel shading. Naruto runs with his torso leaning forward and his arms extended behind him.

JOJO’S BIZARRE ADVENTURE
Make the transformation unmistakable: a muscular torso, broad shoulders, strong thighs, angular facial features, sculptural shadows and confident posing. Use bold graphic colors and dramatic architectural scenery.

Keep the face clearly readable and the head proportionate to the large body. Give him a powerful stride and one brief theatrical pose, followed by a smooth return to running.

ONE PIECE
Use long, elastic arms and legs, a broad expressive grin, rounded forms and playful distortion. Place him in a colorful coastal setting with a ship, harbor details and bright sky.

Allow exaggerated limb arcs and squash-and-stretch. The movement should feel rubbery and adventurous.

DRAGON BALL
Use athletic proportions, angular blond hair, pronounced brows, bold contours and hard-edged cel shading. Create rocky terrain, distant mountains and a vivid sky.

title: Chrome extension spider crawler that summarizes webpage text live
text:
Build a Chrome extension (Manifest V3) called "TL;DR Crawler" that works on any normal web page.

WHAT IT DOES
Click the toolbar icon: a line-drawn spider appears on the current page, follows your cursor (also while scrolling), reads the text it walks over and builds a short TL;DR in a floating panel. Click the icon again: everything disappears and the page is exactly as before.

1. TOGGLE
- background.js: chrome.action.onClicked injects content.js with chrome.scripting.executeScript.
- content.js checks a global flag. If the crawler is already running, it shuts down and cleans up. Otherwise it starts. Only one instance per tab, ever.

2. FIND THE TEXT
- Find the main readable area: prefer <article> or <main>, otherwise the element with the most paragraph text. Skip nav, header, footer, aside, menus, forms, code, ads and hidden elements.
- Collect text blocks (p, li, blockquote, h2-h4) and split them into sentences. Store each sentence as a DOM Range (sentences can span links and bold text, so do NOT wrap them in elements).
- Watch the area with a debounced MutationObserver (1s) to pick up text loaded later (infinite scroll, lazy content).

3. PICK KEY SENTENCES
- Score each sentence: +2 digits, +2 for %, $, €, million, billion; +1.5 for words like first, record, launch, announce, new, only, biggest, fastest, warns, raises, cuts; +0.3 per capitalized name (max +2); -2 if under 40 or over 260 characters.
- Mark the top 25% as key sentences (min 5, max 80), spread so most paragraphs get one.
- Summaries, max 9 words each:
  - If an API key is set: send all key sentences in ONE request to Claude and ask for a JSON array of short, plain summaries (max 9 words, keep numbers and names exactly, no hype). Request again in batches when new text appears.
  - Without a key: fallback summary = the sentence with filler openers removed (and, but, however, also, according to), cut at a word boundary with "…".

4. THE SPIDER
- Shadow DOM host at document root containing a full-screen fixed <canvas> (pointer-events: none, z-index 2147483646) and the panel.
- Look: small rounded-rectangle body, abdomen ellipse, head with two white eyes, outlines in #5ab8ff. 8 legs as 3px blue lines with pink (#ff4f7a) joint dots, two segments each with inverse kinematics, knees bending outward.
- Gait: two alternating leg groups. A foot steps only when it's ~80px from its ideal spot and the other group is planted. Steps last 0.13s with a small lift, landing slightly ahead in the walking direction.
- Movement: target = cursor position + scroll, so it follows while scrolling. Max ~420 px/s, smooth acceleration, stops ~40px from the cursor, turns smoothly toward its direction. If the cursor is idle for 8s, it wanders around the viewport.
- requestAnimationFrame with a fixed 1/120s physics step. Support devicePixelRatio and window resize.

5. CRAWLING
- Every 80ms and on every foot landing, find the text under the spider with document.caretRangeFromPoint (ignore the extension's own elements).
- If that point is inside a key sentence not yet found: highlight it with the CSS Custom Highlight API (::highlight(tldr-found) with a soft yellow background) and add its summary to the panel.
- If a foot lands on a normal word: in ~25% of cases glitch just that word. Wrap only that word in a span (it's a single text node, so it's safe) and apply one random effect: monospace font, blue outline, blue highlight, slight rotation, wide letter-spacing, blur or uppercase. Max 2 effects per word. Record every change so it can be undone.

6. PANEL
- Top-right, draggable by its header, inside the Shadow DOM so site CSS can't affect it.
- Dark (#16181c), mono title "TL;DR" in yellow (#ffd166), a "found / total" counter, a pink progress bar and a numbered list in article order. The newest item flashes yellow and the list auto-scrolls to it. The list scrolls inside a max height.
- Buttons: "Copy TL;DR" (plain text to the clipboard), "Restart" (clears highlights, glitches and the list) and "Close" (full shutdown).
- If a key is set, add "Write TL;DR with Claude": sends all found sentences and returns 3 short lines using only their facts, numbers unchanged. Show a "Thinking..." state, then the answer under the list.

7. API KEY
- options.html: a field for the user's Anthropic API key and a model name, stored in https://t.co/YDJaSAQOTq.local.
- All API calls go through background.js with fetch to https://t.co/ePcSurB2Zg, with headers x-api-key, anthropic-version: 2023-06-01 and content-type: application/json.
- Handle errors quietly: if a call fails, keep the fallback summaries and show a small "AI unavailable" note.

8. QUALITY RULES
- Never break scrolling, clicks, links or text selection on the site.
- Full cleanup on shutdown: canvas, panel, highlights, wrapped word spans, inline styles, listeners, observers, timers.
- prefers-reduced-motion: no glitches, slower walking.
- Plain JavaScript, no libraries. Files: manifest.json, background.js, content.js, options.html, options.js, icons (16, 48, 128).
- Permissions: activeTab, scripting, storage. Host permission: https://t.co/tIh0b4zPlQ*.

At the end, give install steps: open chrome://extensions, enable Developer mode, click "Load unpacked", select the folder, then open options and paste the API key.

title: Three.js island scene for a survival game project
text:
PROMT 5 

Stage 18 — Island 2 as a real playable zone

Goal: the low, hazy islands on the far left of the starting view stop being cheap backdrop geometry and become a real second island you can reach by motorboat, moor at, and walk around on. It should read as the edge of a large swampy mainland: a low mangrove shoreline, a river mouth facing island 1, and a swamp river leading inland into jungle. This stage is only the foundation. River water, jungle and the wooden boat come in later stages.

1. Location and terrain
- Find how the distant islands are built now and replace them with island 2 in the same spot, about 380 m from the boat pier, so crossing at full throttle takes 1–2 minutes. Keep one of the old far islands as scenery.
- Give island 2 its own heightfield module (separate from island 1's grid and with its own seeded RNG, so island 1's placement never shifts). Build the coastline mask, run an exact distance transform, then add noise: a muddy shore 0.2–0.6 m high, a gentle rise inland to about 4 m, and hills/karst in the west up to about 25 m where the river "comes from".
- Carve the river system into the terrain now: Catmull-Rom splines for a main channel, a branch, a backwater and two creeks, each with width and depth tables along its length (about 20 m between sand spits at the mouth, a wider estuary, about 7 m in the hills). Add floodplains with small ponds, and a shallow muddy delta in front of the mouth. River water level is flat (sea level), so one reflection plane stays correct.
- Bake the data grids later stages will need: height, real distance to water, calm-water gradient, sand, channel proximity (for planting) and coast. Add CPU and GLSL accessors so getHeight, getShoreDist, the water shader, the underwater composite, the ripple sim and rain all understand island 2.

2. Level-of-detail zones
- Two zones, island 1 and island 2. Only the zone the player is in gets the full detail set: layered ground, grass, undergrowth, LOD trees, shadows, planar reflection. The other zone gets a cheap far mesh plus tree impostors, faded by aerial perspective.
- Switch smoothly with hysteresis. Build detailed 80 m terrain chunks nearest-first in time-budgeted slices (no frame over about 30 ms) while the player is still at sea, dither them in over the far mesh, and dispose of everything when you leave. When looking from island 2 back at island 1, hide small objects by screen size.
- Shadow cascades, water sim windows, caustics and reflections must follow the player to island 2. Check float32 precision at x ≈ −900 for shimmering or jitter.

3. Sea between the islands
- Rework the soft world boundary so a corridor to island 2 is open while the rest of the sea still pushes you back. Shape the seabed as deep water rising to a muddy shallow at the mouth.
- Near island 2, fade out waves, swell, surf and foam, and shift the water colour from turquoise to murky green-brown with no visible seam. From island 1, island 2 should read as a hazy silhouette w

title: 15-second cinematic handheld sailing-boat scene with two photoreal women
text:
Two women framed by the open companionway of a small wooden sailing boat — one in the near foreground at frame right inside the cabin in a white ribbed tank top and wide cream linen trousers, seated on the varnished steps with one knee up, looking at the camera; the second up on deck through the hatch in a lilac knit polo and white trousers, holding the rigging with one hand and leaning out, facing the camera. Setting: a classic teak sailboat cabin, varnished wood panelling, a brass porthole, rope coils and a folded striped towel in the foreground, the open hatch revealing the sunlit deck, white sails, a stone harbour wall with small moored boats and flat blue sea under a pale sky, soft late-afternoon light. Shot on an early-2000s point-and-shoot digicam with harsh direct on-camera fill flash that aggressively illuminates the near woman and the cabin wood, flattening her features and putting sharp specular highlights on the varnish, the brass and her shoulders; the deck and harbour beyond stay visible but hazy, milky and underexposed relative to the flash. Warm, slightly saturated CCD tones, strong bloom and halation at the hatch edges, minor digital noise. Candid amateur, Y2K editorial, unpolished but stylized. 4:5.

Photorealistic character reference sheet of one young woman, 16:9, plain light-grey seamless background, soft even daylight, no text, no labels. Top row: full body front, three-quarter, side profile, back view, standing relaxed and barefoot. Bottom row: close-up head front, three-quarter, profile, then a four-face expression strip — neutral, soft closed-mouth smile, mid-word talking, easy laugh. Small insets: layered gold necklaces, hands, linen fabric texture. She is in her early-to-mid 20s with sun-kissed light olive-tan skin, dense natural freckles across her nose and cheeks, warm flushed cheeks, hazel-green almond eyes, defined natural brows, a straight nose, and full lips with a soft rosy-nude tint. Her hair is very long, sun-streaked honey-brown with lighter blonde ends, center-parted, with face-framing pieces and a slightly salty, undone texture. Wardrobe: a white fine-ribbed scoop-neck tank top, cream loose-weave linen wide-leg trousers, and two thin gold chains — one with a tiny cross, one with a small oval medallion. Skin realism: visible pores, fine texture, faint unevenness, natural sheen on the cheekbones, no smoothing, no retouching, no beauty filter. Identical face, hair and body across every panel.

Photorealistic location reference sheet, 16:9 grid of six panels, no people, no text. Panel 1: wide exterior of a classic 1960s teak sailing yacht moored in a small Mediterranean stone harbour at golden hour — glossy varnished hull, white sail half raised, stone harbour wall, small white fishing boats, flat blue water. Panel 2 (hero angle): inside the cabin at seated chest height, looking up the varnished teak companionway steps to the open hatch — deep glossy mahogany panelling, a large brass porthole on the right wall, a small brass bell above it, a thick coiled cream-and-navy rope at left, a navy-and-white striped towel folded on a bench in the foreground, a bright slice of deck, rigging, sail and harbour through the hatch. Panel 3: on deck looking back toward the hatch — teak deck planks, cleats, winches, coiled lines, the hatch opening, harbour and low sun behind. Panel 4: close detail of the brass porthole, bell and varnish reflections. Panel 5: companionway steps close-up — worn varnish, a brass drawer pull, a small brass handrail. Panel 6: the harbour view from deck — stone wall, moored boats, flat sea, a pale golden sky with a low sun. title: Cinematic outer-space journey from Earth to a black hole
text:
Cinematic space journey, ultra-realistic, IMAX quality, 8K.

Opening: slow push-in from the dark side of Earth at night, city lights glowing like golden veins, a thin blue line of atmosphere on the horizon as the sun rises behind the planet, dramatic lens flare.

Camera accelerates past the Moon, gliding low over grey craters with long sharp shadows, then shoots outward toward Saturn — massive rings filling the frame, ice particles sparkling in sunlight, the camera flies between the ring layers.

Transition: the camera dives into a vibrant nebula — swirling clouds of magenta, teal and deep orange gas, newborn stars glowing inside, volumetric light rays piercing through dust.

Finale: a supermassive black hole with a glowing accretion disk, light bending around the event horizon (gravitational lensing like Interstellar), camera slowly orbits it as time seems to slow down.

Style: Hans Zimmer-style epic atmosphere, deep blacks, high contrast, anamorphic lens, smooth drone-like camera movement, volumetric lighting, photorealistic, no text, no people.

No stock photos of people, no text over photos, no gradient text, no generic icon-card grid, no purple.

title: Interactive jelly chess game with squishy physics
text:
Build "Jelly Chess": a single self-contained HTML file (three.js bundled inline, no external requests except fonts) with a full chess set made of glossy gummy jelly. Two modes: a two-player hotseat game with complete chess rules, and a toy box where the pieces can be grabbed, thrown, poked and shaken.

LOOK
- Classic Staunton pieces cast in jelly: lathe-turned profiles, rook crenels, bishop slit, queen crown points, king cross, knight with a sculpted bevelled head.
- Real gummy material: MeshPhysicalMaterial transmission with refraction, attenuation colour and distance, clearcoat; a studio environment for reflections; soft key-light shadows that match the deformed shapes (custom depth material with the same vertex deformation).
- Juicy flavour pairs instead of white and black, switchable with a button: Lime & Raspberry (default), Orange & Blueberry, Lemon & Grape, Peach & Mint, Cherry & Pineapple. Use the flavour names everywhere in the UI ("Lime to move", "Raspberry wins").
- The board: glazed ceramic tiles in neutral latte tones so the candy colours carry the picture, set in a wooden tray with a procedural wood texture; files a–h and ranks 1–8 burnt into the rim (each glyph turns round when the board is seen from the other side).
- Markers: little syrup drops in the mover's colour on legal squares, rings on captures, a soft highlight on the last move and the selected square, a pulsing red glow under a king in check.

JELLY MOTION (per-piece springs, vertex shader deformation)
- Lean in x and z, squash and stretch with the volume kept, twist, and a poke dent; taller pieces swing slower, underdamped so they ring for a while.
- Moves are hops: a crouch, a stretched leap, a squashy landing, then the top carries on and wobbles.
- Captures: the victim gets squashed, then hops off to a tray beside the board (at the ends of the board on tall screens). Castling hops the rook too. Promotion morphs the pawn on landing.
- A king in check fidgets; a mated king slumps.

RULES (Play mode, hotseat)
- Full legal move generation, verified with perft (start position 197,281 at depth 4; Kiwipete 97,862 at depth 3).
- Castling, en passant, a promotion picker (♛♜♝♞), SAN with disambiguation, a move list, undo, flip the board, new game.
- Check, checkmate, stalemate, threefold repetition, fifty-move rule and insufficient material, with an end card ("Checkmate. Raspberry wins · 2 moves", plus New game and Look at the board).
- Tap to select and tap a target, or drag a piece onto a square; an illegal drop hops back.

TOY MODE
- Grab and throw pieces (throw velocity from the last ~0.1 s of pointer movement, so holding still before letting go just drops it); tap to poke (a dent and a ring).
- Shake the box, and Set up (everything hops back to the starting position).

title: Cinematic 3D animated comedy scene of a penguin crossing a jungle river
text:
Character-design reference sheet on a clean light cream / pale warm-yellow studio background, neatly organized like an official high-end 3D animated feature-film character model sheet. Every view must show the SAME original penguin character with strict identity and proportion consistency.
Top-left title block reading:
MILO — YOUNG ADVENTURER
TYPE: young penguin
PERSONALITY: curious / optimistic / clumsy / determined
BUILD: tall pear-shaped body / oversized feet
STYLE: premium realistic 3D animated character
AGE APPEARANCE: young
Below the title, include a COLOR PALETTE with labeled swatches for CHARCOAL FEATHERS, CREAM BELLY, GOLDEN NECK PATCH, BEAK, FEET, EYES.
Center-left: large FULL-BODY FRONT VIEW and FULL-BODY SIDE VIEW, standing naturally.
Center: FULL-BODY 3/4 VIEW as the main hero pose and FULL-BODY REAR VIEW.
Center-right: HEAD FRONT VIEW, HEAD SIDE VIEW, and HEAD 3/4 VIEW.
Bottom: an EXPRESSION STRIP showing the same face with HAPPY, DETERMINED, CONFUSED, EXCITED, PANICKED, and DAZED expressions.
Beside it, include three small ACTION POSES: sprinting awkwardly with feet kicking backward, balancing with both flippers stretched outward, and celebrating with both flippers raised.
Character Design
Milo is an entirely original young penguin with a distinctive, instantly recognizable silhouette.
Tall, slightly pear-shaped body rather than a short round body.
Soft charcoal-grey feather covering across the head, back, shoulders and outer flippers.
Large creamy-white belly extending naturally from the lower face through the torso.
Two subtle muted golden-yellow feather patches running down the sides of the upper neck.
A distinctive small messy three-feather tuft on top of his head, asymmetrical and slightly leaning to one side.
Large warm dark-brown eyes with visible brown irises and small natural highlights. Expressive but not excessively oversized.
Narrow, slightly curved charcoal-black beak, longer and slimmer than a typical cute cartoon penguin beak.
Long, thin, flexible flippers.
Oversized pinkish-grey webbed feet that create an intentionally awkward silhouette.
Slightly long legs visible beneath the body when running.
Detailed soft feather texture with individual feather breakup around the chest, neck and flipper edges.
Friendly, innocent facial structure.
Expressions are communicated naturally through eyelids, eyes, head position, beak movement and body posture.
No clothing. No hat. No accessories. No uniform. No shoes. No human hairstyle. No logos. No weapons.
Rendering
Premium photorealistic 3D CGI animated-feature rendering.
Detailed individual feathers, soft feather displacement, physically realistic materials, subtle subsurface scattering around the beak and feet, realistic eye reflections, cinematic studio lighting, gentle contact shadows and extremely clean character-model presentation.
Combine believable penguin anatomy with exaggerated animated proportions suitable for expressive physical comedy.
Milo m

30-SECOND 3D ANIMATED COMEDY
Reference: Use the attached @ Milo character sheet as the exact visual reference for Milo. Maintain his identical face, eyes, three-feather head tuft, charcoal-grey feathers, cream belly, golden neck patches, long thin flippers, pear-shaped proportions, oversized pinkish-grey feet and overall silhouette throughout the entire video.
The reference defines Milo's appearance only.
[GLOBAL]
Duration: exactly 30 seconds.
Aspect Ratio: 9:16 vertical.
Genre: animated adventure comedy.
Core Story: Milo wants to cross a fast tropical jungle river. His first solution, riding a ridiculously tiny wooden plank, fails spectacularly. Refusing to give up, he returns inside a giant hollow coconut used as a boat with two broad leaves as paddles. His second attempt works. Milo navigates dangerous rocks and rapids, becomes overconfident and celebrates his victory, completely unaware that the river leads directly toward a huge waterfall.
Visual Style
Premium photorealistic 3D CGI animated feature-film aesthetic.
Highly detailed soft feathers, expressive character animation, lush tropical environments, realistic water physics, cinematic lighting, vibrant natural colors and exaggerated physical-comedy timing.
Warm sunny daylight throughout.
Natural cinematic depth of field.
Physically believable character weight and momentum underneath the exaggerated animation.
Maintain an entirely original visual identity.
Environment
One continuous tropical jungle river system.
Dense palms, enormous broad leaves, hanging vines, moss-covered rocks, rich green vegetation, turquoise water, distant jungle-covered hills and bright blue sky.
Milo begins on one specific grassy riverbank.
The river continuously flows downstream through rapids toward a waterfall.
Maintain this geography throughout the entire video.
No dialogue.
No text.
No subtitles.
No logos.
No HUD.
No additional characters.
SHOT 1 — 0:00–0:02
Wide lateral tracking shot.
Milo suddenly explodes through two enormous tropical bushes, already sprinting at full speed along the grassy riverbank.
His oversized feet rapidly slap against the ground while his long flippers swing wildly.
Under one flipper he carries an absurdly tiny rectangular wooden plank.
Camera races alongside him.
The fast turquoise river becomes visible ahead.
Milo stares toward it with absolute determination.
SHOT 2 — 0:02–0:04
Medium frontal shot at river level.
Milo dramatically skids to a stop inches from the river.
Grass and dirt kick forward around his feet.
He stares at the powerful rushing water.
Then looks down at his tiny wooden plank.
Then back at the river.
Beat.
Milo gives one extremely confident nod.
He throws the plank onto the water.
It looks hilariously small.
SHOT 3 — 0:04–0:06
Low side-angle tracking shot.
Milo backs up two steps.
Charges forward.
JUMPS.
He lands belly-first across the tiny floating plank.
Water bursts outward.
The plank sinks slightly beneath his weight...

title: 22-second square product launch film with typed captions and glass UI
text:
<inputs>
Ask me for: my product's name, a one-line pitch, my logo, 3-6 screenshots of my product, 40+ images of what it makes (or photos of it), my brand colours and font, an ElevenLabs API key and voice ID, and a royalty-free song with a clear drop (the file and the drop's timestamp). If I skip any, use the defaults: "Ora 2", "an image model made for taste", free Unsplash and Pixabay images, Geist, ink #111214, the voice Samara X (19STyYD15bswVz51nqLf) on eleven_v4, and Pixabay "Cascade Breathe" (129.83 BPM, drop at 75.39s).
</inputs>

<script>
Write a 9-line voiceover in this shape and map every line to my product:
"This is [name]. A [category]... made for [value]. [Verb] in ANY style. Show it a [input] — and it just... gets you. The more you use it, the BETTER it gets. Tune its [setting]. Its [setting]. Its [setting]. Every [output] — exactly how you see it. [Name]. Out now."
Light emotion tags only: [softly] on the quiet lines, [excited] on the [Verb] line. The opener gets no tag and a plain full stop.
</script>

<voice>
Call the ElevenLabs API directly with my key, no MCP. Generate 4 takes of the whole script in one read and let me pick. If one line is off, regenerate only that line 4 times and splice the best one into my take.
Cut every pause over 0.28s down to 0.2s, then level each phrase 85% of the way to the median level, changing gain only inside the pauses.
For word timings, cut the read at every pause of 100ms or more, transcribe each chunk on its own with Whisper and pin each chunk's first word to its measured onset. One Whisper pass puts words up to half a second late.
</voice>

<direction>
A 22 second square launch film, 1440x1440 at 60fps, in the style of an AI lab's launch: a white page, one typeface, black ink, real images, and every caption typed word by word at the exact moment it's spoken.
Every control (the prompt bar, the settings panel, the caption pill) is liquid glass: the scene behind it frosted, its edge bending that scene like thick glass, a top sheen, a bright rim and a soft lift shadow. Glass on plain white shows nothing, so put a slow pastel aura in my brand colours, or a blurred wash of the photo, behind it.
The one word she stresses types in a gradient of my brand colours with a faint glow behind it.
Motion rules: the camera always drifts (a 1.0 to 1.04 push per scene, and when one scene hands its content to the next, the next starts at the zoom the last one ended on), nothing pops in (fades of at least 0.3s, eased), images switch on 16th notes with a click each, scene changes land on phrase starts, and the music's drop lands on the [Verb] line. No full stops on screen.
Banned: selection-box highlights, beat-snapped slams, white flashes, 3D, templates.
</direction>

<structure>
Seven scenes, each hung on the voice:
1. "This is [name]": a collage of my images drifts out as the name types in big, then the category line replaces it.
2. "made for [value]": full-bleed flashes of my best images on 16th notes into the drop, with the line typed over them in white.
3. The drop: a glass prompt bar types a short prompt, then the result card switches style on every 16th, with a black style chip that rolls to each new name and a strip of thumbnails.
4. "Show it a moodboard": 9 images fly into a 3x3 grid, then ring around the result as "It gets you" types.
5. "The more you use it, the better it gets": two typed lines, the stressed word in the gradient.
6. The settings: a glass panel of 3 sliders, each moving as she names it. The picture shifts hue, rolls new seeds on 16ths, then turns poster, and a blurred wash of its own colours shifts with it behind the glass.
7. "Every [output], exactly how you see it": 120 of my images burst from the centre behind a glass caption pill, then collapse into my logo as the name types, with "Out now" underneath. Hold 2s.
Swap the prompt bar, the results and the sliders for my product's real input, outputs and settings.
</structure>

<sound>
Start the song so its drop lands on the [Verb] line, and anchor the beat grid there.
Duck the music under the voice with a 3-band sidechain (lows 30%, mids 85%, air 55%; 0.3s hold, 50ms look-ahead, 0.5s release), then move each phrase's mids until the voice sits about 9 dB over the music between 300 Hz and 4 kHz.
One downloaded Mixkit SFX per event, placed by its measured peak: a click on every image switch, a key on every typed letter, a soft landing on the stressed word, whooshes, and impacts on the drop and the logo, trimmed around their peak (many are 4 second risers). Fade the music on a dB curve under the end card. Loudnorm to -14 LUFS.
</sound>

<build>
1. One HTML canvas. Every frame is a pure function of time inside seek(t), and every caption and cut reads the word table.
2. The glass: snapshot the canvas behind the shape, blur it about 14px for the body, draw a lightly blurred copy magnified about 1.06x in a 12px band along the edge, then add the milk, sheen, rim and shadow.
3. Render with Playwright at 60fps with 8 motion-blur subframes, then encode with ffmpeg.
4. Before you show me anything: a contact sheet of stills, a frame-diff scan for single-frame pops (only the 16th-note runs may jump), and the voice-over-music ratio for every phrase.
</build>

<gotchas>
A [warmly] opener comes out whispered and [excited] sounds fake. A highlight box behind a word looks like a Windows text selection. If a scene's camera restarts at 1.0 mid-handoff, the zoom snaps. A 0.05s fade reads as a pop-in.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for the inputs, write the script, send me 4 voice takes to pick, then show me 8 stills before the full render

title: Interactive plush frog toy with grooming mechanics
text: Build "Plush Frog" — Material Studies No. 011.  One self-contained HTML file, raw WebGPU/WGSL, no libraries, with a clean fallback card when WebGPU is missing. All labels in English.  SHAPE. An original plush frog (not a copy of any existing toy) as a signed distance field: a soft bean of a body, two eye bumps smooth-unioned on top, haunches folded at the sides, stubby front feet, flattened where it sits on the table. Skin = surface nets of the SDF (one Newton step, gradient normals).  SEWN-ON PARTS, all embedded in the simulation lattice so they ride along with every squeeze: – two glass safety eyes: near-black beads with a dark amber ring round the pupil and mirror-bright gloss; they stay rigid (follow the polar rotation of the averaged deformation gradient, never squash); – an embroidered smile: a round thread tube laid along a curve projected onto the face; – a felt lily-pad beret with a notch, draped over one eye bump (its height settled at build time so the underside just clears the skin), with five cupped felt petals and a wool-knot heart.  PHYSICS. XPBD on the CPU, 60 Hz, 6 substeps. Hex lattice in the body's principal frame, boundary nodes snapped to the surface, barycentric embedding of every render vertex. Co-rotational shape matching per 8-node cell (warm-started rotation, strain stiffening), soft tet volume constraints (the stuffing compresses a little, unlike jelly), a firmer fabric shell. Edge damping, deformation damping relative to rigid motion, rolling resistance, sleeping. Floor with Coulomb friction.  FUR. Shell fur: the skin drawn ~40 times as instanced shells, outermost first. Strands are jittered points in rest-space cubes (~0.8 mm spacing); each shell keeps the fragments within a tapered cone around each point, so thickness and length vary naturally; per-strand tilt and crimp, a vertex-level wave; alpha-to-coverage under 4× MSAA. Rest-space regions: cream belly patch, pink dyed cheeks, a groove for the smile, a back seam, stitched toe lines, pile pressed flat under the felt cap.  FUR MOTION. Per vertex: a combed lie in rest space carried into the world by the local deformation gradient, plus a tip offset on a damped spring driven by gravity and the skin's own acceleration — toss the frog and the coat swings. Laid-down pile stands lower.  SHADING. Wrapped diffuse through the pile, darker toward the roots, two Kajiya–Kay lobes, a velvet term (pile seen against its lie looks darker and denser, with it, it shines), a soft halo in the outermost wisps, a per-vertex soft key shadow on the shells. Procedural photo studio, PCSS floor shadow plus contact AO from a top-down height map, felt with fibre fuzz and sheen, Khronos PBR Neutral tone mapping.  TOOLS. – Hand: soft patch grab with wide reach, twist with scroll or a second finger, pinch to zoom, orbit by dragging the empty table. – Comb: stroking lays the pile the way you brush (the stroke is carried back into rest space through F⁻¹); "Smooth fur" puts it back. – Squish:

title: Side-by-side boar animation refinement comparison in Blender
text:
Use Blender MCP to refine an existing rigged boar animation against a side-view video reference (144 frames at 24 fps, 6 seconds).

First inspect the scene, rig, rest pose, bone hierarchy, mesh weights, and existing animation. Create a verified backup before making changes.

Set up a synchronized side-by-side comparison in Blender: reference on the left, model on the right, with matching frame numbers. Review all 144 frames and match the visible motion as closely as the model’s proportions allow. Explicitly identify any poses inferred because of occlusion or missing depth information.

Animate complete leg chains from the shoulders and hips, with appropriate body movement and weight transfer. Preserve bone lengths. Match footfall timing, hoof placement and orientation, swing height, stride length, and joint bending. Avoid excessive bending of supporting legs, ground penetration, foot sliding, and unnatural hoof tilt.

Validate the front and hind legs separately before smoothing. Previous attempts improved the front legs but left the hind legs with short strides, insufficient swing flexion, and trajectories poorly positioned relative to the pelvis. Smoothing preserved these errors instead of correcting them.

Once the gait is correct, improve continuity without changing footfall timing or ground contact. Check interpolated and subframe poses using the deformed hoof mesh, not only bone positions. Treat numerical smoothness and contact checks as supporting evidence; also inspect the rendered motion.

If working from v4, preserve the approved front legs, torso, head, and tail animation, and modify only the hind-leg chains. Use the reference to determine hind-leg timing; do not assume a fixed offset from the front legs.

Deliver the updated .blend file and synchronized comparison video. Briefly report what changed, what failed and how it was fixed, what was verified, and any remaining mismatch. Do not claim an exact 1:1 match unless the comparison supports it.

title: 12-shot Solo Leveling fantasy fight animation
text:
STRUCTURE: Exactly 12 shots with 11 hard cuts; each shot is internally continuous and begins from the exact positions, distance and facing established by the previous shot.

ENVIRONMENT: Huge dim Gothic throne hall about 40m long with two rows of massive square stone columns, tall narrow arched windows, warm-white diagonal sunlight beams filled with dust, dark polished stone floor, iron wall torches, dark-red hanging banners, a huge gold-relief double door at the east end, and a rough dark-grey north wall with a square pillar near the door.

SCREEN DIRECTION LOCK: All side views shoot from the south toward the north; east/gold door always remains screen-right, west always screen-left.

YOUNG WARRIOR: One adult male, about 22, lean athletic build, 1.78m, short fluffy black hair with bangs above brows, dark-brown eyes, clean-shaven determined face; charcoal hooded zip jacket with hood down, dark-grey T-shirt, dark jeans and worn dark sneakers.

His only power is brief blue magical electricity and particles around his palm/body during awakening or forceful actions; never a constant aura.

He is normally unarmed; only at the beginning he briefly holds one ornate gold dagger which dissolves into blue particles and never returns.

DEMON: One adult humanoid bipedal demon about 2.3m tall, lean but powerful, covered in segmented dark-crimson lacquered carapace with spikes and small hooks; integrated horned faceplate with two backward-curving horns and two narrow glowing white eye slits.

A heavy dark-crimson segmented crest extends from the back of the helmet like rigid armored feathers; it is not soft hair and never turns pink.

Hands are crimson armored claws with five pointed digits each; feet are armored clawed feet.

Weapons: one massive black two-handed greatsword with gold rivets and fine gold lines, plus one short dagger with broad grey blade, black ribbed grip and gold end caps.

The demon always runs and walks upright on two legs, never on all fours.

IDENTITY LOCK: Both characters remain identical throughout in face, body, hair, clothing, materials and proportions; no cloning, morphing, face swaps, costume changes, extra limbs, fused bodies or altered anatomy.

SPATIAL TRACKING: Warrior begins about 6m from the gold door facing west; demon approaches from west and stops about 18m from the door, leaving about 12m between them. Greatsword is planted at the 18m position with dagger beside it and both stay there permanently. Demon charges to warrior at 6m, carries him 3m east, and slams him at about 3m from the door. Warrior later throws demon about 6m west so demon lands about 9m from the door. Final close combat pushes warrior about 3m north onto the pillar beside the gold door. Final slide carries warrior about 4m west. No teleporting or unexplained repositioning.

SHOT 1 | 0.00-1.00: Extreme close-up of the warrior’s eyes in front of the gold door; he looks up toward the west, focused and calm; slight camera push; CUT.

SHOT 2 | 1.00-3.80: Low tracking shot over the demon’s rear-right shoulder; demon walks east dragging the black greatsword, blade scraping sparks and scratches across the floor; small warrior visible far ahead near the gold door; camera advances with demon; from 3.20-3.80 demon stops in the hall center about 12m from warrior; CUT.

SHOT 3 | 3.80-6.80: Begin close on warrior’s right hand holding the ornate gold dagger; 3.80-4.60 he releases it and it dissolves into blue magical particles immediately after leaving his palm; 4.60-5.20 brief blue electricity erupts around the open palm then fades; 5.20-6.80 camera pulls back/up into an over-shoulder medium shot as he lowers stance into an unarmed fighting guard; one brief blue pulse crosses his body and disappears; demon remains about 12m away; CUT.

SHOT 4 | 6.80-10.00: Low-angle medium shot of demon; 6.80-7.60 white eye slits glow as head turns toward warrior; 7.60-8.40 demon swings greatsword in a half-circle and drives it point-down into the stone on its right, cracking the floor and throwing dust/rubble; sword remains upright; 8.40-9.20 demon draws the short dagger; 9.20-10.00 opens claw and drops dagger beside the planted sword, where it bounces twice and stays; CUT.

SHOT 5 | 10.00-14.00: Side wide tracking shot, demon screen-left and warrior screen-right, about 12m apart; 10.00-10.80 demon crouches unarmed with claws open; 10.80-11.30 launches across the distance at supernatural speed, each footstep cracking stone, and drives right shoulder into warrior’s abdomen; 11.30-12.30 ONLY SLOW-MOTION SECTION: warrior folds over the demon’s right shoulder, head/arms hanging behind and legs in front, while demon keeps both feet on the floor and runs about 3m east; 12.30 return to real time; 12.30-12.60 demon dumps warrior from shoulder and warrior’s back hits first; 12.60-14.00 floor explodes into a cracked crater, dust and rubble spread outward, demon crouches beside the crater then rises and looks down; CUT.

SHOT 6 | 14.00-17.00: Strongly tilted low handheld close shot showing both full bodies; 14.00-14.40 warrior lies in crater while demon stands about 1m above him; 14.40-15.00 warrior plants hands and explosively jumps up; 15.00-15.50 warrior grabs ONLY the edge of demon’s left shoulder armor with his right hand, pivots hips and throws demon over his right shoulder toward the west; 15.50 warrior visibly opens hand and releases, creating immediate separation; 15.50-17.00 demon flies left/west while warrior stabilizes at crater edge watching; CUT.

Stage 19.2 — Passenger plane crash on island 2 

Goal: integrate a standalone plane-crash simulator, a single HTML file of about 2200 lines built by another AI, into the game as a live event. title: Procedural jelly kitten knight in a grassy field
text:
Build "Knight Kitten": a single self-contained HTML file, native WebGPU, fully procedural (no models, no textures, no libraries).

The scene: a tiny jelly kitten knight sitting in a grassy field.
- The kitten wears a little suit of armour and a bow.
- It holds a sword far too big for it, and a cape is sewn to its back.
- The kitten, the armour, the bow and the sword are all one signed distance field filled with a single lattice, so no part can come loose. Material regions are painted in rest space: jelly, armour, blade, grip, guard and pommel, bow.
- Candy-bright glossy eyes; tabby stripes and a cream muzzle, chest and toes inside the jelly.

Physics (XPBD):
- The body is a soft lattice: co-rotational shape matching on hexahedral cells plus tetrahedral volume constraints, a fixed 60 Hz step with substeps, edge damping and sleeping.
- The armour is firmer than the jelly.
- The sword is steel that bends: overlapping shape-matching clusters along it, with the hilt held in the kitten's grip in the torso's best-fit frame.
- The seat keeps its footing on the grass and the toy rights itself after a wobble.
- A drag stretches the kitten. "Lift" mode picks the whole kitten up so it dangles and jiggles, then lands and finds its footing again.
- The cape is an XPBD cloth (stretch, shear and bend constraints from a flat pattern) sewn to points embedded in the lattice.
  - Spheres riding the body keep the cape off it, and it rests on the grass.
  - Per-triangle aerodynamic wind acts on it.
  - The cape can be grabbed; a hard pull tugs the kitten along.

Rendering:
- The jelly is a refractive volume: front depth plus the nearest back face, absorption by thickness, a glowing deep colour, gloss and the environment refracted through it.
- The kitten is skinned on the GPU from the lattice nodes and their deformation gradients.
- The sun shadow map also stores the coloured light the jelly lets through; a top-down height map gives contact shading under the kitten.
- An instanced grass field around it sways in the same wind formula as the physics.

Weather presets, each with its own sun, sky and wind:
- Mist (soft hazy light);
- Wind (gusts that lean on the toy and blow the cape);
- Rain (falling streaks and splashes on the ground);
- Storm (dark sky, heavy rain, lightning flashes).

Make all four look unmistakably different.

Interaction:
- Drag the kitten to stretch it; drag the background to orbit; zoom.
- Grab the cape.
- A Lift toggle to carry the kitten.

UI:
- A minimal glassy UI: weather buttons (keys 1–4), jelly palettes Honey, Rose and Icy blue, Softness and Wind sliders, Pause (Space) and Reset (R).
- Responsive on phones; adaptive quality.
- NaN-safe WGSL: clamp every pow and smoothstep input and clamp the HDR result, so no black specks appear on real GPUs.

You are a senior real-time 3D artist and Three.js engineer. Build a detailed, realistic, interactive mid-engine supercar in the existing project using Three.js and WebGL.

title: Playable Flappy Bird clone in a portrait browser game
text:
Create a complete, polished, playable browser game inspired by the classic Flappy Bird. Use original artwork and sound effects while faithfully recreating the core gameplay, pacing, and retro visual feel.

TECHNOLOGY
Use HTML5 Canvas, CSS, and JavaScript.
Make the game work without a backend or external services.
Avoid unnecessary frameworks and dependencies.
Organize the code clearly and include instructions for running it locally.
Deliver a finished game with all required files, not just a mockup or code snippets.

CORE GAMEPLAY
The player controls a small bird that moves forward automatically through an endless series of pipe obstacles.
Keep the bird at a fixed horizontal position while the environment scrolls from right to left.
Apply constant gravity to the bird.
Each flap gives the bird an immediate upward velocity. Set the velocity rather than adding unlimited upward acceleration.
Allow flapping with Space, the Up Arrow, a mouse click, or a touchscreen tap.
Use consistent physics across different frame rates, preferably with a fixed simulation timestep.
Rotate the bird slightly upward when it flaps and gradually downward as it falls.
Add a simple looping wing animation.

OBSTACLES AND COLLISIONS
Generate pairs of green pipes with an opening between them.
Randomize the vertical position of each opening while keeping all openings reachable.
Keep a safe distance between pipe openings and the top and bottom boundaries.
Spawn pipes at regular intervals and remove them after they leave the screen.
Detect collisions with pipes, the ground, and the top boundary.
Use slightly forgiving collision boxes that match the visible bird reasonably well.
End the run immediately when a collision occurs.
Give the player one point after the bird fully passes a pipe pair.
Ensure each pipe pair awards a point only once.

GAME STATES
Implement clear transitions between these states:
Ready:Show the title, an animated hovering bird, and a short “Tap or press Space to start” instruction.
Keep the background scrolling.
The first input starts the game and triggers a flap.

Playing:Show the current score prominently at the top center.
Hide menus and instructions.
Keep controls immediate and responsive.

Game Over:Stop obstacle movement and disable flapping.
Play a brief collision effect and let the bird fall to the ground.
Display a result panel with the current score and best score.
Include a clearly visible restart button.
Add a short input cooldown so the collision-triggering input cannot accidentally restart the game.
Restart without reloading the page.

Paused:Pause when the browser tab becomes hidden.
On return, show a resume overlay and wait for explicit input.
Prevent large physics jumps after resuming.

VISUAL DESIGN

Use a cohesive retro pixel-art style with original assets.
Use a portrait-oriented play area with a logical resolution around 360 × 640.
Include a bright blue sky, subtle clouds, distant scenery, green pipes, and a scrolling ground strip

title: Interactive jelly-sea diorama with dinosaurs, volcano, fish, and underwater creatures
text:
Build "Dino Jelly", an interactive material study: one self-contained HTML file, native WebGPU + WGSL, no libraries, no external requests (no fonts, CDNs or images). It belongs to an editorial series called "MATERIAL STUDIES": quiet paper backdrop, serif italic headline, small uppercase sans labels, a glassy control panel.

The subject is a square slice of jelly-sea cut out like a dessert: a sandy volcanic island with ferns and cycads, and four procedurally animated gummy dinosaurs:
- a brontosaurus wading the shallows
- a pterodactyl that dives for fish
- a plesiosaur you watch through the cut faces
- a pack of five little raptors on the beach
You toss gummy fish for them, rumble the volcano, stir the sea and tip the whole block.

━━━ 1. DELIVERABLE & CONSTRAINTS ━━━
- One HTML file (~220 KB). CSS, JS and WGSL inline, plain JS, no build-time dependencies in the output.
- WebGPU only. If navigator.gpu, the adapter or the device is missing, or init throws, show the fallback overlay (§15). Handle device.lost the same way.
- Fixed-step simulation:
  · water at 1/120 s, bodies at 1/240 s, with an accumulator and a catch-up cap
  · animals once per frame with dt clamped to 0.05
  · render once per rAF
- Cap the backbuffer at ~2.4 MP.
- Expose window.__dj with: world, block, water, palms, bodies, dinos, volcano, cam, view, st, setPalette, reset, resetView, setPause, project, toss, rumble, pick(x, y), advance(seconds). advance steps 1/60 repeatedly. A test-only st.freeze flag stops the sim without changing input handling.
- Everything lives in block-local coordinates (y up, base at y=0), so the jelly wobble and the block tilt carry the animals too.

━━━ 2. WORLD & TERRAIN ━━━
- Block: side 5.2 (HALF = 2.6), rest water level WL0 = 1.3, wobble height 2.0.
- Water grid: GN = 168.
- terrainH(x, z), analytic and smooth:
  · Seabed: 0.86 − 0.32·smoothstep(−3.8, 4.2, x+z), plus gentle noise. It is deepest towards the +x/+z faces the camera looks through.
  · A broad shallow shelf: centre (−0.22, −0.26), radii 1.95 × 1.8, top at WL0 − 0.17 (tiny undulation). It blends into the seabed over normalised radius 0.8 → 1.0, giving a reef drop-off.
  · The island: centre ISLE = (−0.5, −0.55), radii 1.32 × 1.16. Top at WL0 + 0.13 − 0.05·r, blended in with 1 − smoothstep(0.66, 1.06, r). Gentle beaches.
  · The volcano at (−0.8, −0.9), foot radius 0.64, height 1.0. With vr = dist / 0.64:
      h += 1.0·(1 − vr)^1.6 · (1 + 0.07·sin(7θ + 0.6)·smoothstep(0.25, 0.9, vr))
         − 0.62·(1 − smoothstep(0.09, 0.24, vr))
    This gives gullies and a crater. The rim sits ~0.6 above the beach.
  · One sea stack at (1.7, −1.3): +0.2·exp(−d²/0.045).
  · Fine sand ripples underwater.
- Result:
  · ~10% dry sand
  · ~18% ankle-deep shelf
  · a deep L-shaped band 0.6–0.76 deep along the two visible faces, the plesiosaur's water
- Helpers:
  · terrainNormal (finite differences)
  · terrainGrid (water-cell centres)
  · isDry(x, z, level, margin)
  · slopeY(x, z)

text:

First check that AE, Python, ffmpeg and a heavy Japanese gothic + mincho font are available. If anything is missing, tell me how to install it (free Google Fonts like Dela Gothic One are fine).
</setup>

<rules>
- 144 BPM (1 beat = 10 frames at 24 fps). Every cut lands on a beat.
- One strong colour pair per screen: Gunjo (ultramarine) #1F4BFF / Konkon (deep navy) #0B1F4D & Yamabuki (golden yellow) #FFC627 / Kinari (ecru) #F3F1EC & 墨 #1C1A1A / Enji (crimson) #7A0E2E & 桃 #FFB3A8 / Fukamidori (deep green) #1F4F2A & Moegi (spring green) #C6E23A / 朱 #FF6A1F
- Motion comes in fast and holds briefly.
- No explanatory text in the video.
</rules>

<idea>
Treat kanji as architecture: things built from parts that can be taken apart and rebuilt.
Let one shot's last shape become the next shot's first shape, so the whole piece feels like one continuous thought.
Give it an arc: an opening, a build-up, a peak, one quiet moment, and an ending that loops back to the start.
</idea>

<ingredients>
Pick a few of these and decide the order yourself. You don't have to use them all, and you can add your own.
- Kanji built from plain bars, changing into other kanji
- Kanji large enough to touch the frame edges, cropped like a poster, but keep about two-thirds of each character on screen so it still reads
- Traditional Japanese patterns (Tatewaku, Seigaiha, Asanoha …)
- Calligraphy: stroke counts, stroke order
- Genkō yōshi (manuscript paper), vertical writing
- Split-flap departure boards, the twelve zodiac signs
</ingredients>

<sound>
Synthesise everything (no audio files) in the Japanese in scale: hyoshigi, taiko, bells, whooshes. Place sounds at the same frame numbers as the cuts. Leave one stretch where the beat drops out.
</sound>

<constraints>
- Patterns from shape-layer properties and repeaters, never drawn by hand. Animate on normal keyframes so I can retime things.
- Put all colours on one controller, and give me controls for the main movements.
- Use matchName, not display names (works in Japanese or English AE). Render with aerender's default template. Wrap scripts in try/catch.
- Shape layers start at comp centre; set anchor/position to [0,0] when plotting in comp coordinates. Text caps at ~1296 px, so scale up beyond that. Check every character exists in the chosen font.
