title: Dark neon glitch-art effect on a video with looping soundtrack
text:
Apply a dark neon glitch-art effect to the attached video (Python + ffmpeg, frame by frame):

1. Cut out the subject with rembg (isnet-anime for anime/illustration, isnet-general-use for real footage). Make the background pure black.
2. Posterize the subject to 5 brightness levels and recolor it with a 3-color palette on black:
   main color for cool/neutral areas (cyan #14b8f0), mid color (violet #6438c4), accent for warm/red areas (magenta #ff2ad4).
   Keep it dark: most of the image black or navy, only the highlights glow. Let the color-patch edges crawl slightly with noise.
3. Add a magenta rim light on the subject's left edge.
4. Datamosh: wherever the current frame is empty, keep the previous frame shifted a few px down and faded (melting ghost trails). Also copy ~3% of 24px blocks from the previous frame with a small random offset.
5. Vertical drips: in ~30% of the columns, smear bright pixels upward (up to ~300px) and downward (~150px). Mix 2–8px wide drips with thin vertical scratch lines in the palette colors, denser near the subject.
6. Light grain + vignette. Keep the original resolution and fps, export as H.264 MP4.

Generate an original vaporwave-glitch soundtrack (~-12 LUFS) / make it a seamless loop where the last 1s drips into the first 1s column by column.

title: Self-running isometric Plants vs. Zombies lawn battle in one HTML file
text:
Create one complete, self-contained HTML file for FRONT LAWN DEFENCE, a self-running three.js vignette of a Plants vs. Zombies battle on a back lawn, as a tiny isometric scene with no interaction.

THE LOOK, a tiny isometric "small plays" vignette:
- A three.js scene seen through an ORTHOGRAPHIC camera at a fixed isometric angle (about 30 degrees down, 45 degrees around). The camera never zooms or shakes.
- Render the scene at LOW RESOLUTION (about 360 pixels tall) into a render target with NearestFilter, then scale it up to the window by a whole-number factor with crisp nearest-neighbour pixels, so every pixel is a sharp square.
- The scene sits on one small, irregular, organic patch of a sunny back lawn with five neat striped rows of mown grass, a stone garden path along one side, a wooden fence along the far edge and a few flower beds, floating in the middle of a plain WHITE page (#ffffff) with plenty of white space around it (the patch spans about 60 percent of the frame width). Its edges dissolve into the white through an ORDERED DITHER (a 4x4 Bayer pattern): scattered single pixels break up the border, with no hard outline and no drop shadow.
- Carefully modelled low-poly shapes with soft, simple shading: one bright sunny directional light with real shadows plus a gentle ambient fill, so objects read clearly as small 3D forms.
- A clean palette of about 20 to 24 colours declared as constants: two bright lawn greens for the stripes, warm grey path stone, honey fence wood, peashooter green with a darker leaf collar, sunflower yellow petals and a brown face, wall-nut tan, cherry-bomb red, snow-pea icy blue, zombie grey-green skin with brown coats, red ties and blue trousers, an orange traffic cone, a grey metal bucket, a red lawnmower, glowing golden suns and pale grey-white smoke.
- BRIGHTNESS: keep the whole scene bright and readable, with a generous ambient fill and soft shadows.
- CHARACTERS: every character is a tiny but carefully SHAPED 3D figure (about 10 to 16 low-res pixels tall, bigger where the brief says so), built from spheres, capsules, cylinders and tapered shapes, never from plain boxes, and instantly RECOGNISABLE as the famous game character from its colour scheme, silhouette, proportions and signature props alone. Each moves with its own personality and timing, with readable poses. Never draw disembodied or close-up hands.
- SIGNATURE MOVES: every special move has its own distinct, readable effect (its own shape, colour and timing), so a viewer can tell the moves apart at a glance.
- DAMAGE STAYS: scorch marks, cracks, craters, dents, debris and broken pieces stay where they happened until the restart, so the scene tells the story of what has happened.
- NO GORE: never blood or gore. Characters that are beaten fall, tumble, fly off, or vanish in a puff of smoke or light.
- No text, letters, numbers, logos, emblems with lettering, HUD or UI anywhere, never a s

title: Interactive 3D swimming pool with flowers, ripples, rain, and whirlpool
text:
Build a single-file HTML + three.js interactive scene called "Bloom Pool": a sunlit swimming pool seen from a pitched perspective camera. You drop tropical flowers onto the water and play with them.

Pool and look:
- A rounded-rectangle pool with a shallow end on the left and a deep end on the right.
- Glassy mosaic tiles: a field, a border, and a band at the waterline. Each tile has a bevel and a soft glaze highlight.
- Stone coping with a bullnose lip overhanging the water, deck pavers around it, and splash-darkened stone near the edge.
- A dappled shadow from a palm crown leaning over one corner.
- Size the pool and fit the camera to any screen, portrait or landscape.

Water:
- A real-time ripple heightfield updated at about 90 Hz.
- Refraction of the tiled floor through the surface.
- Animated Voronoi caustics on the floor.
- Fresnel reflection of the sky and sun, and of the pool's own edge (the tiled wall band and the coping).
- Crests and troughs, foam from splashes, a coping shadow and a meniscus along the walls.
- Gentle circulation from the return jets.

Flowers (five species, modeled procedurally from petal profiles):

- Pink lotus: cupped petals around a seed pod and a ring of stamens.
- Spotted tiger lily: six recurved tepals, long stamens.
- Ruffled hibiscus: dark eye, long staminal column.
- Waxy plumeria: a five-petal pinwheel.

Each flower is a small physics body:
- Drop it from a card at the bottom, or drag it over the water. It falls with turbulence and lands with a splash, droplets and rings.
- It floats and bobs, radiating ripples. It glides with a wake, and floating flowers collide with each other.
- A breeze turns them. They spin into a whirlpool.

title: Home network control demo with Claude Code
text:

If you can't run commands on this computer (you're not Claude Code or a similar agent), say so in one line, tell me to paste this into Claude Code on a computer on my home Wi-Fi, and stop.

If a VPN is on, ask me to pause it. Ask me whether I also have a guest or IoT network. For each device, tell me what it is, with brand and model where you can, and how sure you are. If only a chip maker shows (Espressif, Tuya and the like), ask me what that device is.
Then list what you found and ask me which devices I also have that aren't on the network (an IR-only AC, a fridge, a microwave and the like); for those, offer the next best option (an IR blaster, a Wi-Fi sensor).
Then ask me which ones to make mine, and for each one I pick, make it mine: control from this chat, and fix what bugs me. If I say "just diagnose", change nothing.

Rules for every device
- Only my own devices on my own network. If this computer isn't on my home network (a cloud session, a virtual machine, or WSL without mirrored networking), say so and stop. To find them: reach every address in my own subnet once (one ping each; ask me first if the subnet has more than 256 addresses), then read the ARP table (a device that ignores ping still shows up there); then mDNS (Bonjour) and SSDP (UPnP); then the router's client list if I've given you its login. If a VPN is on, ask me to pause it: it can hide my home network. Ask me whether I also have a guest or IoT network. Never scan or touch any other network.
- On macOS, if pings or connections to my devices fail with "No route to host", tell me to allow this app under System Settings > Privacy & Security > Local Network, then retry.
- One device at a time, in the order listed (or the order I pick), with the router's Wi-Fi changes last. Finish it, or tell me it's stuck, before the next.
- Back up first: save each device's current settings in its own folder under "rea-home-devices" in my home folder before any change. Keep that folder private: it can hold passwords and tokens, never share or upload it. Keep README.md and CLAUDE.md there listing every tool you made and how to run it, so a new chat started in that folder can use them.
- Before each change, show the old and new value and wait for my yes. Read the value back after. Keep a way to undo every change.

title: Interactive offshore jelly diorama with platform, turbines, boats, and storm events
text:
Build "Offshore Jelly" — a single-file interactive WebGPU diorama in the "Material Studies" series: a stretch of North Sea cut out as a cube of translucent jelly, sitting on a studio floor. Everything is procedural (no external assets, no network), one HTML file with inline JS/WGSL.

THE BLOCK
- A wobbly jelly cube you can grab by its sides and tip; it springs back. Sliders: firmness, damping, wind (0–20 m/s).
- Inside: a shallow-water simulation for the sea surface (waves, wakes, foam, whitecaps), seabed with sand ripples, scour rocks, kelp, boulders, starfish, crabs, urchins, a pipeline, cables and a small wreck. Caustics on the seabed. Dragging the water stirs up waves.
- Waves come from the wind: several wave trains whose height grows with wind speed.

THE SCENE
- A production platform on a four-legged steel jacket (braces, risers, conductors, boat landing, marine growth below the waterline): main and cellar decks, process module, derrick, living quarters, lifeboats, a pedestal crane with a laydown area, a flare boom with a flickering flame and smoke.
- An octagonal helideck with an H, a net, perimeter lights and a windsock.
- Five offshore wind turbines on monopiles: transition piece with yellow platform, boat landing ladder, davit, tower, nacelle, three-blade rotors with red tips, blinking red aviation lights. Rotor speed and power output (MW) follow the wind.
- A rocky skerry with a lighthouse whose beam turns; seals haul out on it.

WHAT HAPPENS
- Supply run: a platform supply vessel comes in from standby, holds station next to the jacket on dynamic positioning (thruster foam), and the crane does four lifts — containers swing on the hook, are set down on the platform and back-loaded onto the boat's deck. Then she sails back to standby.
- Helicopter: flies in from the west, turns into the wind, lands on the helideck; a deck officer walks out; passengers get off. A second press sends it away (spin-up, lift, outbound). Rotor and tail rotor spin, downwash flattens the water.
- Crew boat: a small catamaran sails out to a turbine, pushes its bow onto the boat landing, and technicians climb the ladder onto the platform. Next time she picks them up and brings them home.
- Storm: the wind builds to a gale, waves get big with whitecaps and spray, rain falls, the room darkens, lightning strikes blades, the lighthouse, the derrick or the sea with a flash and thunder. Above cut-out the turbines feather their blades and stop (0 MW); the helicopter is grounded. Then it eases and the turbines restart.

LIFE
- Schools of fish around the jacket and wrecks, gulls that perch on railings and take off on the horn, gannets that plunge-dive for fish, a pod of porpoises, seals, moon jellyfish, crew walking the decks.

CONTROLS & UI
- Buttons: Supply run, Helicopter (take-off when landed), Crew boat, Storm. Space = ship's horn. Tapping a turbine switches it on/off, tapping the supply boat or helideck calls them. Orbit by drag, zoom by wheel/pinch.
- Tallie

title: Pixel-art 3D backyard four-square game with ball physics
text:
Build a single-file HTML + three.js (r160) scene called "Chalk Square": four square played with a football in a back yard on a floating island. It is a real 3D scene rendered as crisp pixel art.

Rendering: an orthographic isometric camera (drag to turn in 90° steps, scroll or pinch to zoom). Render into a small low-res target with a depth texture, then upscale with texelFetch to whole screen pixels. Add depth-based outlines and quantize every pixel to a fixed ~60-colour palette in OKLab, with an optional Bayer dither. Toggle "Pixel art / Raw 3D", with a pixel-size slider and Palette / Dither / Outlines checkboxes.

Yard: patched, cracked asphalt with a kerb, grass and dirt around the island edge. Around the asphalt:
- a row of lock-up garages with painted, numbered doors and a flat roof that overhangs them;
- a brick transformer booth with a warning sign;
- a poplar with a bench and a grandmother on it;
- a chin-up bar, a carpet rack with a rug, bushes;
- a lamp on a pole and a lamp over a garage door.
Pigeons walk and peck, and flap up onto the roofs when the ball or a kid comes near. A cat on the garage roof follows the ball with its head.

Chalk: a data texture over the asphalt. It holds the 4.8 m square split into four zones (King, Queen, Jack, Dunce) with letters and a crown, plus hopscotch and doodles. Each texel stores its order along its stroke, so the lines can be redrawn progressively.

Game (8 kids, each with a skill, power and style: power / trick / safe / lob):
- Four kids play, four wait in a queue. The King serves by dropping the ball and kicking it after the bounce.
- The ball must bounce once in your zone, then you kick it into another zone. With the two-touch rule you may first cushion it up.
- You are out for: a ball that lands out, lands in your own zone, bounces a second time, or (if set) lands on a middle line. Otherwise a ball on the line is replayed.
- The kid who is out goes to the back of the queue. Everyone below moves up a zone, and the next kid in line enters at Dunce. A kid fetches the ball and throws it to the King.

Ball and AI: real ball physics (gravity, bounces, rolling, softer bounces in puddles, the walls). Each receiver simulates the ball forward, picks the moment it is at foot height, runs to stand behind it and kicks. Shots are a drive, a lob, or a dink just over the line, aimed away from the target kid; everyone picks on the King. Aim and power errors grow with a fast ball, a stretched contact and lower skill, and occasionally a kick is shanked.

Kids: box-rigged with two-bone IK. Poses: run, ready crouch, a kick that strikes at the ball's height, cushion, hold, throw, clap, argue a call, and a crouched walk while drawing chalk.

Time and weather: Day / Dusk / Night (the lamps light the court), Dry / Rain.
- Rain: streaks, splashes, darker asphalt, puddles that mirror the yard via a mirrored render pass, and the chalk washing out.

title: Interactive home-device diagnosis site on a TV
text:
Everything below is about my own devices on my own home network. I just don't know their brands or models.

If you can't run commands on this machine (you aren't Claude Code or a similar agent), tell me that in one line, ask me to paste this into Claude Code on a computer connected to my home Wi-Fi, and stop there.

Start by finding what's on my network: ping every address in my own subnet one time (check with me first if the subnet is bigger than 256 addresses), then look at the ARP table, then mDNS (Bonjour) and SSDP (UPnP), and last the router's client list if I've shared its login with you. If a VPN is running, ask me to pause it. Ask whether I also have a guest or IoT network. For every device, tell me what it is, the brand and model when you can tell, and how confident you are. If all you can see is a chip vendor (Espressif, Tuya and similar), ask me what that device is.

Next, show me the list and ask which of my devices aren't on the network at all (an AC that only takes IR, a fridge, a microwave and so on). For those, suggest the closest alternative (an IR blaster, a Wi-Fi sensor).

Then ask which devices to bring under my control, and for each one I pick, do it: I run it from this chat, and you fix whatever annoys me about it. If I say "just diagnose", don't change anything.

Rules that apply to every device
My devices on my network only. If this machine isn't on my home network (a cloud session, a virtual machine, or WSL without mirrored networking), tell me and stop. Discovery order: ping every address in my own subnet one time (check with me first if it's bigger than 256 addresses), then the ARP table (devices that ignore ping still appear there), then mDNS (Bonjour) and SSDP (UPnP), then the router's client list if I've shared its login. If a VPN is running, ask me to pause it, since it can hide my home network. Ask whether I have a guest or IoT network too. Never scan or touch any network that isn't mine.
On macOS, if pings or connections to my devices fail with "No route to host", ask me to allow this app in System Settings > Privacy & Security > Local Network, then try again.
Work on one device at a time, in the order of the list (or the order I choose), and leave the router's Wi-Fi changes for the very end. Either finish a device or tell me it's stuck before moving on to the next.
Backups come first: before changing anything, save each device's current settings in a folder of its own inside "rea-home-devices" in my home folder. That folder stays private because it may hold passwords and tokens: never share or upload it. Keep a README.md and a CLAUDE.md in it listing every tool you built and how to run it, so a fresh chat opened in that folder can pick them up.
Before any change, show me the current value and the new one and wait until I say yes. Read the value back afterwards. Always keep a way to undo each change.

title: Beat-synced manga-style edit of Makima footage
text:
Turn the attached footage into a beat-synced, manga-style music edit and send me the finished MP4.

INPUTS (fill in or leave blank; if blank, choose sensibly and tell me what you chose)
- Source footage: [attached]
- Music: [attached track / use the source audio]
- Aspect ratio: [default 4:3 1440x1080; 9:16 1080x1920 for vertical], 24 fps
- On-screen text / credit: [optional]
- Palette: [default: paper #f8f2ea, ink #141012, main accent red #d0141e (shadow #7c0a12), highlight yellow #ffd60a (shadow #f29a00)]

GOAL
The edit should feel like a living manga page: ink lines, screentone, flat accent colours, bold graphic backgrounds, and hard cuts locked to the music. It must look designed, not like a filter over video.

1. STUDY THE MATERIAL
- Go through the footage frame by frame using contact sheets. Catalogue every usable moment: framing, pose, motion peaks, internal cuts, and strong details (eyes, hands, silhouettes, close-ups, crash zooms).
- Analyse the music: BPM, beat grid, downbeats, phrases, sections, energy curve, accents, fills, ending.

2. LOCK THE LOOK (applies to every shot)
- Mask the subject on every frame (rembg isnet-anime for anime or illustration, a human-segmentation model for live action). Check mask quality before relying on it.
- Ink lines via XDoG/DoG, with thickness scaled to the framing.
- Paper base. Mid-tones become halftone dots: fixed screen angle, area-correct radius. The deepest shadows become solid ink.
- Strict palette: paper + ink + one main accent + one highlight.
  - Map the subject's most distinctive colour to the flat main accent.
  - Map glowing or brightest elements to the highlight.
  - Everything else stays monochrome.
- Tune tones per shot so faces read clean (mostly paper, light screentone).
- Give subject cut-outs a thin ink outline when composited over graphics.

3. DESIGN YOUR OWN SHOT VOCABULARY
Based on what this footage does well and what this music needs, define 6-10 recurring shot types. Each type pairs a kind of source framing with a graphic treatment. Draw from this palette or invent your own:
- extreme close-up of a detail with impact shake
- silhouette over a bold graphic (concentric rings, rays, burst)
- clean black-and-white manga panel with a lightened background
- subject cut-out over a graphic ground (halftone texture, printed-page texture, blobs, speed lines, flat colour)
- typographic panel (large vertical CJK or bold type, plus small secondary lines; all text original)
- impact marks (!!, stars, sparkles)
- black or flash frames
- glitch frames (channel split, slice offset, magenta/yellow)
- tinted frames (pink, red, mono)
- halftone-dissolve transitions
- punch-ins and crash zooms
Rules:
- Every type must use something the footage genuinely does well.
- Save the strongest images for the strongest musical moments.
- Briefly justify each type.

4. PLAN A FRAME-ACCURATE EDL BEFORE RENDERING
List start/end frame, shot type, source fra
